Why £1m-a-season deal will be hard for Pollock and Hearn to find

BBC News Tue, 04 Aug 2026 16:29:15 GMT

Pollock holds the record as the youngest English try-scorer in Six Nations history

Salary cap regulations might not be high on everyone's holiday reading list, but agent Eddie Hearn might be interested if he's keen to get Henry Pollock's £1m pay-day.

The Prem salary cap is currently £6.4m per club. In basic terms, your whole squad's salaries have to add up to £6.4m or less.

There's an outside chance the Northampton back row could get a salary of £1m next season, if a club out there has that amount of space in the cap.

The only team thought to be in this bracket, according to the last published salary cap report in 2024-25, would be Newcastle.

However, we don't have Newcastle's latest data since the Red Bull takeover and the signing spree on the likes of Raffi Quirke and Hoskins Sotutu.

Clubs in the 2026-27 season also have to spend at least £5.4m, dubbed the new salary cap floor - this leaves less wriggle room if you wanted to bring in one player on big money.

As he negotiates for a new contract, if the 21-year-old England forward wants to stay at Northampton, it looks like they don't have the cap space for a £1m deal.

They could make space by significantly reducing the salaries of Pollock's team-mates who renegotiate this year, although that might not be very popular or sensible business.

So, this is where we enter the world of 'excluded players', or marquee players if you're old school, whose salaries are exempt from the £6.4m cap.

Pollock to demand £1m a year at Northampton - Hearn

This video can not be played

Could Pollock really be paid £1m a season? It's complicated...

Before we get too deep, it's worth knowing that a current Prem player moving to a different Prem club is not the same as a player coming in from outside the league.

Basically, don't think that Pollock can be compared to Scotland's Finn Russell at Bath, as there are different rules.

Time to grab a pen and paper. In the Prem salary cap regulations section 3.26 on excluded players, the first problem Pollock has is that to become the excluded player he must have "been a player of that club for at least two full salary cap years prior to the salary cap year in which they are nominated to be an excluded player".

This means Pollock can't just become Northampton's excluded player next season, they have to declare him to be that player in the future. But why, I hear you cry.

It's to stop clubs poaching players off each other and back-loading player contracts.

We learnt about this during the Covid pandemic, when clubs agreed bigger pay-days with their players in advance of the new lower salary cap regs being introduced, so that their salary didn't count in the reduced cap.

It also prevents sides from manipulating the cap. For example, you can't pay player X £5m in year one of an excluded deal, then just £100 in year's two and three, rinse and repeat with a new big name every year. Not allowed.

The way the cap stops clubs doing this is a process of "averaging".

Allow Instagram content?

This article contains content provided by Instagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. You may want to read Meta’s Instagram cookie policy, external and privacy policy, external before accepting. To view this content choose ‘accept and continue’.

If you want to read regulation 3.28.2, it's long, wordy and not very sexy.

The summary is that over three years the average pay of the excluded player is key to what ends up in and outside the cap.

If a player earns £100,000, £150,000 then £200,000 across three years, the average is £150,000.

Then as the excluded player, if you then want to pay them £1m, the extra £850,000 would actually be included in the cap as it is above the average.

These rules mean it's actually quite hard for players to move around the league and command the excluded player spots.

To conclude the excluded player regs, it's also worth knowing that we're not allowed to know the identity of any excluded players.

You can guess, assume, even ask them, but technically "a club is not entitled to know the identity of the excluded players of other clubs".

This means that if Northampton already have a player nominated for the excluded player spot they would probably have to unpick a huge amount of spreadsheet calculations to move it over to Pollock.

To those outside the sport much of this will seem like madness and an unfair market. However, the salary cap is basically designed to stop clubs making poor financial decisions or over-stretch themselves. The demise of Wasps, Worcester and London Irish being the forefront of this.

Prem Rugby told BBC Sport: "The salary cap is designed to prevent clubs from over-spending. It helps control inflationary pressures from club costs and ensures the viability and competitiveness of clubs.

"This year the Prem is forecast to post record revenues of more than £200m for the first time, with that number forecast to grow again year-on-year."

With six different Prem winners in seven seasons, you can't argue that the league isn't competitive.

Clubs like Saracens have long championed salary cap increases and now that the league's stability has been assured following the removal of promotion and relegation, this is likely the next chapter in the salary cap debate.

Prem Rugby said: "Any change to the wider cap structure would always go through a full club consultation and be up for discussion amongst the men's professional Rugby Board before any decision is made.

"The removal of promotion and relegation is a separate strategic decision aimed at giving clubs long-term investment certainty, as is evident with the new ownership of Red Bull at Newcastle and Black Knight Rugby at Exeter Chiefs - as well as the new investment from Sir James Dyson at Bath."

Some players can command big commercial deals outside rugby, and these deals will eclipse their club earnings multiple times over.

The big examples away from Pollock right now are the USA's Ilona Maher, South Africa's Siya Kolisi and England's Ellie Kildunne.

A Pollock £1m pay-day in club rugby is possible, but highly unlikely at Northampton, for now.

BBC News Tue, 04 Aug 2026 16:02:37 GMT

Fires are believed to have been deliberately started on a mountain where crews have been tackling a blaze since the weekend.

The fire at Llanwonno, near Ferndale in the Rhondda Valley, began on Saturday afternoon with emergency services remaining at the scene.

It remains a major incident due to the scale of the fire and "challenging conditions" on the mountain, including low cloud, mist and rain.

South Wales Fire and Rescue Service (SWFRS) said there were reports of "deliberate fire setting" on the mountain overnight on Monday, while firefighters continued working to contain the blaze.

Locals have not been forced to evacuate, but a rest centre has been set up for people who do not wish to stay at home because of poor air quality.

A spokesperson for SWFRS said it continued to work with partner agencies to contain and extinguish the wildfire on Llanwonno mountain and prevent further spread, helping to protect nearby properties and communities.

"There were reports of deliberate fire setting on the mountain [on Monday night]," they said.

"Firefighters worked throughout the night in challenging conditions to tackle the fire and protect properties."

Resident Caryl Holmes said most of her family live around the area, with her daughter's house "practically on the mountain".

"I've been checking in on everybody making sure the fire wasn't near their homes, but it was near my daughter's," she said.

"It was so close and very frightening to be honest. She wasn't allowed to come home 'til it was put out."

She said the fire was particularly bad on Monday night when "the smoke was so thick I couldn't breathe" and added that the firefighters had been "amazing".

Ian Putland said even with the windows closed he could smell the fire.

"I heard about it a couple of days ago, and didn't think it would affect me... but then I came out yesterday and saw ash on the car and it indicated how close the fire was," he said.

"I was then alarmed with all the fire people about."

He added that he was "frustrated that the fires had been started deliberately".

"There's the wildlife killed, people are being put in danger and it takes emergency services away. It is a real waste of resources."

Christian Hadfield, area manager at SWFRS, said crews had been at the incident since Saturday but declared it a major incident on Monday in order to protect homes in the area.

"We are putting fire breaks in and monitoring the area," he said.

He added there were reports of "pockets of deliberate fire setting" which put the crews "under really critical conditions and stretches the service".

The fire was "unpredictable and complex work", he said, and firefighters could be there "for many days to come".

Hadfield said a specialist firefighting helicopter had been secured to help crews fight the blaze but could not be deployed due to the poor weather conditions.

SWFRS said road closures remained in place and members of the public were asked to avoid the affected area.

Anyone with any information is being asked to contact South Wales Police.

Justice secretary apologises to families affected by early release scheme

BBC News Tue, 04 Aug 2026 15:58:13 GMT

Justice Secretary Alex Norris has apologised to families affected by the early release scheme, saying they were "carrying the can from previous failures".

Families, including a man whose pregnant partner died after being hit by a speeding driver, criticised the prisoner early release scheme, saying it comes "at the expense of victims".

Andy Burnham announced that prisoners convicted of rape, grooming, and serious child sex offences will be excluded from the scheme in England and Wales. The prime minister said he wanted to exclude more, but prison overcrowding prevented this.

Calvin Buckley said he was "shocked and disappointed" the killer of his partner and unborn child could be released early.

The mother of PC Andrew Harper also said she was "devastated" to learn two men jailed after her son was killed will still be eligible.

The prime minister said making more prisoners exempt was not possible without the prison system collapsing and putting the public "at much greater risk".

Justice Secretary Alex Norris also warned a prison capacity crisis would be likely if fewer prisoners were allowed early release.

Norris later said he spoke to the families as "it is really important to express that this shouldn't be where it is".

He also said he was confident the prisons would have adequate room now that about 1,000 extra prisoners will not be released early.

"We have modelled it very carefully," he said.

PC Harper, 28, was killed in 2019 when he was dragged by a car down a country road as three teenagers fled the scene of a quad bike theft in Berkshire.

His family previously said they had received a letter from the Ministry of Justice confirming that two of the offenders could be included in the early release scheme.

While the driver of the vehicle, Henry Long, received a 16-year sentence and would not be eligible, Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers, who were passengers in the car and sentenced to 13 years for manslaughter could apply for early release after serving half of their sentences.

The Sentencing Act was amended in January, with the eligibility for early release based on the length of fixed sentence, rather than the type of offence.

The act already excluded some of the most serious and dangerous offenders, such as murderers serving life sentences or those on extended sentences.

But last month the prime minister promised to "review the policy" and paused the scheme after a backlash from survivors.

Announcing the changes on Monday, he said: "I fully understand the anger, anxiety and distress that's been caused. I've heard that loud and clear."

But PC Harper's mother Debbie Adlam, told BBC Newsnight: "It feels like we're letting Andrew down again" to hear his killers might still be eligible for release.

"We've been through the justice system, we thought we'd done as best as we could.

"Now we're standing up to fight again... so I just feel really let down, for Andrew's sake as well as ours."

She added that Norris had called her to explain the situation and apologise.

Later, on BBC Breakfast, Adlam called for more support from the probation service, stressing: "I need to know at the very, very least if they are going to be released that we're kept in mind of what's happening and we are informed".

Other families have also criticised the early release scheme.

Calvin Buckley's partner Frankie Jules-Hough and unborn child died in May 2023.

"Our justice is being taken away, I understand there's a crisis, I agree that it needs to be addressed, but not at the expense of victims," he told BBC Breakfast.

Claire Corkery, whose parents, Sue and Tom, were killed by a speeding driver in January 2024, said "it's almost like a tiered system, treating what has happened to us as less serious".

The justice secretary said 5,000 extra releases will take place in 10 batches from October.

But the Prison Governors' Association (PGA) said it was "unclear" how many prisoners will have their sentences recalculated.

"We don't know if it is tens, hundreds or thousands," it said, adding that there will now be "huge pressure on prison and probation staff to get the work of identifying prisoners now excluded and recalculating their sentences done".

The justice secretary told the Today programme approximately 1,000 prisoners will now not be released early following the revision to the scheme.

"If we drew it any wider we would have a prison capacity crisis," Norris explained.

Prisoners released on licence, Norris stressed, will be subject to "very significant controls on their lives," adding victims will be consulted about these.

Lissie Harper, PC Harper's widow, said it was "disgusting" that his killers could be eligible for early release.

She said she was "beyond appalled and bristling with anger to hear that Andrew's killers are soon to be free to roam the streets".

And Thames Valley Police Chief Constable Jason Hogg said the decision not to exclude them was "demoralising for all police officers".

Under the revised plans, rape and child sexual offences will now also be excluded from early release.

This move does not require changes to the existing legislation before October, the government said, but it may make amendments in the future to exclude certain offenders from being released.

Offenders of other crimes serving longer sentences of four years or more will be eligible for release halfway through their sentences rather than two-thirds as had previously been the case.

Those serving less serious sentences could be freed after a third of their time, rather than half.

The changes are due to be phased in, beginning with prisoners serving sentences of fewer than 575 days, going up to inmates jailed for 12 years or more being eligible for early release in June 2027.

The number of individuals released each time will depend on the prison population, which the government says will evolve between now and implementation.

Separately, those who serve the full sentence and are convicted of rape or serious child sex offences will face stronger surveillance after leaving prison, the government said.

The government also announced an extra £10m will go to front-line victim support services, including a new national helpline.

Burnham, who became PM on 20 July, made the announcement a day before going on holiday overseas.

He is taking a break from day-to-day duties, but staying in contact with officials, the BBC understands.

After the exemptions were announced, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch wrote on social media: "Yet again victims are learning their fate from press releases" and warned "killers, violent offenders, men who have terrorised their partners and more" will still leave prison early.

Meanwhile, a prison officer told the BBC that "delaying the releases until October could mean we simply run out of space".

The Victims' Commissioner for England and Wales, Claire Waxman, accepted the exemptions will feel "like a real injustice" for PC Andrew Harper's family.

She called on the prime minister to show "proper leadership," adding "we seem to keep going from crisis to crisis and it's always victims and bereaved families that pay the price".

Chief executive of the Prison Reform Trust Pia Sinha told the Today programme there were "no happy solutions", adding, "in 2029 we will have a mismatch between supply and demand.

"If we keep adding exceptions and exemptions to that, we will diminish the number of people that can be released and we will be back within months to another capacity crisis."

Domestic Abuse Commissioner Dame Nicole Jacobs criticised the decision to not exclude domestic abuse perpetrators.

"It is critical that no abuser is released in October unless I am confident that victims' safety is not being compromised," she said.

Mass funeral in Gaza for 112 Palestinians killed in 2023 Israeli strike

BBC News Tue, 04 Aug 2026 15:07:52 GMT

Large crowds turned out in Gaza City for a mass funeral for 112 people, mostly women and children, who were killed in an Israeli strike on a residential block in late 2023, early in the Gaza war.

The bodies - belonging to members of two extended families - have only recently been recovered from under the rubble in a two-week-long operation.

Dramatic footage showed the remains lined up in rows, each victim covered with a Palestinian flag and some with a photo of the dead, before relatives carried them away.

The funeral is said to be the biggest of its kind to have taken place in Gaza.

"I think this is a feeling that was supposed [to be felt], a feeling of pain, grief and loss," said one mourner, Ali Abu Sharia. "After we managed to retrieve them and bury them, perhaps we can be partially relieved despite the pain of loss and all we're still living through."

Forty-four children, 38 women and seven people with disabilities were listed among the dead from the Abu Sharia and Hassayna families, who are one clan.

They were killed when a residential block in the Sabra neighbourhood of Gaza City was attacked by Israel on 22 November 2023.

It was a day of heavy bombardment, six weeks after the 7 October Hamas-led assault on southern Israel, which led to 1,200 people being killed and 251 being taken hostage.

The BBC has asked the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) for information on what was targeted but has not yet received a response.

Since the start of the war, at least 73,377 people have been killed in Gaza, according to the Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.

In Gaza, the recovery work was carried out by the Civil Defence, which operates under the Hamas-run interior ministry. Its efforts have been supported by the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC).

"We provide material support - literally the gloves, shovels, protective equipment and body bags they use," said Patrick Griffiths, spokesperson for the ICRC.

"We provide training, supporting them to do their work safely, in line with professional practice ensuring the deceased are treated with dignity. And we've supported them by renting - for hundreds of hours - two of the only excavators available for this work in Gaza."

"It's not an answer any family wants to receive - confirmation that your loved one has been killed," Griffiths added. "But it's essential towards them receiving closure and being able to mourn their loss in their own way."

Last month, the BBC filmed the start of the operation to uncover bodies in Sabra. A single bulldozer picked through the rubble and then more delicate work was done by hand.

"This multi-storey building has been levelled. There were maybe more than 180 civilians inside. Most of them, around 90%, were killed," Civil Defence spokesman Mahmoud Basal said at the time.

"On that day [of the strikes], the Civil Defence crews couldn't get to the site because it needed co-ordination [with Israel via a third party such as the ICRC] and there was great danger in reaching the area."

Relatives of the dead were at the scene to guide the recovery crews during the recovery work. They said they had retrieved as many bodies as they could immediately after the attack and were relieved to be able to give others a proper burial.

"It's a devastating and sad feeling that resonates with everyone who was here," said Nahed al-Hassayna, as he showed the BBC the rubble of his family's living room.

"The kids – what did they do?" he asked, holding up the possessions of two of his young relatives. "This was a school backpack for Omar, and this was Ibrahim's shoe. Why? Why were they killed?"

"I'm the sole survivor of my family," said Yousef Abu Sharia, standing nearby. "Today, I'm talking to you [as] the one who lost my mother, my father, my uncle and my cousins and all my family. I lost them under this rubble."

It is believed that dozens more bodies are yet to be recovered at the site.

Across the Gaza Strip, thousands more people are unaccounted for. The remains of many are thought to be under the rubble left by intense Israeli air strikes during the war.

What's behind having to release some prisoners early?

BBC News Tue, 04 Aug 2026 15:04:59 GMT

The government has changed its plan to release thousands of offenders in England and Wales well before the end of their sentences in an attempt to make space in prisons.

People sentenced for rape, serious child sex and grooming offences will now not be eligible for early release from October.

But some prisoners who are not excluded could be freed after serving a third of their total custodial sentence rather than after 40% or 50% of their term.

This is not the first time a government - Conservative or Labour - has had to release prisoners early to make space in England and Wales' overcrowded prisons.

BBC Verify has looked at the reasons why ministers feel the need to resort to these measures.

The prison population in England and Wales on 3 August was 86,495, which was 97% of useable capacity.

The Ministry of Justice (MoJ) has warned the prison population will overtake capacity as soon as this November.

In the long-term the MoJ has projected that the capacity of all prisons will rise to around 99,000 by 2032 as a result of more prisons being built by this government.

But it also projected that the prisoner population would rise to about 104,000 by 2032 if the Sentencing Act 2026 - which provides for earlier release - did not come into force.

That is why new Justice Secretary Alex Norris says there is a "prison capacity crisis" which means the government has to implement the latest early release scheme.

Norris has said that 5,000 prisoners are now due to be released from October - down from 6,000 due to the new exclusions.

The MoJ has projected that the Sentencing Act will mean the prisoner population remains below the capacity of the prison system, rising only to around 96,000 by 2032.

The England and Wales prison population has risen significantly in recent decades with a significant uptick starting in the 1990s before reaching a record high in 2024.

The Institute for Government (IFG) think tank says this is partly the result of longer sentences.

In 2023, the average prison sentence at Crown Courts in England and Wales - which deal with more serious offences - was more than 25% longer than those handed down in 2012.

For some crimes, the increase was greater. Sentences for robbery in 2023 were 13 months longer on average than in 2012 - an increase of 36%.

Longer sentences mean more people being held in prison at any one time.

Former Conservative Justice Secretary David Gauke, who led an independent sentencing review for Sir Keir Starmer's government, argues this is the result of a "bidding war" by political parties since the 1990s over who can imprison people for longer.

Gauke also points out that the prison population has been rising at a time when overall crime in England and Wales has been falling, according to the official Crime Survey.

So despite the fall in crime more people are being sent to prison - and for longer.

Another reason for upward pressure on the prison population is that more people than before are being returned to prison for breaching the conditions of their release.

There were 51,419 licence recalls in England and Wales in the year ending March 2026, up from 40,259 in the previous year - a 28% increase.

Cassia Rowland from the IFG said most recalls are for breaches of licence conditions, such as missed appointments, rather than offenders committing further offences or posing a serious risk to the public.

"The probation service is overwhelmed, with high caseloads and lots of vacancies putting often inexperienced staff under huge pressure," she said.

Successive governments have pledged to increase the number of prison places - but delivery has often fallen short of those promises.

Between 2010 and 2024, when the Conservatives were in power, around 13,000 new prison places were created.

But around 12,500 places - notably those built during the Victorian era - were closed after falling into disrepair.

That means an estimated net total of only around 500 new prison places were added over 14 years.

In a 2024 report, the National Audit Office (NAO) cited the MOJ's "unrealistic timelines", and government bodies not working together to prioritise delivery, as reasons for the slow pace of prison building.

Although three new prisons have opened in the past four years - adding approximately 5,000 more places - further expansion to existing prisons has been delayed by a major supplier going into administration, according to the Prison Reform Trust.

Pia Sinha of the Prison Reform Trust told BBC Verify: "Successive governments have found it difficult to increase prison capacity because new prisons take years to plan and build, often facing planning hurdles and local opposition."

The Labour government has pledged to build 14,000 new prison places by 2031. The MoJ told BBC Verify that it had delivered about 3,200 places as of July.

However, it has not said how many prison cells have been taken out of use so we cannot say whether there has been a net gain or loss of spaces.

Analysts argue that without a major change in thinking about the appropriateness of prison as punishment, or a significant long-term increase in prison building, the system in England and Wales will remain close to capacity.

And that means governments will continue to be under pressure to implement early release schemes to avert a capacity crisis.

Which area has the best grades? Key takeaways from Scotland's exam results

BBC News Tue, 04 Aug 2026 13:52:54 GMT

The results are in. More than 130,000 Scottish students have found out how they did in their exams.

From the gender split to council-level trends, BBC Scotland has been digging into the numbers behind the results.

Here are five things we have learned from the 2026 Scottish exam results.

The number of pupils achieving an A, B or C grade at National 5, Higher and Advanced Higher has increased slightly on last year.

The figure for the National 5 qualifications, taken by the majority of pupils at 15 or 16, rose from a 78.4% pass rate in 2025 to 79.2% this year.

The rate for Higher increased from 75.9% to 76.7%, and the rate for Advanced Higher rose from 76.7% to 77.6%.

The gap between the level of results achieved by students in the least deprived parts of Scotland and those in the most deprived closed a little in this year's figures - but still remains significant.

The "attainment gap" is a measure of the difference between the grades of the top 20% better-off students and those who live in the bottom fifth of the Scottish Index of Multiple Deprivation (SIMD).

The way SIMD is used has been changed this year which resulted in some revision of previous figures.

The latest stats show that at National 5, the gap is 15.6 percentage points, down from 16.4.

That's because 86.6% of better-off students got an A to C grades this year as opposed to 71% of those in the most deprived areas.

At Higher, the gap is 15.9 percentage points, down from 16.8 last year.

And at Advanced Higher it is 12.1, down from 13.3.

This year's stats also show that female students have achieved higher pass rates at all levels than their male counterparts.

At National 5, the pass rate for girls was 80.9% as opposed to 77.5% for boys.

At Higher, it was 79% for female students and 74% for male.

However, both these figures represented a small closing of the gender gap.

At Advanced Higher, the gap between female (80.3%) pass rates and those of males (73.9%) widened.

Council-level data also shows a geographical split in attainment levels.

The figures show East Renfrewshire Council had the highest proportion of A to C passes at National 5, at 90.6%.

Other council areas above 80% were: East Dunbartonshire (86.2%), South Ayrshire (83.5%), Stirling (82.6%), Aberdeenshire (80.8%), South Lanarkshire (80.6%), West Dunbartonshire (80.3%) and Perth and Kinross (80.2%).

Qualifications Scotland data also shows the attainment gap between rural and urban classification.

Large Urban Areas had the highest proportion of student attaining grades A to C at National 5 levels with 80.3%, while Remote Small Towns had the lowest at 71.6%.

It is the same trend for Highers but with a smaller gap. The stats showed that 77.8% of students in Large Urban Areas achieved grades A to C while for Remote Small Towns it was just 72.2%.

Find and compare your council using the interactive table below.

Independents (private schools) also continue to outperform those at education authorities (state schools), with the figures showing a clear gap in pass rates at all levels.

More than 90% of entries at private schools achieved grades A to C this year at National 5, Higher and Advanced Higher level, while state schools remain below 80%.

Students with an additional support need (ASN) also continue to lag behind those without.

The latest figures show the attainment gap at National 5 level between those with and without ASN was 8.9 percentage points in 2026.

It's a similar picture at Higher level with the ASN attainment gap being 6.2 percentage points.

However, the gap narrows at Advanced Higher level with a 1.2 percentage point difference between those with and without ASN.

Children with ASN include those who have a Co-ordinated Support Plan, Individualised Education Programme or child's plan, and are assessed or declared disabled, or as having another support need.

Scottish exam pass rates rise as students find out results

BBC News Tue, 04 Aug 2026 13:51:26 GMT

Pass rates for Scottish exams have increased as students across the country received their results.

More than 148,000 learners have been finding out the results of their Nationals, Highers, Advanced Highers and Skills for Work Awards.

Qualifications Scotland - which replaced the Scottish Qualifications Authority last year after a number of controversies - said a record number of vocational and technical qualifications were awarded.

Figures show that the poverty-related attainment gap has narrowed compared with last year.

Admissions service Ucas said a record number of Scottish students aged 18 and under had been accepted into university or college. In total, 32,370 Scottish students of all ages secured places, up from 31,850 in 2025.

Education Secretary Màiri McAllan said it was a "proud day" for young people and the education system.

She added: "These are incredibly positive results across the board, with academic passes up at every level as well as record numbers of vocational qualifications.

"This is testament to the breadth and strength of Scotland's education system, the professionalism of our teachers and school staff and the hard work of our young people."

Statistics showed the National 5 pass rate had risen by 0.8% in 2025 to 79.2% this year.

The pass rate for Highers was up 0.8% to 76.7% while Advanced Highers rose by 0.9% to 77.6%.

A record total of 120,485 vocational and technical qualifications were achieved at levels 1-6, an increase of 9.1% compared to 2025.

More than 131,000 people sat exams in over 460 schools, colleges and training centres this year.

The attainment gap between the results achieved by students in the least deprived parts of Scotland and those in the most deprived closed a little in this year's figures - but still remains significant.

At Nat 5, the gap is 15.6 percentage points, down from 16.4%. The gap is the difference between the 86.6% of better-off students who got A to C grades this year, compared to 71% of those in the most deprived areas.

At Higher, the gap is 15.9 percentage points, down from 16.8 last year, and at Advanced Higher it is 12.1, down from 13.3.

Donna Stewart, chief qualifications and examinations officer, praised learners for their hard work and commitment.

"The rise in overall attainment at all three National Qualification levels and the increasing attainment in vocational and technical qualifications will rightly be welcomed in classrooms and staff rooms across Scotland," she said.

"The diversity of qualifications being achieved today is evidence of the appetite for skills-based, practical qualifications along with traditional subjects."

Opposition politicians said more needed to be done to improve outcomes for young people.

Scottish Labour's education spokeswoman Katherine Sangster welcomed the improvement in results, but said there was "no room for complacency".

"No child should be held back by their postcode or their background, but it's clear far more must be done to tackle the damaging inequalities in our education system," she said.

Scottish Conservative MP Andrew Bowie said "plummeting teacher numbers and spiralling levels of school violence" had made it a difficult year for pupils.

He added: "This has created a challenging environment for pupils to get the grades they hoped for, which is why they deserve a huge amount of credit for achieving great results.

"However, it's clear some pupils are still facing a postcode lottery when it comes to educational achievement."

The Scottish Greens called for "high-stakes exams" to be replaced with continuous assessment.

Laura Moodie, the party's education spokeswoman, said: "We need an education system that recognises achievement throughout the year, not just on exam day."

Scottish Liberal Democrat education spokesperson Duncan Dunlop said: "The new education secretary needs to address the teacher job mismatch, make sure kids are learning skills that equip them for the future and finally deliver on efforts to tackle the poverty-related attainment gap."

The Educational Institute of Scotland (EIS), the country's largest teaching union, said the results were "testament to the hard work of learners and their teachers alike".

General secretary Andrea Bradley said: "They should all be proud of their achievements, and we should all be equally proud of them for their hard work and the results that they have achieved."

She added that the "persistence" of the attainment gap was "a huge concern as well as a huge challenge".

This year's exam results are the first under Scotland's new exams body, Qualifications Scotland.

The organisation replaced the Scottish Qualifications Authority, which was scrapped after a series of controversies, including the downgrading of some students during the Covid pandemic.

In the Borders, Hawick High School's head boy Aleksander got As in all five of his Highers and now hopes to study medicine.

"It is a great relief," he said.

"I am doing three Advanced Highers now in sixth year and if they go to plan I will hopefully get into Edinburgh University to study medicine.

"I really wasn't sure I would get As – particularly in Maths as I didn't like the exam, but it turned out to be my best result."

Andrii Lutsyk, 18, has spent the last year studying an HNC in social sciences with criminology at North East Scotland College.

He achieved an A in his final HNC grade and now plans to study history at the University of Edinburgh after the summer.

Andrii, who arrived in Aberdeen in 2022 as a Ukrainian refugee and hopes to return one day, said: "I am quite surprised with my grade.

"I am very happy and very proud of myself and everyone who has been helping me through this long journey."

If you have a conditional offer for university or college that you don't meet, you can apply to Ucas' clearing process, external, which is used by universities and colleges to fill empty places.

Skills Development Scotland (SDS), the agency which supports training and skills for work, will also operate an advice line on 0808 100 8000.

It will be open from 08:00 to 20:00 on Tuesday and Wednesday, and from 09:00 to 17:00 on Thursday and Friday.

Advisers will be able to offer guidance on vacancies at colleges and universities; the clearing system for universities; apprenticeships; jobs; volunteering; or staying on at school.

Drinking culture embedded in cricket - Stokes

Ben Stokes played 122 Tests, 114 one-day internationals and 43 T20s for England

Ben Stokes says "cricket has a drinking culture and that has not changed", but does not believe the England team has a problem with alcohol.

Former England captain Stokes, 35, announced his shock retirement from international cricket in June - during the third and final Test of the series against New Zealand.

The all-rounder's departure came weeks after he missed England's second Test against the Kiwis following an incident in a London nightclub involving him and bowler Gus Atkinson.

That was the latest in a number of off-field episodes involving the England team.

A midnight curfew was introduced following the Ashes tour, with the policy updated to advise England players to avoid drinking alcohol on the day before and the day after matches - following the incident involving Stokes and Atkinson.

Asked whether the England team had a drinking problem, Stokes told the For the Love of Cricket podcast:, external "No, that is such an extreme thing to put on a team."

He added: "I think cricket has a drinking culture and that hasn't changed.

"We are in 2026 now, where the game has gone more professional over the years, and one thing that has just stayed within cricket is its relationship with alcohol - from club cricket it works its way up. It has just stayed there and has been embedded within the sport.

"The relationship between alcohol and cricket is just something that hasn't moved on as the game has become more professional.

"For people who think the English cricket team has a drinking culture, I would say no. I would just say cricket has a culture that is associated with alcohol."

Booze, beach, beaten - how England lost the Ashes

England advised to avoid alcohol around matches

Stokes was found not guilty of affray in a high-profile trial in 2018, after being involved in a fight outside a nightclub in Bristol.

He told the court that he had been drinking but was not drunk.

Stokes said he gave up alcohol for a period when he was recovering from injury in 2025.

He previously said that, while it was unlikely that he would give up alcohol entirely, he had learned to manage his behaviour with it.

"I think it can be a problem. I don't know what you do to change it," he added.

"I've had, I don't want to say problems, but I've had relationships with alcohol at times over my career that have been potentially dangerous, if that makes sense. But that is completely different to me now.

"There's this relationship with alcohol within cricket that has been the same from the 1980s. As the game has got better and better, that thing has stayed around. That is my opinion on cricket and alcohol."

Speaking to former England team-mates Stuart Broad and Jos Buttler, Stokes said he would love to become coach of the national team in the future.

"I'm doing my level three coaching now while I'm still playing, because I want, when the day comes that I'm not playing any more, I'd love to be able to have all that stuff signed off and done," said Stokes.

"I know what I want to do in terms of staying within the game, which is to be a coach. And would I love to be coach of England one day? Absolutely.

"I just really like the idea of being, again, like, in some form of leadership away from playing."

Fleming new England Test coach with Root captain

Root in 'very different place' over Test captaincy

Stokes return would not surprise England chief Key

England were beaten 2-1 by New Zealand and the series defeat followed the 4-1 Ashes loss in Australia, meaning they have not won a Test series since late 2024.

Stokes has rejected suggestions he could reverse his England retirement for the 2027 Ashes and, when asked whether he had definitely retired, Stokes said: "Definitely".

He also expressed surprise at Harry Brook not replacing him as England Test captain.

Batter Brook, 27, was promoted to Test vice-captain for last winter's Ashes tour - before it emerged that he had been struck by a nightclub bouncer in Wellington the night before a white-ball game in New Zealand in November.

However, Joe Root was given the Test captaincy for the second Test against New Zealand, which Stokes missed, and has now been given the role permanently.

Stokes had backed Brook, who leads the white-ball sides, to succeed him in the role.

"I think just if you think someone's going to be a good captain or a good leader, then just give them it," said Stokes.

"I understood the reasoning but I was still like, well, what message is that sending to him?

"He's vice-captain. And then the captain is not playing, but he's not captain. What?"

Root's first spell as Test captain was between 2017 and 2022 and he captained England to a record 27 Test wins in 65 matches.

He will work with new England Test coach Stephen Fleming, the former New Zealand captain, in the role.

Root stepped down from his first stint as skipper in April 2022, following a 10-wicket defeat by West Indies.

At that time, England had won just one of their past 17 Tests, including a 4-0 Ashes humbling in Australia, while also navigating Covid restrictions - with Root saying the job "took its toll" on his health.

"I wish him [Root] nothing but success. I hope he goes on and achieves amazing things in his role as captain and I think he's going to really enjoy it with Flem [Fleming]. He's a great man," said Stokes.

"I've worked with Flem before but I told Joe, I said my only worry is just you. And that's all I really care about now, just because I have seen what he went through and how much he put himself through for someone.

"He's just always put the team first - he always comes second. And that's just my only concern with it, is just obviously knowing what he went through last time he was in charge of the team. I don't want to see that ever happen again because I care for Joe a lot, but I wish him all the success in the world.

"I'm sure he's going to do great. So I'm looking forward to seeing what the team does going forward."

Fleming replaced Brendon McCullum as coach of England's Test team.

McCullum was fired following a string of poor results and several off-field incidents involving his players, but remains in charge of England's white-ball sides.

There were rumours of a rift between him and Stokes during the latter stages of their time together for England, but both have denied that was the case.

McCullum said he told his former captain that he considered him a "good friend", while Stokes said the pair are "mates".

"We never once fell out," said Stokes.

"Did we have discussions with each other that we had different views on and different opinions on? 100% and we both admit that. I think Baz has even said that himself.

"Did we have a fallout? Absolutely not."

Man 'driven insane' by noise admits killing fish

BBC News Tue, 04 Aug 2026 12:08:21 GMT

A man who admitted using motor oil and detergent to kill his neighbour's fish, after being "driven completely insane" by the noise of a water pump in the pond, has been sentenced.

Gerry Duffy, 76, of Hadley Road, Barnet, north London, pleaded guilty on the day of his trial at Willesden Magistrates' Court to three counts of damaging property and one count of unlawfully destroying fish in March.

The court heard Duffy climbed into Andreas Ptohides' garden to break the water pump "out of sheer frustration and lack of sleep", having warned his neighbour he would take matters into his own hands.

Duffy was given a two-year conditional discharge and ordered to pay £565 in compensation to his neighbour.

Duffy, who worked as a builder before his retirement, lives in a studio flat which backs on to the garden owned by his neighbour, the court heard.

Shahid Iftakhar, prosecuting, said the "neighbour dispute" between Duffy and Ptohides, potentially caused £565 of damage.

He said: "The defendant has previously complained to the complainant about noise coming from his garden and has said words to the effect of, 'if you didn't deal with it, I would' – there was a warning before the incident."

The prosecution added that Duffy was captured on CCTV having "climbed into the complainant's garden and damaged the water pipes and pumps".

In mitigation, Elliott Stern told the court his client had tried to deal with the dispute without resorting to killing the fish.

Mr Stern said: "The man has been driven completely insane by this noise, he's spoken to the complainant several times.

"They initially said they would stop the water pump going but then turned around and said that's not good for the fish."

An environmental officer came to the house and told Duffy he either had to "move or close his window", the court heard.

"Out of sheer frustration and lack of sleep, Mr Duffy, out of character, I would say, lost his mind and committed various damages," said Stern.

Family funeral held after suspected triple murder

BBC News Tue, 04 Aug 2026 12:02:37 GMT

A funeral service has been held for a woman and her two daughters who are believed to have been murdered.

Nothabo Zandile Tshuma, 42, and her daughters Natalie, 15, and Nala, five, were found dead in Great Denham, near Bedford, on 6 July.

At the funeral service in a church in Bulawayo, Zimbabwe, mourners spoke of the mother's kindness, her love for her family and determination to succeed.

Inside the packed hall, dozens sang mournful songs as the three white coffins stood in the centre of the room, each placed beside a smiling photograph.

An inquest into the deaths found the mother and her two children had died from head injuries.

Ndodana Mkhanyisi Tshuma, 45, was arrested in Johannesburg on suspicion of murdering his wife and two children; he remains in custody in South Africa. He is also facing a separate gun-related charge.

At the same time, UK authorities are working to have him extradited to stand trial for the murder allegations.

Speaking to the BBC, family spokesperson and relative Leon Khumalo described Nothabo, who had built a life in the UK over many years, as "the family's pride and joy."

He said: "She was the glue of our family and was dearly loved by many".

Khumalo said his family was grappling with the loss, which had taken "two generations from them" in one gruesome incident.

At the funeral service, the speakers spoke fondly of her kindness, her love for her family and determination to succeed.

One said: "When she moved to the UK from Zimbabwe, we were all incredibly proud. It filled us with so much joy as a family to see her build a great career and respected career."

Another relative described Natalie as "an intelligent young girl who showed great promise. She was gentle and loved sport".

Speaking about Nala, he added: "She was full of infectious joy and laughter."

The family have said they want justice for the deaths, and the truth to be revealed through the court process.

Tshuma's case resumes on 27 August; he is yet to plead.

Surgeon struck off after wrongly connecting organs

BBC News Tue, 04 Aug 2026 10:31:45 GMT

A doctor who botched an operation so badly it was described as "not compatible with life" has been struck off the medical register.

Dr Yasser Adly Abdel Rahman, an NHS locum surgeon from Egypt, carried out the flawed emergency bowel procedure on a young man.

It meant the contents of the patient's bowel, leaving his stomach, were re-deposited back into his stomach through a circular "closed loop", the Medical Practitioners Tribunal Service (MPTS) heard.

The patient was left in "uncontrollable pain" and could have died but for another surgeon correcting the error in a second operation, the misconduct hearing, sitting in Manchester, was told.

Rahman at no time considered that something may have gone wrong surgically, the tribunal heard, despite the patient's parents and other medics expressing concerns.

A former consultant general and colorectal surgeon, acting as the General Medical Council's expert witness, said the procedure carried out by Dr Rahman was "not known to man" and his error was "as bad as it gets".

Rahman, who qualified in 1993 from Ain Shams University in Cairo, Egypt, did not attend the hearing and was not legally represented.

He claimed he had been made a "scapegoat" after a "witch hunt" following the operation, carried out at the Royal Oldham Hospital, where he was working as a locum on 25 August 2020.

The MPTS imposed an order restricting his work as a doctor in July of the following year, but Rahman broke the conditions of the order as he then applied for and secured a job as a locum at Affidea Express Care Clinic in Ireland in February 2022, the tribunal found.

This breach of the order imposed on his work was an "aggravating" feature, the tribunal ruled, to already "significant" errors in surgery and post-op care, the hearing was told.

The tribunal concluded in a ruling last month that Rahman's misconduct was "fundamentally incompatible with continued registration" and erased him from the medical register allowing him to work as a doctor.

What will happen when a SpaceX rocket collides with the Moon?

BBC News Tue, 04 Aug 2026 09:13:37 GMT

The Moon has endured countless blows over millions of years. Asteroids and meteors have given the satellite its signature pockmarked surface and network of craters. More recently, it has also experienced impacts from the plucky little probes and landers that Earthbound space agencies have sent hurtling its way.

Now on Wednesday, scientists expect the Moon will experience yet another collision, this time from a drifting SpaceX rocket that has been travelling at around 2.43 kilometres per second, or about 5,400mph.

The upper stage (section) of one of SpaceX's Falcon 9 rockets will "impact" the Moon on 5 August, according to Nasa's Centre for Near-Earth Object Studies (CNEOS).

The US space agency reached the conclusion after independent astronomers, using public data, noted that a portion of the rocket from a January 2025 launch was on an accidental collision course with the Moon.

"There is no danger to Earth," said spokesperson Jimi Russell. "Nasa will continue to track the booster for training purposes, as well as later observe the impact site for scientific purposes."

SpaceX launched this specific Falcon 9 rocket as part of a US and Japanese mission to carry a pair of lunar landers and scientific equipment to the Moon last year.

Part of the Falcon 9 is reusable and designed to return back to Earth for its next mission. But parts of the rocket are shed in space and remain there, stuck in orbit unless they eventually collide with another celestial body.

The piece in question is the upper stage of the rocket, and is about the size of a five-storey building, with a mass on Earth of at least 4,000kg (8,800 lbs).

Astronomer Bill Gray, who first discovered the trajectory, wrote on his blog that he believed het object will land near the Einstein Crater, which is on the part of the Moon that receives daylight and is visible from Earth. He predicts it will create a crater more than 17m (56ft) in diameter.

The impending collision - predicted to happen at about 02:35 EDT (06:35 GMT) on Wednesday - is expected to captivate astronomers, both amateur and professional.

"It's something really huge smashing into the Moon. It's not remotely dangerous, we can just watch the show," says Dr Matt Bothwell, public astronomer at the University of Cambridge.

"It's going to impact and it's going to send up a huge plume of dust, maybe 50km into the air or more, and that's going to spread sideways over time," Bothwell said.

Given the Moon's lack of atmosphere and far weaker gravitational pull, the moment of impact will be "more impressive than any [similar] explosion on Earth", Bothwell said.

Nothing will slow the object down, like the atmosphere would do here on Earth - and nothing will prevent the estimated million kilograms in debris from rocketing up into space.

While the impact will probably not be visible from Earth with the naked eye, people with access to a sophisticated telescope may be able to see a flash radiating off the Moon's surface, Bothwell said.

More significant would be the educative potential of the impact, Bothwell noted. He said this moment would present a unique opportunity to study what happens when an object hits the Moon.

Scientists are therefore gearing up to watch the event closely.

Big telescopes in the Americas, plus Nasa's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter and South Korea's Danuri probe, will track the flash, plume and new crater, and a citizen‑science project is signing up keen amateurs to film the impact too.

By catching the dust plume in action, astronomers hope to turn this accidental crash into a useful experiment.

Watching how much material gets thrown up, how high it goes and how it falls back should sharpen their models of lunar impacts, and even give clues about what lies just beneath the surface at the impact site, where fresh subsurface material will be exposed for the first time.

Bothwell, the astronomer, also said the collision would provide a cautionary tale about the issue of ever-accumulating, human-made space clutter.

"I think more people should be more worried about space debris," Bothwell said. "Every single year we put more stuff in orbit. Sometimes the satellites just collide, and they shatter into more pieces. I think there's a worry about a runaway cascade, if we put so much stuff in orbit."

According to the European Space Agency (ESA), there are around 54,000 objects floating in space that measure larger than 10cm. In total, humans have launched about 17,000 tonnes of objects into space since the Space Age began in 1957.

The last dead rocket to impact the Moon was in 2022, when the Chinese Long March 3C upper stage from the 2014 Chang'e 5‑T1 mission hit the far side of the Moon - which faces away from Earth.

Decades earlier, Nasa launched objects into the Moon on purpose, in order to collect data for the Apollo missions.

Analysis: Trump challenged by cold reality from top allies

BBC News Tue, 04 Aug 2026 09:11:39 GMT

It's been a humbling few days for Donald Trump, even if the American president is reluctant to acknowledge it.

In a series of setbacks, Trump has faced adversity in matters both large and small; two of which he cares about dearly and one that could determine his and his party's political fate for the remaining two years of his presidential term.

From a flawed attempt to renovate a Washington landmark to questions about his pick to head the justice department to increasingly complicated efforts to end his war in Iran, the president has been handling tricky issues - many of his own making.

Trump's response has been a familiar one. A first term refrain - that the president makes his own reality with "alternative facts" - is still the operative one. He sticks to beliefs even in the face of conflicting evidence.

Unlike his first term, however, when many of his most notable conflicts were with dissenters in his own administration, this time around he has butted heads even with those who have proven themselves the most loyal to him.

On Friday, US Attorney Jeanine Pirro, a former Fox News host and stalwart Trump ally, moved to drop felony destruction of property charges against former Olympian David Hearn, who federal prosecutors had accused of intentionally damaging the Reflecting Pool near the Washington Monument.

"The damage was the result of a botched installation and not vandalism," she wrote in a 20-page court filing announcing her department's decision. She attributed her decision to prosecute Hearn as the result of misleading information provided by the Department of Interior.

Trump may embrace alternative facts, but the evidence Pirro confronted - what she would have had to defend in court, before a judge and potentially sceptical jury - provided scarce support for her case. And so she abandoned it.

Trump had enthusiastically endorsed the vandalism explanation, however, and he stuck by it. In a Truth Social post on Saturday, he criticised Pirro's decision to drop the case and did so again in comments from the Oval Office on Monday.

"She folded like an umbrella," he griped.

If the Reflecting Pool case was an instance of Trump being forced to face legal reality, up on Capitol Hill it was an unpleasant political reality that confronted him.

One of Trump's closest allies – his former criminal defence attorney Todd Blanche – was hitting stiff headwinds in his bid to become attorney general on a permanent basis.

Two Republican senators, John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina, had joined Democrats to block Blanche's nomination. They were demanding Blanche provide a letter formally disavowing any attempts to revive the proposed $1.8bn (£1.34bn) fund to pay individuals who claimed to have been the targets of politicised government prosecution.

Tillis called it a "payout pot for punks" amid concerns it could be used to compensate people prosecuted over the US Capitol riot by Trump's supporters in 2021.

In another Saturday Truth Social post, Trump wrote that he would keep Blanche on as acting attorney general and "push hard" to get Congress to pass legislation authorising the fund.

"It will immediately be back on the table, and I will get it done," he wrote, suggesting that no matter what the ultimate outcome of Blanche's nomination, Trump is unlikely to ever let the issue go.

The political maths in the Senate, however, was undeniable. By the next day Blanche had acceded to the senators' request, releasing two letters that Tillis and Cornyn said satisfied their concerns.

In comments from the White House on Monday, Blanche escaped the scolding that Pirro the prosecutor received. Trump said he "didn't look at" Blanche's documents. "I understand there's been a sign-off, but I don't know what they agreed," he said.

While the Reflecting Pool prosecution and the so-called "anti-weaponisation fund" may be topics of intense presidential interest, they barely register as concerns for the larger American public.

That is decidedly not the case with the war with Iran, where Trump is once again accusing Iran of deceit amid another round of on-again, off-again negotiations and threats of overwhelming American military action.

On Monday, after asserting the previous day that he had called off "an attack that would have been the biggest attack since World War II" at the behest of Iranian officials and Arab intermediaries, Trump took to Truth Social to condemn what he said was Iranian duplicity after Iran denied any new direct negotiations.

"They ask for a meeting, some would say 'beg', talks begin, with more scheduled in the immediate future, and they say, openly and proudly, that they're not having any discussions," Trump wrote.

If Iranians are misrepresenting the status of talks it wouldn't be the first time - but it also wouldn't be the first time Trump has seemingly taken their assurances at face value and heralded a new diplomatic breakthrough.

US officials told the BBC's partner CBS News on Monday that no "new" or novel negotiations with Iran were planned. An Iranian official said the country's only current talks were with Oman, over the future of shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.

The latest twists in the war have become a familiar pattern with little progress, as polls continue to show American disapproval of the conflict and concern that Trump is not achieving his war goals.

Those recent public-opinion surveys suggest the war has become a growing drag on the president's overall popularity. A recent Associated Press poll puts Trump's approval at 33%, aligned with similar findings by CNN, Quinnipiac and YouGov. That matches or is below Trump's ratings after the Capitol riot and is above only Richard Nixon – who resigned from office in disgrace - among second-term US presidents in modern American history.

Trump, however, has repeatedly dismissed surveys suggesting his historic unpopularity.

"My REAL Polling Numbers, not those made up by the Fake News Media, are the best they have ever been," he posted to Truth Social on Monday.

In three months, voters will head to the polls for congressional midterm elections. And Trump has shown surprising strength at the ballot box in the past, even in the face of seemingly daunting poll numbers.

While Trump may be grappling with – and, at times denying - recent adversity, that will be the ultimate measure of his political fate. And if Republicans struggle, it may provide yet another reality that Trump, despite his best efforts, must eventually face.

The once-impossible black holes that could break thermodynamics

New Scientist August 04, 2026

The following is an extract from our Lost in Space-Time newsletter. Each month, we dive into fascinating ideas from around the universe. You can sign up for Lost in Space-Time here.

Physics is littered with the remains of theories that once seemed destined to explain everything. A theory can dominate for decades, even centuries, only to be wiped out when new experimental results arrive or a fitter idea comes around. Before long, they’re relegated to little more than fossils in the scientific record.

Thermodynamics, though, is like the crocodile of physics – an unchanging ancient beast that has survived the field’s great mass-extinction events: the arrival of quantum mechanics, the fusion of space and time into one fabric, the discovery of the expanding universe. Thermodynamics has persisted through them all. Even Albert Einstein believed it would outlast quantum theory and general relativity, two fields he helped establish.

Advertisement

Now, it may finally have met its real test: an extremal black hole, a theoretical variety of cosmic behemoth that sits at the limits of the theory of general relativity. One of the basic laws of black hole thermodynamics suggests that nature could never make such a beast. But recent work has shown that nature may have found a loophole.

To see why that would be such a big deal, we need to return to the early 1970s, when our modern understanding of black holes was only beginning to take shape. Jacob Bekenstein, then a graduate student at Princeton University, pointed out that matter falling into a black hole seemed to disappear from the observable universe, taking its entropy with it.

Entropy tells us how many microscopic arrangements can produce the same observable state. Imagine a glass of water sitting on a table. To us, it has an obvious temperature, volume and pressure, but the molecules within can be arranged and moving in an immense number of different ways while the glass, overall, looks exactly the same. It’s worth mentioning that entropy is a very powerful tool – counting these arrangements can help us unpick what the microscopic components of a system are. According to the second law of thermodynamics, the total entropy of an isolated system always increases over time. So what happens when something falls into a black hole, crossing a threshold beyond which nothing can ever return? Is it just gone from the account of entropy in the cosmos? Certainly not without breaking the laws of physics. So, Bekenstein proposed a radical solution: black holes must possess entropy of their own.

Physicist Stephen Hawking initially objected. If a black hole had entropy, thermodynamics implied that it must also have a temperature – and anything with a temperature should radiate. That was awkward, given that the defining feature of a black hole was that nothing escaped it. But then physicists, including Hawking, crunched the numbers and saw that once they included quantum mechanics, black holes did emit a faint glow, now known as Hawking radiation. They had a temperature after all.

This physicist is hunting for the biggest black hole in the universe

And when doing the maths, physicists noticed a striking resemblance between the laws that governed black holes and the laws of thermodynamics, which concern the transformation of work, entropy and energy in engines. In fact, there were rock-solid correspondences between the behaviour of black holes and the first two laws of thermodynamics, which state that energy cannot be created or destroyed and that entropy can never decrease in a closed system.

Physicists had little reason to think the third law would be any different. In ordinary thermodynamics, the third law says you can never cool a system all the way to absolute zero. The colder it gets, the harder it becomes to remove the last scraps of heat, until reaching zero would take an impossible amount of time or effort.

Black holes were thought to play by the same rule. A black hole is characterised by just three numbers: its mass, electric charge and spin. From those, you can work out the area of its event horizon, its temperature and its entropy. And, in line with the third law, it seemed that a black hole could never quite reach zero temperature, or stop emitting Hawking radiation altogether.

But in 2024, Christoph Kehle at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and Ryan Unger at the University of California, Berkeley, proved that such extremal black holes, as they’re known, could indeed exist. So, the third law of black hole physics may not be much of a law after all.

“Extremal black holes were thought of as an idealised, unattainable limit: something you could write down as a solution, but which could never be reached [through any real physical] process, but we proved that wrong,” says Kehle.

We didn’t think this third law for black holes was true just because it mirrored thermodynamics. It also seemed to keep the rest of physics safe.

Charged and rotating black holes can have two horizons. The outer one is the familiar event horizon, the point beyond which nothing can return. Deeper inside lies the Cauchy horizon. Cross that and general relativity stops telling you what happens next: even perfect knowledge of the past would no longer be enough to predict the future.

Mathematical physicist Roger Penrose thought the Cauchy horizon would always stay safely inside the event horizon, keeping the singularity at the core of the black hole hidden from the rest of the universe. He called this idea cosmic censorship: a kind of built-in protection mechanism that stops us witnessing a place where the laws of physics have broken down – a so-called naked singularity.

But the black hole’s gravitational pull is counteracted by its charge and rotation. Increase either of these properties and the Cauchy horizon expands while the event horizon contracts. Eventually, the two coincide at a limit known as extremality. The gravitational intensity at the event horizon – a quantity known as its surface gravity – then falls to zero. Because a black hole’s Hawking temperature is proportional to this surface gravity, an extremal black hole has zero temperature and emits no thermal Hawking radiation.

Does time come from the entire universe running computations?

Extremal black holes ride on the edge of this cosmic danger zone – right as the Cauchy horizon threatens to eclipse the event horizon and reveal a naked singularity – and were thought to be impossible. But Kehle and Unger found two ways around this.

Their models showed that an extremal black hole could form if you physically added charged matter to a black hole gradually, or fired a beam of charged particles into a region of empty space and caused it to collapse into an extremal black hole directly. Crucially, these mechanisms didn’t risk creating a naked singularity.

“The fact [that this work proves] extremal black holes can form dynamically tells us that these objects are not just mathematical limits. They can genuinely arise within classical gravity,” says Chiara Toldo at the Free University of Brussels in Belgium.

That matters because these strange objects may provide a bridge between black holes in the messy, evolving universe and the highly idealised ones that have long appeared in string theory and quantum mechanics.

For decades, physicists have wanted to know what black holes are made of. Their entropy suggests that there must be many possible arrangements of microstates, corresponding to the same black hole. But what, exactly, is being rearranged?

That question is one reason theoretical physicists such as Toldo have been interested in extremal black holes for some time. Much of their appeal comes from their zero temperature, which would usually mean zero entropy. But despite having zero temperature, extremal black holes can still possess entropy. That makes them unusually clean models for exploring what a black hole’s microstates might actually be.

“[String theory] gives you powerful techniques with which you can count the states inside a black hole,” says Toldo. “You can try to start figuring out what the states inside the black hole are” and what they’re made of. But until now, much of this work dealt with extremal black holes as idealised mathematical models. Showing that one can form dynamically brings those ideas a step closer to the kinds of objects that might genuinely arise in our universe.

Subscriber-only newsletter

There may even be a way to spot one. As matter tumbles towards a black hole, it can be squeezed and heated so violently that it gives off a burst of radiation. This is nothing like Hawking radiation: it comes from the infalling material itself. Around an ordinary black hole, the resulting disturbance soon dies away. But an extremal horizon lacks the usual damping effect, allowing part of it to linger and even grow. Last year, researchers showed that this should leave a distinctive fingerprint in the faint tail of radiation travelling out to distant observers.

But actually detecting an extremal black hole remains a distant prospect. For now, the more immediate implications are theoretical. If the third law of black hole physics can be broken, then the analogy between black holes and thermodynamic systems may not be as exact as we thought.

Kehle and Unger’s work has exposed more than a gap in our understanding of black holes. It raises the more unsettling possibility that we don’t fully understand thermodynamics either.

“This work made me realise that I understand black holes better than I understand classical thermodynamics,” says Kehle. “For example, when the third law says you can’t cool a system to absolute zero with a ‘finite sequence of operations’, what actually counts as an operation? There could be something more fundamental lurking there that we don’t know about.”

“We’ve disproved the third law as it was written, but we don’t yet understand this problem in any sense. There’s still a lot to be done,” says Unger.

Random wobbles in time could finally solve gravity’s greatest mystery

Darwin proved right about gnat-trapping carnivorous plant

New Scientist August 04, 2026

More than 150 years after Charles Darwin proposed that saxifrages were a group of plants that practiced carnivory, researchers have meticulously gathered the evidence to confirm he was right.

“Talk about an amazing feeling,” says Doug Soltis at the University of Florida. “To have the opportunity to confirm a prediction of Darwin is both humbling and very exciting.

“I would like to think Darwin would be pleased [and say] ‘I was right – again.’”

Advertisement

The long-overlooked insects that could save our crops

To formally qualify as a carnivorous plant, a species must possess adaptations that enable it to attract, capture and digest its prey and absorb nutrients from it. Perhaps the world’s most renowned carnivorous plant is the Venus flytrap (Dionaea muscipula).

In 1875, four years after detailing his theory of natural selection in his book On the Origin of Species, Darwin wrote about his fascination with two species in the genus Saxifraga, which were known to catch insects.

The genus has around 450 species and is found in Arctic and alpine regions of the northern hemisphere as well as in the South American Andes.

Free newsletter

However, despite attempting several experiments to prove the plants digested the insects, Darwin was unable to substantiate his hunch.

To take up the challenge, Soltis and his colleagues studied specimens of Saxifraga candelabrum from Wufeng Mountain in Yunnan province, China – a different species from those studied by Darwin, but in the same genus.

During field surveys, the botanists observed that the Saxifraga candelabrum plants were capable of trapping small insects, using hairs covered with a sticky secretion. Bigger insects – those more useful to the plants for pollination – weren’t captured by the goo.

Mature plants had an average of more than 70 insects stuck to them, primarily various species of gnat, which suggested a potential carnivorous habit, says team member Hang Sun at the Chinese Academy of Sciences.

The Selfish Gene at 50: Why Dawkins’s evolution classic still holds up

The team first tested whether the secretions produced by the hair-like structures that trap insects contained digestive enzymes capable of breaking down the prey, and found they did.

Next, by infusing insect prey with a nitrogen isotope, the scientists were able to demonstrate that nutrients from the digested insect had been taken up by the plant.

Finally, genetic studies showed that Saxifraga shares common genes with other carnivorous plants – a sundew (Drosera spatulata) and a flycatcher bush (Roridula gorgonias) – that control prey attraction, digestion and nutrient uptake.

“Together, these genomic data provide independent evidence that S. candelabrum is a true carnivorous plant,” says Sun.

Soltis expects the team’s research will lead to a re-examination of other species in the genus, including the ones Darwin studied, and the wider Saxifraga family.

“Many members of the family have these hairs, and I would not be surprised if others are also carnivorous,” Soltis says.

Nature Communications DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-75288-y
