Political parties told to remove signs advertising meetings in Napier

New Zealand Herald August 04, 2026

Signs like the Act Party's public meeting sign have to be removed in Napier but are still allowed up in Hastings. Photo / Jack Riddell

Three political parties have been told by the Napier City Council that their signage or billboards advertising public meetings are not allowed in the city until closer to the election.

Act Party’s Tukituki candidate, Rob Douglas, on Saturday posted a Facebook video of him standing in front of a billboard advertising David Seymour’s public meeting at the Hawke’s Bay Racecourse on September 5.

In the video, Douglas said he was removing billboard signs because “the Napier City Council have created some dumb regulation which means we can’t have billboards up advertising meetings for the Act Party”.

Douglas shared with Hawke’s Bay Today an email sent to him at 1.40pm on Friday, by a Napier City Council staff member.

The email said the council believed Act’s public meeting signs breached a rule in Napier’s district plan.

The rule states temporary signs on private property for “electioneering, election advertisement and similar purposes” must not be erected more than nine weeks before polling day.

The council considered the public meeting signs to meet the definition of “similar purposes”, and said all non-compliant signs had to be removed by 5pm on Sunday.

A Napier City Council spokeswoman said public meeting signage was treated the same as basic candidate hoarding signage, “as defined in the Proposed District Plan”.

National’s Napier MP, Katie Nimon, confirmed she had also had to remove billboards advertising a public meeting with Christopher Luxon at the Napier War Memorial on August 20 from inside Napier city boundaries.

The Napier City Council also recently told Labour’s Napier candidate, Dr Alex Hedley, the motorhome he was using as a mobile campaign office with his face and election details on the side wasn’t allowed in the city until closer to the election.

He told Hawke’s Bay Today he had been keeping it in storage at his election office since the reprimand.

The council spokeswoman said Act, National and Labour were observed to have election-related signage in place and were emailed the council’s signage rules.

Billboards could go up in Napier for the general election on November 7 from Saturday, September 5.

“The nine-week limit balances candidates’ ability to communicate with voters while ensuring election signage doesn’t dominate city spaces for an extended period,” the Napier City Council spokeswoman said.

Hastings does not appear to have any intention of following Napier’s lead.

A Hastings District Council spokeswoman said the billboards promoted a community meeting and, provided the billboards were advertising a genuine meeting, the council did not “regulate or dictate the political content” of the meeting.

Douglas said it was frustrating the party could advertise in Hastings and Central Hawke’s Bay, but not Napier.

“They should have bigger fish to fry than wasting ratepayers’ money searching for public meeting signs they can take down.”

Act’s Napier candidate, John (Johno) Ormond, said the council had significantly reduced the window political parties had to advertise.

“Too many national and local government staff spend their days finding new ways to say ‘no’ to their constituents,” he said.

Jack Riddell is a multimedia journalist with Hawke’s Bay Today and has worked in radio and media in the UK, Germany, and New Zealand.

Legendary hotel’s revamp gets it a perfect score

Sydney Morning Herald August 05, 2026

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

After navigating a chaotic Florence airport and some hairy hairpin bends in our hire-car, arriving at this newly renovated Renaissance villa – its facade attributed to the school of Michelangelo – feels even more like a serene escape from life’s mundane realities. Architect and designer Luigi Fragola says it was the stillness of the villa that first struck him as he walked through the 15th-century estate: “What fascinated me was the silence – that silence of places that have truly lived.”

Formerly a convent, at one time Napoleon’s headquarters and more recently a private home, the building, set high in the Fiesole hills above Tuscany’s capital, has been painstakingly reimagined. It’s also now the hotel du jour for the rich and fabulous (model Alexa Chung and DJ Isabella Massenet were at the reopening party). Given the Lamborghini, Porsche and Ferrari in the driveway, I’m also somewhat relieved we were upgraded to a Mercedes instead of the Opel Astra I’d booked online.

Sign up for the Traveller newsletter

The latest travel news, tips and inspiration delivered to your inbox. Sign up now.

While original cloisters, stone fireplaces, restored frescoes and heavy curtains speak to its weighty history, works by Italian artists – hand-painted murals by Francesca Guicciardini, watercolours by botanical artist Maria Rita Stirpe, wall coverings by Elena Carozzi – bring present-day personality. The terraced gardens, with 180-degree views as far as Brunelleschi’s cupola crowning the Duomo, are a highlight: lavender and rosemary scent the gravel pathways, while the lemon trees are the healthiest I’ve seen, weighed down with enormous fruit.

We’re staying in a garden suite that’s seemingly built into the hillside, jasmine hedges camouflaging our private alfresco area from passers-by. There are, of course, rooms in the villa itself (39 altogether), but being enveloped in nature feels wonderfully therapeutic. The green Cipollino marble in the bathroom and local Impruneta terracotta floors echo the gardens outside, while raw linens and a chalky palette reflect Fragola’s restrained approach. Artisanal details include hand-painted tapestries, silks from Venice-based Rubelli and ornate scagliola [a 17th-century plastering technique] tabletops by Tuscan workshop Bianco Bianchi.

It’s appropriate that a fresco of The Last Supper adorns the original refectory where a sumptuous buffet breakfast is laid out – there are so many irresistible cakes and pastries alongside cured meats, cheese, yoghurt, juices, fruit and yes, eight types of honey (the villa has its own beehives), that you need never eat again. And that’s without ordering eggs Florentine from the a la carte menu.

Under a striped awning at the alfresco pool grill, try a vibrant Caprese salad or linguine alla Nerano (with zucchini); at Ristorante San Michele it’s all about the caponata, the eggplant parmigiana and the Chianina beef used in the tartare. The sheer volume of local and seasonal ingredients is impressive.

Dishes get more intricate at Antesi, the eight-table fine dining restaurant in the 16th-century loggia, where executive chef Alessandro Cozzolino conjures an ambitious culinary journey called the “cuisine of time” – the elaborate presentation occasionally taking precedence over depth of flavour.

For a more casual experience, the intimate Bar Doccia offers an excellent drinks list including several non-alcoholic aperitivi, alongside substantial snacks. As is traditional, if you order a couple of cocktails you’ll also be served bowls of olives, almonds and chips but maybe treat yourself to a couple of croquettes blanketed in shaved white truffle for good measure.

You don’t have to travel far to dip into the area’s history: nearby Monte Ceceri is where Leonardo da Vinci came to study local birds of prey and eventually tested his “great kite” flying machine. The hotel offers several immersive experiences including a hike through those woodlands, a calligraphy masterclass and a paper-making workshop, while its shuttle bus will drop you in the centre of Florence at Piazza della Repubblica (so much easier than attempting Fiesole’s narrow, winding roads yourself). Wellness devotees are also looked after, with three treatment rooms including a double suite at Italy’s first Guerlain spa, and, up in the woods, an Energy Chapel, Sungazing Lounge and yoga deck designed by super-cool Milanese lifestyle brand La DoubleJ.

The celebration of Italian craftsmanship and the level of thoughtful detail at this historic Franciscan convent, combined with the sublime peace of its gardens, make a stay here unforgettable.

Government contracts to require job creation instead of green targets under new rules

The Guardian Tue, 04 Aug 2026 21:30:00 GMT

Louise Haigh says taxpayer money must benefit local communities amid backlash from environmental groups

Ministers will scrap the requirement for companies to prove their green and progressive values before they are awarded government contracts, and instead ask firms to prove they will help young people back into work.

As part of a government push to reduce the number of people not in education, employment or training (Neets) in the UK and boost regional growth, public sector buyers will double the consideration they give to whether companies will get more people into jobs, rather than if they can show they are improving social and environmental wellbeing. Government procurement contracts account for about £90bn of taxpayers’ money spent each year.

Louise Haigh, the first secretary of state, said the move would help small businesses who often find themselves locked out of contracts because of the requirements, which big businesses know how to get around.

“Every pound of taxpayer money should be spent in a way that benefits local communities – creating good jobs and giving young people the skills they need for the future,” said Haigh. “For too long, securing government contracts has been a tick-box exercise that fails to deliver the positive change that people feel in their pocket and see in the places they live.

“We are doing things differently. These new rules will ensure the £90bn that is spent each year through government contracts supports British jobs, skills and people in every postcode.”

Central government departments are required to weigh up the social value of government contracts, which counts for 10% of the decision. Under new measures this will be increased to 20%, but instead of considering social good, government buyers will be pushed to secure contracts with companies creating local jobs that pay above the minimum wage, offer training, work experience or plug local skills gaps.

Contracts worth less than £1m will be exempt from the requirement, which ministers hope will make it easier for smaller companies to compete.

The plans were criticised by environmental and green campaign groups, which said that job creation should not be a trade-off with protecting the environment.

“Protecting the environment and helping young people into good work are mutually beneficial and one shouldn’t come at a cost to the other,” said Greenpeace UK’s head of politics, Ami McCarthy. “Companies should be held to account with environmental targets to help achieve a better future without leaving young workers behind.”

Friends of the Earth’s head of campaigns, Rosie Downes, said: “Encouraging companies to create good local jobs is crucial, but it shouldn’t be an either/or with efforts to safeguard our environment.

“Communities are already paying the price of environmental inaction, with the UK on course for record levels of heat-related deaths this summer and our natural world in sharp decline.”

Sarah Williams, the director of strategic partnerships at Green Alliance, said: “The UK is facing a growing youth unemployment crisis, so businesses should be encouraged to create good jobs and opportunities for young people. But scrapping requirements on climate and sustainability is simply not the answer. It’s not an either/or choice.”

The move is also likely to spark concern among anti-trafficking and equality campaigners. A Labour source said the government knew it would face criticism for scrapping some of the current social value indicators.

“What companies have to do at the moment feels too much like a box-ticking exercise and it’s just red tape instead of being useful,” they said. “We are trying to make sure that the government pound is being used to invest in companies that want to invest directly in young people in their areas, and it brings real results and doesn’t just look good on paper.”

Suppliers will be assessed on their commitment to backing British jobs and developing skills, and specifically targeting support for young Neets, care leavers and people with long-term health conditions.

Man charged in Washington state with starting largest wildfire in the area

The Guardian Tue, 04 Aug 2026 20:52:04 GMT

Suspect had a prior conviction for reportedly shooting his father in Arizona, after he told his son to do the dishes

Authorities on Monday charged a man in Washington state with starting a wildfire that has consumed almost 4,000 acres and forced tens of thousands from their homes.

Aaron Farinacci, 37, of Spokane, was arrested and charged with first-degree arson for setting the Old Trails fire, the largest of three devastating wildfires burning through the region.

He was found in possession of waterproof matches and a butane lighter – and was identified by witnesses who spotted him kneeling in grass close to where the blaze began over the weekend.

At a press conference on Monday night, John Nowels, the Spokane county sheriff, said Farinacci had been apprehended quickly.

“As it happens in so many critical cases, it was citizens who were paying attention to their surroundings, being aware and willing to step up and say something that led to the relatively quick apprehension of Mr Farinacci,” Nowels said. “This was fantastic, very quick work by everybody involved.”

Nowels also offered details of the suspect, including that he had a prior conviction in Arizona for manslaughter. According to the Phoenix New Times, the victim was Farinacci’s father, who was shot and killed at their Mesa home in 2010, reportedly after telling his son to do the dishes. Farinacci was later found injured by a self-inflicted gunshot wound.

Farinacci, then aged 21, pleaded guilty in 2012 to manslaughter and aggravated assault. A judge found he was mentally fit to assist in his own defense, though defense lawyer Jose Colon continued to raise questions about his mental health and said that he had been hospitalized multiple times for psychiatric treatment, court records show.

Beth Farinacci, who had married Aaron Farinacci’s father, said second-degree murder, not manslaughter, would have been a more appropriate way to resolve that case.

“Manslaughter is for when someone accidentally kills another person. It is not for someone who intentionally points a loaded gun at their father and shoots him in his face and back,” she wrote in a letter to the judge.

It was also reported that Aaron Farinacci had been contacted by police twice before during fire investigations.

Spokane police responded to reports of several fires on 8 July 2025, near Farinacci’s apartment. The area near the Spokane River involved several “bus-sized” fires and prompted a significant emergency response, according to a police record.

The Washington state patrol made contact with Farinacci the following month while pursuing a suspect in a wildfire at Riverside state park. They found him on a park bench, “seemingly out of breath from possibly running”. They took photos of him. He was wearing a green T-shirt just like the one he was seen wearing on Saturday, the document says.

Farinacci was expected to make his first court appearance Tuesday, Nowels said, as crews continued to battle the fires that have expanded across the county.

The Old Trails fire started Saturday north-west of downtown Spokane. The blaze jumped the Spokane river and ripped through neighborhoods that some residents were able to return to on Monday.

“There’s nothing to save,” said Miriam Sim, 76, as she and her husband, Daniel Sim, surveyed the ruined home where they had lived since 2005.

In one Spokane neighborhood, blackened vehicles, a boat twisted by the heat and melted plastic recycling bins remained. Across the street, lawns were still green and houses were spared, as residents continued to run hoses or sprinklers to water their properties.

More than 67,000 people were told to evacuate the three fires – Old Trail, Autumn Lane and Fairview – that by early Tuesday had burned about 16 sq miles (41 sq km) of Spokane, although orders in some areas were downgraded late on Monday.

Sign up to Breaking News US

after newsletter promotion

Elsewhere across the state, where extreme high temperatures and a fourth year of drought conditions have taken hold, there were at least 15 wildfires burning, covering at least 390 sq miles.

Washington state’s entire congressional delegation wrote to Donald Trump on Monday urging the president to approve an expedited emergency declaration. Bob Ferguson, the state’s Democratic governor, said he spoke to the White House over the weekend after making his own emergency declaration.

“Hundreds of people have completely lost their homes and farms, and many are prohibited from returning to their homes or neighborhoods as crews continue to extinguish smoldering embers,” the politicians’ letter said.

No deaths or major injuries have been reported, although Cpl Mark Gregory, a spokesperson for the Spokane sheriff’s office, said Monday that 14 remained unaccounted for. They were, he said, probably people who had not been in contact since evacuating and were not truly missing or in danger.

More than 1,000 firefighters, many from out of state, arrived by Monday to help tackle the blazes, a number expected to double in the coming days, authorities said. Crews continued to fight the fires by land and air, with Nowels warning the public during the Monday press conference not to interfere with aerial operations by using drones.

A bulletin issued by the National Weather Service (NWS)’s Spokane office on Tuesday morning warned that challenging conditions would persist through the remainder of the week.

“Extensive amounts of smoke will continue over the region, maintaining unhealthy air quality,” it said.

“Dry conditions and breezy winds increase Friday and Saturday across portions of central Washington, bringing elevated fire weather conditions.”

The ECB will not schedule any bilateral cricket against Afghanistan, however, and this summer organised a tour of England for the Afghan Refugee Women’s team, as well as inviting them to the T20 World Cup final at Lord’s. The Afghanistan women players fled the country with the majority relocating to Australia after the Taliban retook control in 2021 and enforced a ban on female sport.

While Afghanistan are the only ICC full member not to operate a women’s cricket programme the world governing body has not banned them. Australia, South Africa, and New Zealand also refuse to play Afghanistan in bilateral series, however, with Ireland joining West Indies, Zimbabwe and the four Asian ICC full members in granting them fixtures.

The ECB’s relationship with Cricket Ireland has been delicate for some time, as England have declined an invitation to join a proposed new Euro Nations Cup tournament also involving Scotland, the Netherlands and Italy next year due to their congested calendar.

The deadly 2025 Eaton fire in the Los Angeles area was caused by equipment belonging to the utility company Southern California Edison, fire officials said in a report released on Tuesday.

Los Angeles county fire officials found that the cause of the fire that killed 19 people and destroyed or damaged more than 9,000 homes and businesses was a tower that was not in service, according to the report.

“After 18 months of thorough review of all evidence, alongside retained electrical and metallurgical experts, the investigation concluded that the cause of the wildfire conflagration was due to the electrical arcing events that took place on the out-of-service Southern California Edison (SCE) tower,” the agency said in a statement.

It took firefighters nearly a month to extinguish the blaze, which scorched 22 sq miles (57 sq km).

Kathleen Dunleavy, a spokesperson for Southern California Edison, said the utility had received the report and was reviewing it.

“We have taken our potential role in the start of this fire seriously from the very beginning,” Dunleavy said. She said SCE previously acknowledged “it was likely our equipment was associated with the ignition of the Eaton fire”.

She said the utility continued to support the community as it recovers.

SoCal Edison has claimed in lawsuits earlier this year that Los Angeles county agencies failed to send timely evacuation warnings to residents in east and west Altadena. Eighteen of the 19 people who died in the fire lived in west Altadena.

The utility also has claimed water agencies, including Pasadena Water and Power, did not provide enough water as the fire spread, leaving firefighters with limited resources. Los Angeles county declined to comment about the latest court filings.

The Los Angeles county arson fire investigation unit jointly conducted the investigation with California department of forestry and fire protection. It found electrical arcing on the utility’s out-of-service tower sparked the dry brush below and that the utility was responsible for maintaining and operating its electrical lines and equipment “in a manner that would minimize the risk of catastrophic wildfire posed by them.”

The blaze was sparked during extreme weather conditions that included high temperatures, low humidity and powerful winds. Two “electrical arcing events” occurred in quick succession, causing an unknown burning material to fall from the tower to the ground below, according to the report.

Within 12 seconds, dry grass and brush was ignited and the fire swiftly developed “into a conflagration engulfing the areas of the San Gabriel Mountains, Altadena, Pasadena, Sierra Madre and La Cañada Flintridge”, the report said. It took more than two weeks to fully contain the wildfire.

The report cites an interview with a Pasadena resident who called 911 on 7 January after spotting flames across the canyon from his home’s rear window. The caller described it “as a 10in x 10in fire at the base of a high-voltage electrical tower”, the report said.

The Eaton fire burned at the same time as the Palisades fire, the most destructive blaze in Los Angeles to date and among the five worst in California’s history. The blaze killed 12 people and destroyed more than 6,800 homes and buildings in Pacific Palisades. The fire ripped through hillside neighborhoods, destroying mansions with spectacular ocean views.

The man accused of sparking the Palisades fire will be tried again this fall after his first federal arson case ended in a mistrial in June. Prosecutors said Jonathan Rinderknecht used a barbecue lighter on 1 January 2025 to spark a blaze that burned undetected deep in root systems before flaring back up 7 January.

Changes to body morphology to improve aerodynamics are banned under International Cycling Union rules. The UCI’s commissaires were looking for padded chest fairings that would artificially improve airflow and reduce wind resistance.

In June the male rider Jan-Willem van Schip was disqualified in a French race for inserting a water bottle into the front of his racing jersey on the basis that it enhanced his aerodynamics and speed.

The UCI directive that selected riders have extra checks before the stage to Dijon came at the instigation of some teams who had noticed changes to rider physiques before time trials.

Stijn Steels, director of the AG Insurance-Soudal team, said he first noticed suspicious padding at the Paris Olympics in 2024. “There was a rider who suddenly had huge breasts,” Steels told the Belgian newspaper Het Laatste News.

“Last year, many riders filled their bust area completely with ice or other items to create a larger volume, which gives a much better aerodynamic effect. It’s only a few watts difference [in power], but a few watts matter a lot in a time trial. It’s possible and it does make a difference, but I wouldn’t risk it.”

Stephen Delcourt, manager of the race favourite Demi Vollering’s FDJ United-Suez team, said: “We never play with the rules like this. If they want to have controls for this, it’s because someone is doing it. Every season everybody does more work in wind tunnels and looks at equipment from the handlebars, the bike, the helmet. But we don’t play with the rules, we are always transparent.”

The former world champion Marianne Vos, teammate to the defending Tour de France champion, Pauline Ferrand-Prévot, supported the clothing checks. “It’s good that they try to enforce the rules,” Vos said. “Everybody is looking for the best aerodynamics, so there are some games. But there are rules to live by.”

In a statement to the teams taking part in the Tour Femmes, the UCI said “particular attention” would be paid to ensure cyclists complied with regulations over “non-essential items or other accessories worn by a rider that could alter their physique”.

Vos said of the checks: “I don’t think it’s really body searching, so I don’t have a problem with it, as long as it’s not too invasive.”

Rolf Aldag, team manager to Kasia Niewiadoma, winner of the Tour Femmes in 2024, saw little difference between the clothing inspections and standard doping controls. “You have to enforce the rules,” Aldag said. “Otherwise, don’t make them. If there’s something to check, then it should be checked. They do that every time they do a doping control. So do we question doping controls?

“If we question it due to the privacy of an athlete, then you have to skip doping controls too, which we all agree that we should not do. It’s the same rule for the men and they would also be checked. I think there’s nothing wrong with that.”

Bert Blocken, professor of aerodynamics, aerospace and mechanical engineering at Scotland’s Heriot‑Watt University, said a chest fairing can alter airflow around the body and reduce aerodynamic drag, allowing riders to conserve energy.

“You don’t gain tens of seconds on a time trial, but over 20-30km, it can make a decisive difference,” Blocken said, adding that it could mean a gain of 0.78 seconds per kilometre.

The UCI’s directive has led to accusations of sexism as no clothing checks were carried out either before, or after, the men’s Tour de France time trial, between Évian‑les‑Bains and Thonon-les-Bains on 21 July.

Roodhooft said: “When you see that the men try things with water bottles placed in strategic spots, then I can imagine that women are thinking about it as well. Still, it’s not good that it happens because it’s still cheating.”

Infantino is steadily losing backing from countries who previously had sent letters to endorse his continuation for a fourth term in charge. It is understood that Greece is the latest federation to have pulled its support, following the lead taken by countries such as England, Wales, Finland and Serbia. More European federations are expected to follow in the coming days, while a number of nations in Concacaf – the North and Central American and Caribbean confederation – are also giving serious consideration to withdrawing their backing.

Prince Ali’s statement, published on X, painted the picture of a small country facing a litany of roadblocks when it came to receiving help from the global governing body. Jordan competed in their first World Cup this year but he explained some of their fans had not received visas, despite purchasing tickets, and expressed anger at being taxed by the US for being based in the country.

Other countries are understood to have been put under concerted pressure to formally back Infantino before the Fifa election in March, although details of how it was applied remain unclear in those cases.

Grafstrom’s email had urged Fifa staff to keep morale high after what was perceived to be a successful World Cup. His message stopped short of criticising Infantino by name and promised to shield colleagues from the strife enveloping their organisation.

“A sad and reproachable series of events – which were thankfully concluded with the FFE project permanently abandoned – for as much as we feel dismayed by them, should not overshadow this reality,” read a section of the email.

He referred to “a turmoil, which is difficult to comprehend and accept” and said: “Individuals, unstable moments and unfortunate episodes come and go. The institution, its mission and its responsibility towards world football continue, and that is why we should always keep our professionalism, sense of perspective and composure.”

Wenger, who assumed his current position in November 2019, confirmed he had been among the many senior Fifa staff sidelined by Infantino’s plan. “I was not involved in this strategic plan and first became aware of the project through media reports,” he said.

“The decision to withdraw the project was absolutely necessary and beyond question, because I firmly believe in an independent Fifa that serves our game with commitment, transparency, and integrity.”

Fifa was contacted for comment regarding Prince Ali’s accusations.

The US and Europe hope a deal is imminent to reopen the strait and they are putting pressure on Oman to accept a temporary agreement that officials in Muscat fear will leave Iran retaining near permanent dominance of the vital oil shipping channel. Ships would enter the strait in a route close to Iran, but leave on a route that passes through Iranian and Omani waters.

But far from being feted over an imminent diplomatic victory, Pezeshkian was instead forced to deny that he had repeatedly offered to resign, verbally and in writing, during a television interview marking his second anniversary in the job.

Pezeshkian accused some of wishing to create a rift inside Iran and said: “If I want to resign, I will officially announce that I have resigned. I will not resign, I will stand.”

The resignation claims, which have been front page news in Iran, were made by Mohammad Bagher Kharazi, who is linked by marriage to Mojtaba Khamenei, the new supreme leader.

He said Pezeshkian had become frustrated at being excluded from decision making, made worse by the supreme leader’s reluctance to reveal his whereabouts for fear of foreign intelligence agencies. Khamenei was badly injured in the Israeli bombing on the first day of the war that killed his father and has not been seen or heard in public since.

Kharazi claimed Pezeshkian had threatened to quit so many times that Khamenei warned him he would accept the next resignation threat, a claim Khamenei’s office eventually said on Tuesday was “fundamentally false and untrue”.

Pezeshkian insisted in the interview that he was in complete harmony with the military and said those that claimed 30,000 people had been killed in the January protests never took up the offer to provide proof.

The interview, marking the halfway point of his turbulent presidency, appeared to be an attempt to dispel the impression that his belief in consensus was a weakness, or that he had been sidelined by hardline war leaders.

Kharazi is the brother-in-law of Massoud Khamenei, the younger brother of the supreme leader. Critics say he has a record of making unsubstantiated allegations and despite his family connections to the supreme leader, it is not clear if he has seen him since his elevation to the post in March.

Mehdi Tabatabaei, a senior member of the Iranian president’s office, described the reports as “complete nonsense and lies”.

He said: “Two years have passed since their failure in the arena of national elections, yet they are still seeking revenge against the will of the nation. They have become puppets of Iran’s enemies.”

BP boss is unsentimental in pruning portfolio and clear on North Sea advice to Burnham

The Guardian Tue, 04 Aug 2026 17:56:21 GMT

Meg O’Neill is overseeing rapid clearing of the decks at BP after strategic muddle of recent years, with ‘message’ for new PM

BP boss urges Burnham to prioritise UK oil and gas

Revealed: major oil firms make $93bn profits amid war and climate crisis

BP will ignore “sentiment” and “history” in pruning its portfolio of assets, says its new-ish boss, Meg O’Neill. She demonstrated as much last week when putting the company’s 60-year-old North Sea oil and gas business up for sale, explaining on Tuesday that “it just doesn’t compete” in the internal battle for capital.

Now comes a disposal that sends an equally unsentimental message about priorities. The US biogas business, Archaea, which was a prized acquisition in the brief green-tinged era of Bernard Looney, is on the block less than four years after BP bought it for $4bn (£2.98bn).

Back in 2022, Looney, O’Neill’s predecessor-but-one, cooed over Archaea, which taps methane from landfill sites. It was “a fantastic fast-growing business” that would add “distinctive value” and “support our net zero ambition”. One hefty write-down later, the operation is judged surplus to requirements because it’s too capital-hungry for a group in debt-reduction mode.

The clearing of the decks at BP is happening quickly after the strategic muddle of recent years. A sale of the solar power unit Lightsource is close but, as with the North Sea assets, it’s not just the green assets that are a target. A major refinery in Gelsenkirchen in Germany has gone. So, too, the Austrian fuel stations. And the sale of the lubricants business Castrol was under way before O’Neill arrived. By the end of the year, reckons BP, it will have reached its target to get net debt below $18bn, 12 months ahead of schedule.

The process will have been massively assisted, of course, by the boom in profits and cashflow that followed the surge in oil and gas profits with the Iran war. BP’s profits more than doubled to $5.73bn in the three months to the end of June.

Cue understandable outrage among campaign groups but zero surprise on the part of City analysts. BP sold its oil at an average of $94 a barrel in the second quarter, up from $67 in the first, enjoying only a slightly smaller increase in the price of natural gas. Profits were obviously going to be enormous, just as they have been at other oil majors. That is doubly so when constraints in the global flow of oil meant refining the stuff – where BP is also big – became a licence to print money in the period.

For O’Neill, the next question from investors will be when she is going to rejoin other majors and restart share buy-backs, which were cancelled in February when the strain on the balance sheet was more acute than it is now. She dodged the question on Tuesday – but shareholders will expect an answer from a straight-talking chief executive soon-ish.

Still, she was clear in the advice she had given to Andy Burnham if the new prime minister wished, as he says he does, to take a “pragmatic” approach to the North Sea.

“The message I left him with was: the UK gets 75% of its energy from fossil fuels today, so that’s oil and natural gas,” O’Neill said. “The first barrel of oil we consume and molecule of natural gas we need should be coming from the UK North Sea, where we generate jobs, we generate tax revenue, we generate all those additional positive impacts.”

That is the case for more (or just more stable) domestic volumes, even as the UK keeps decarbonising: you do it to minimise imports, particularly of liquefied natural gas with its higher associated emissions. The UK’s net import dependency was 43.5% in 2025.

There’s no chance of O’Neill reversing BP’s exit from the North Sea, it seems, but the other implied message in her comments about the competitiveness of the basin wasn’t hard to grasp. If Burnham wants to boost domestic supplies, it won’t be enough just to approve Adura’s Jackdaw and Rosebank fields for production. There will also have to be a rethink on the energy profits levy, AKA the windfall tax that dates from 2022, to incentivise investment.

Politically speaking, it is tricky to lower the level at which windfall rates apply at a moment when the Iran war has created a fresh corporate profits bonanza globally. Burnham has said he was “looking at” the levy. It is one of the unavoidable big choices for October’s budget.

All 173 people have now been returned to Boulogne.

Revealed: major oil firms make $93bn profits amid war and climate crisis

The Guardian Tue, 04 Aug 2026 17:49:16 GMT

Iran conflict windfall over three months reignites calls for companies ‘cashing in on human misery’ to pay for environmental damage

Eight of the biggest oil companies amassed profits of more than $90bn (£67bn) in just three months as the Iran conflict sent energy prices soaring and the emissions-fuelled climate crisis caused deadly heatwaves.

The windfall war profits have reignited calls for oil and gas supermajors such as Saudi Aramco and BP to pay for the environmental damage caused by “cashing in on human misery” and fund a rapid transition to renewable energy.

Guardian analysis found that the eight listed oil producers made almost $93bn (£69bn) in the three months to the end of June – the first full financial quarter after the US-Israeli war on Iran triggered a surge in global oil prices to highs above $126 a barrel.

The companies have used the biggest disruption of fossil fuel supplies in the market’s history to almost double their combined profits from just under $50bn in the same period last year, with campaigners warning that millions of households are left paying the price in higher bills and climate chaos.

The data suggests the eight oil companies – Aramco, BP, Shell, Equinor, TotalEnergies, Eni, Chevron and ExxonMobil – made more than $700,000 of profit every minute over the spring quarter.

While their market valuations were swelling by about $600bn to above $3tn, temperatures built towards a run of deadly heatwaves, all made more likely and more severe by burning fossil fuels.

Carbon emissions from the world’s biggest fossil fuel firms were directly linked to fatal spells of hot weather for the first time by scientific analysis published last September. It found the emissions from any one of the 14 biggest companies were each enough to cause more than 50 heatwaves that would otherwise have been virtually impossible.

The biggest oil profits in the spring quarter were raked in by Saudi Arabia’s state-owned oil company, Aramco, which reported a 34% increase in its quarterly net income to more than $33bn, even as its infrastructure was damaged by drone and missile strikes from Iranian and Houthi forces.

Saudi Aramco’s fossil fuel production has made it responsible for more carbon emissions than any company in history, according to the database Carbon Majors, followed by Chevron and ExxonMobil and with Shell and BP in the top 10. Saudi Arabia has for decades led successful efforts to block and delay international climate action.

On Tuesday, BP became one of the last big oil companies to publish its results for the April to June period, reporting quarterly profits of $5.73bn – the highest since the first year of Russia’s full-scale war on Ukraine and more than double the $2.5bn of the previous three months.

Patrick Galey, the lead on fossil fuels at Global Witness, said: “BP’s sky-high profits are a scandalous reminder of who’s been cashing in on human misery this year. While wildfires threaten communities across the world, drought bites and energy costs spiral, ordinary families are paying the price for big oil’s prioritisation of shareholder wealth over a livable planet.”

He added: “It’s time to make oil giants pay up to repair the climate breakdown they’re driving. Think how many fire and flood defences we could build, or how many solar panels we could install, if big oil paid their fair share in taxes.”

Rosie Downes, the head of campaigns at Friends of the Earth, said: “While BP banks another round of enormous profits, millions of households are paying the price through sky-high energy bills and a climate crisis accelerating rapidly out of control.”

BP’s new chief executive, Meg O’Neill, defended the company’s profits by saying it was “focused on the things we can do to try to help address the situation” such as reliably producing more of the oil products that were in short supply.

The company has been cutting the amount it spends on green energy since it dropped its environmental ambitions in a “fundamental reset” early last year, reducing its annual energy transition budget from $5bn to $1.5bn-$2bn.

In recent years BP has spun off its UK offshore windfarms into a joint venture and sold its US onshore wind business, and on Tuesday it announced it would sell its $4bn US biogas business, which captures methane from landfill sites and is the largest renewable gas producer in the US.

It is in advanced talks to sell its solar power business, Lightsource, to a consortium backed by Kuwait’s sovereign wealth fund, according to the Financial Times.

On Friday, BP put its North Sea oil and gas business up for sale after more than 60 years operating it, reigniting calls for the UK government to rule out the development of two controversial North Sea fields in the ageing basin.

Shell last week reported its second highest quarterly profits ever as its net income jumped to $9.84bn, despite producing less gas from its Qatar gas plant due to billions of dollars’ worth of damage caused by the war. Equinor’s profits climbed to $3.2bn in the same period, up from $1.8bn in the spring quarter last year.

In the US, the profits reported by Chevron and ExxonMobil provoked criticism from Donald Trump. The US president accused the pair of “making too much money” from his war on Iran and warned that they would be made to return profits to the public, as he nears the November midterm elections with flagging approval ratings.

Chevron reported net income of $12.2bn for the second quarter, a more than fivefold increase on the same period last year. ExxonMobil reported a profit of $14.5bn, double what it made in the same period a year ago and its highest quarterly profit since Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine.

Galey said: “You know big oil is taking us for a ride when one of their biggest allies, Donald Trump, is telling them to rein their profiteering in.”

The impacts this summer include Europe’s worst ever heatwave, another categorised by scientists as “impossible” without human-caused global heating. About 20,000 people are estimated to have died due to the extreme temperatures, including close to 3,000 in the UK in May and June alone.

South Korea and Japan have also experienced record-breaking heat of up to 42.5C, with the Korean weather agency instructing people to “immediately stop all outdoor activities”, while the climate crisis pushed up temperatures across much of Africa in July. Global heating makes every heatwave more intense and more likely, and rising global temperatures kill one person a minute around the world, a report in the Lancet estimated in October.

The UN climate chief, Simon Stiell, said: “Around the world, climate-driven disasters are reaching nightmare proportions. What needs to be done is clear: leave coal, oil and gas behind faster, scale up renewables, and protect people where the impacts are already hitting hardest.”

Europe’s succession of heatwaves has sucked soils dry and led to extreme drought, damaging food supplies from maize to sunflowers to salad. At least 9m tonnes of grain are expected to be lost, with the UK, for example, facing its worst harvest on record.

The arid conditions have also enabled huge wildfires in France, Spain, Portugal and Greece, causing billions of euros of damage. The blazes send toxic air pollution soaring and in the US and Canada the fires from 15-23 July are estimated to have caused about 4,000 deaths within a week of exposure. The climate crisis is making fire weather worse and about 1.5 million people a year have their lives shortened by wildfire smoke.

In south Asia, the climate crisis is supercharging extreme rainfall – air that is 1C warmer holds 7% more water. More than 40cm of rain fell in 24 hours in Chattogram in Bangladesh in early July, for example, leading to flash flooding. Floods and landslides have taken lives and livelihoods in Pakistan and India. There have also been dozens of fatalities in north-west China, where many thousands of people have been evacuated due to heavy storms.

The eight oil companies were contacted for comment.

Farmers and landowners are calling for a temporary ban on disposable barbecues in England and Wales, as they warn of the risk of igniting wildfires.

The call, which has also been made by firefighters and is backed by the Liberal Democrats and many Labour MPs, comes as much of England faces further hot dry weather, despite rain in some areas.

The deputy president of the National Farmers Union, Paul Tompkins, said wildfires were an urgent concern as farmers counted the cost of lost or poor harvests caused by record heatwaves supercharged by the climate crisis over the last three months and the worst drought in many areas since 1976. Dry conditions have meant vegetation is much more prone to ignition through carelessness or deliberate fire-starting.

Tompkins said: “A stray match or single spark, and months of hard work can be wiped out in just minutes; crops destroyed and harvest ruined, vital machinery and infrastructure damaged and livestock put at serious risk.

“Beyond the immediate losses, there could be long-term consequences for soil health, grassland productivity and confidence of farm businesses already facing significant pressures.”

He called for retailers to remove disposable barbecues from sale, and for local authorities to issue public space protection orders prohibiting the lighting of barbecues, campfires and camping stoves.

The MP for High Peak in Derbyshire, Jon Pearce, wrote to retailers this week, asking them to stop selling disposable barbecues. Most big supermarkets have already halted sales and some have not sold them for years.

But they are still widely available in smaller shops, from some hardware and DIY stores and online.

Wildfires have affected every region of the UK this year, with more than 20,000 hectares (50,000 acres) estimated to have burned. There have been fires in the Rhondda Valley in Wales this week and the Cairngorms in Scotland last week, while a blaze in Suffolk came within a few miles of the Sizewell B nuclear plant. Fires have been going on for months. Blazes hit the Mourne Mountains in Northern Ireland, areas near Aberdeen, and the Brecon Beacons national park in Wales.

Tompkins also called for more grazing in moorland areas to reduce vegetation, but conservationists are wary of overgrazing in delicate habitats.

Some observers have blamed rewilding for the increasing wildfire risk, a claim rebuffed by experts who said rewilding land could vastly reduce risky conditions. The financier and conservationist Ben Goldsmith pointed to the reintroduction of beavers in some rivers, which has increased the surrounding land’s ability to store water and helped to avoid some of the worst impacts of the drought.

Jones, in an interview with the Guardian, said he had recently launched an inspection of offender tagging, and had seen that the system was coming under strain and needed to be upgraded to “minimise the risk to the public”.

“Some of the systems are pretty clunky and it’s far too reliant on people looking for the information rather than the information being fed or pushed to practitioners as a matter of course,” he said.

“Tagging has potential to improve public perception of victims’ safety. But only if it used properly and if there is a wider system and enough staff to support that. If not, there is a risk that you give false assurances to the public.”

The number of people in England and Wales being electronically monitored has doubled to 28,700 in five years, and the number of newly tagged each year is expected to rise to 22,000 from 2027. Jones said this expansion needed a huge increase in staff to monitor offenders.

An early review of Jones’s inspection, across six regions in England, found:

Probation officers wrongly assuming they would be notified about breaches of exclusion zones, when they were required to conduct a specific search.

Data was not being actively monitored or analysed to reduce risk to the public.

“Significant complexity” was involved in managing the monitoring process, leaving probation officers “overwhelmed and disengaged” by the volume of correspondence.

Jones said: “My concern is this: have the processes and the system kept apace with the number of people being tagged? Because ultimately all tagging gives you is information about where somebody is at a particular point in time. You are relying on having sufficient police officers and probation officers to look at that information and make a decision about how it informs your picture on the activities of that individual.”

Last month the National Audit Office found that the rapid expansion of electronic tagging to reduce pressure on prisons would put public safety at risk unless there were robust improvements.

Jones also called for the government to ensure that there were enough staff in approved premises, which are hostels set up to monitor 2,000 of the most serious offenders when they are first released from prison.

“Our research shows that approved premises work. [They] are extremely effective at managing people after their initial release from custody. What a missed opportunity if those premises cannot remain open because of our insufficient staff,” he said.

After a review of the plans, rapists and serious child sexual offenders, including grooming gang perpetrators, will no longer be eligible for the early release scheme. Alex Norris, the justice secretary, has apologised to families affected, saying they were “carrying the can from previous failures”. He acknowledged the proposals had “created harm” for those grieving, such as the wife of PC Andrew Harper, Lissie.

Hundreds of people living on the slopes of Guatemala’s Fuego volcano have evacuated their homes after a huge eruption spewed lava and plumes of ash.

Central America’s most active volcano erupted on Monday morning, with conditions intensifying by nightfall and prompting authorities to issue the country’s second-most severe alert warning.

By Tuesday, rivers of lava were streaming down the 3,763-metre (12,346-foot) volcano, which is located less than 100 kilometres (62 miles) from Guatemala City. Ash rose six kilometres (3.73 miles) into the red sky.

“Since early morning it was active. That night, the alarm was raised that we needed to evacuate,” a local resident, Alejandro Garcia, 68, told AFP.

Villagers left of their own accord out of fear, Garcia said, describing terrifying scenes of lava tumbling down the mountainside.

Firefighters said they transported at least 350 residents of the El Porvenir and Las Lajitas villages to the eastward San Juan Alotenango municipality.

Evacuees are staying in a community hall, where makeshift beds have been set up, while the number of people taken to other nearby towns remains unknown.

“If there were any chance of moving to a different house, it would be better, because you’re always afraid since the volcano doesn’t give any warning,” Lidia Ortiz, 40, said at the shelter.

Escuintla, to the south, was sheltering dozens more families, including children, local authorities reported.

“If an evacuation is ordered or conditions pose a risk to your life, follow the principle of self-evacuation,” Conred spokesperson Valeria Urizar said in a video posted on social media.

The country’s Institute of Volcanology warned of hot volcanic debris flows down Fuego’s slopes, with communities on the western and southern flanks at the greatest risk.

Fuego had been erupting for 23 hours straight by Tuesday morning, it said, although the intensity was easing.

“We’ve already gotten used to having the volcano constantly active, but this time it was really too much,” 50-year-old resident Sonia Vasquez said.

Guatemalan authorities urged “precautions with air traffic”, but there has so far been no impact on the capital’s international airport.

The education ministry ordered the suspension of face-to-face classes in communities within two municipalities near the volcano.

Traffic police also closed a road encircling the mountain range that connects the south coast with the colonial city of Antigua, the country’s main tourist destination and a Unesco World Heritage site.

Guatemala lies on the Pacific ‘ring of fire’ and experiences frequent seismic and volcanic activity.

There have been several such mass evacuations in recent years because Fuego erupted.

Authorities evacuated more than 500 people last year after Fuego spurted gas and ash, with residents moved to shelters from communities near the crater.

Another eruption in 2023 pushed around 1,200 people to evacuate.

In 2018, 215 people were killed and a similar number left missing when rivers of lava poured down Fuego’s slopes and destroyed a village.

The Guardian view on Burnham and the devolved nations: a test for the new politics in Westminster

The Guardian Tue, 04 Aug 2026 17:30:06 GMT

The prime minister has unveiled his plans for English devolution. The picture in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland is much less clear

After early statements of intent on homelessness and social care, Andy Burnham capped his opening two weeks in office by addressing what one might call the English question. Plans for greater fiscal devolution to England’s mayoral authorities, unveiled last week, are part of what is perhaps the primary raison d’etre of Mr Burnham’s government: the need to rebalance power and resources, in a country where they have been skewed disproportionately towards London and the south-east. As the designated administrative hub of that political project, the creation of No 10 North in Manchester symbolises the ambition.

Beyond England’s borders, however, the picture is much less clear. May’s elections in Scotland and particularly Wales were a disaster for Labour and Mr Burnham’s predecessor, Sir Keir Starmer. Progressive nationalist parties now rule in each of the devolved nations. How the prime minister chooses to engage with them will be a test of the kind of politics of compromise and consensus-building he has said he is committed to.

Early meetings with John Swinney and Rhun ap Iorwerth, the Scottish and Welsh first ministers, have been reported as positive by both sides. But the challenge for Mr Burnham will be how to combine a conviction that power should be devolved as locally as possible, with the need to respect the status and prerogatives of different national administrations. The prime minister has argued that “the people of Dundee and Bangor feel just as distant from Holyrood and the Senedd as they do from Westminster”. That seems like a stretch, but Westminster should not in any case claim the right to bypass the devolved administrations in attempting to solve the problem.

Sir Keir at times adopted precisely that approach, at one point warning ministers against being “overly deferential” to the Scottish and Welsh governments. That didn’t do Labour’s popularity much good in either country. Wales has a population of roughly the same size as Greater Manchester, yet the Welsh government does not, for example, have the powers the mayoral authority does over policing. If Mr Burnham is to be consistent in his devolutionary logic, that kind of anomaly should be addressed.

Inevitably there will be frustrations, rows and disagreements, not least over calls for the Barnett formula funding arrangements to be updated. The Scottish National party, Plaid Cymru and Sinn Féin will all have a powerful motive for taking credit for what goes right, and blaming Mr Burnham’s government when things go wrong. Matters in Wales are further complicated by the minority status of the Plaid government, which Welsh Labour has refused to support and which has yet to succeed in passing a budget.

But Mr Burnham’s direction of travel can be the right one for the devolved nations as well as the English regions. A confidence-building early move would be to repeal contentious powers granted by the post-Brexit United Kingdom Internal Market Act 2020, which allow London to distribute funds across the UK in a variety of policy areas. As the Institute for Government has suggested, Mr Burnham could instead fund the devolved governments to establish their own priorities.

Devolution, and the possibilities it could unleash, were at the heart of Mr Burnham’s rise to Britain’s highest political office. Entirely understandably, his first moves have reflected the regional backdrop to that ascent. He should also follow his instincts in the rest of the United Kingdom.

The Guardian view on 80 years of public funding for the arts: more vital than ever

The Guardian Tue, 04 Aug 2026 17:25:06 GMT

Arts Council England has been much criticised in recent years. A new chair offers hope for a weary cultural sector

“I do not believe it is yet realised what an important thing has happened,” the economist John Maynard Keynes wrote in The Listener in July 1945. “Patronage of the arts has crept in. It has happened in a very English, informal, unostentatious way – half baked if you like.” He was referring to the wartime Council for the Encouragement of Music and the Arts (Cema), which would become the Arts Council of Great Britain. Keynes died a few months before it was granted a royal charter on 9 August 1946. A body to secure and distribute government cultural investment was created – an important thing, indeed.

The Arts Council initially funded 46 institutions, including the Royal Opera House and Bristol Old Vic, the first publicly funded regional theatre in the UK. Over eight decades it has contributed to the making of world-renowned treasures such as the Southbank Centre and Royal Shakespeare Company. Today it supports nearly 1,000 organisations from the Proms to Glastonbury, local libraries, comedy venues and community arts centres, as well as individual artists. In 1994 it was devolved into national councils. This week Dawn Airey, the former head of Channel 5, took over as chair of Arts Council England (ACE) from Sir Nicholas Serota.

Given the Arts Council’s fundamental dependence on the economy and political will, it is no surprise that his nearly decade-long tenure was turbulent. Under the Conservatives, ACE’s budget was reduced by about 30%. As Sir Nicholas put it in an introduction to Made in England, a collection of essays marking its 80th anniversary, the health of the culture sector relies on “one sobering, practical reality … money”.

In recent years, ACE has been accused of crippling bureaucracy, favouring grassroots organisations over prestigious establishments, and straying from Keynes’s foundational “arm’s length” principle. “The Arts Council is not altogether on our side,” John Gilhooly, the director of the Wigmore Hall, told the BBC. It pulled out of the Arts Council last year. English National Opera and other classical music organisations suffered major budget cuts in 2022. Contrary to ACE’s promise to take high-quality culture to “every corner of the country”, cuts to Glyndebourne resulted in the cancellation of its 2023 tour.

Let’s Create, the controversial strategy set up in 2020 to diversify and redistribute funds outside London, was blamed for many of these problems. It was scrapped in response to last year’s critical Arts Council review by the former Labour arts minister Lady Margaret Hodge, who accused it of stifling “innovation and creativity”. But inclusive ambitions should not be abandoned with the red tape. Access and excellence are not mutually exclusive.

For all its shortcomings, Lady Hodge concluded that the Arts Council “remains a vital national body”. It is even more important in times of austerity: without public funding, many institutions would not survive. With a new chair – and a new prime minister – this is a moment of hope for a weary creative sector. A petition by Campaign for the Arts urges Andy Burnham to follow the example of Clement Attlee’s Labour government, which established the Arts Council “from the rubble of the second world war”, to make “arts and culture an integral part of their plan to rebuild the nation”. There is much to be done before the Arts Council celebrates its 100th birthday. Without Keynes’s “half baked” scheme, England would be much poorer, in every sense.

Labour members ‘have tougher view on welfare than you might think’, poll suggests

The Guardian Tue, 04 Aug 2026 17:17:38 GMT

Survey finds party members see health, the economy, cost of living and climate crisis among biggest challenges

Andy Burnham has inherited a Labour membership that is sceptical about increased welfare spending, supportive of higher defence spending, and ranks the climate crisis as one of the country’s biggest challenges, according to new polling.

The survey of 788 members between the end of June and the end of July shows them ranking health (43%), the economy (42%), cost of living (39%) and climate change (29%) as Britain’s most important issues, ahead of welfare benefits (7%) and immigration (6%).

Despite the internal rows within the parliamentary Labour party (PLP) on welfare spending and general public pushback, 47% of members surveyed by ThinkLabour believe the government is spending too much on welfare, compared with 21% who believe it does not spend enough. When asked whether they would prefer the government to fund its current welfare bill differently, 52% said taxes should be raised. Additionally, 70% of Labour members said only high earners should be taxed while 24% supported higher taxes on everyone to fund the current bill.

The survey reveals members overwhelmingly backed more spending on social care, with 73% saying the government should spend more on this through higher taxes, either on higher earners alone or through general taxation. It found 68% of members wanted Britain to spend more on defence, and among the supporters for higher defence spending, 61% backed paying for this through higher taxes.

Three-quarters of Labour’s members said they had backed Keir Starmer in the 2020 party leadership contest. The survey did not ask members about Burnham’s leadership. However, a poll conducted just before Starmer’s disastrous local elections performance revealed Burnham had a net favourability of 72% among members at that time, suggesting he would be likely to win any leadership contest he could have fought in. Burnham won the leadership unopposed within the PLP so a vote from party members was not required.

The data is likely to be watched by those in government and it is understood these findings have been shared with senior strategists in Downing Street.

ThinkLabour, formerly known as Labour Together, has become increasingly linked to Burnham’s premiership. The former CEO Alison Phillips recently left the thinktank to become the prime minister’s deputy chief of staff, alongside the former director of devolution JP Spencer, who is now working in No 10 North. Ed Owen, a former Labour adviser during the Blair administration, is the interim CEO.

Christabel Cooper, ThinkLabour’s interim director of political strategy, said: “Labour members have a tougher view on welfare than you might think. They will be aware that welfare is something the Labour government has to get right if it is going to win a second term. And they also understand the importance of defence in a deeply uncertain world.

The Guardian Tue, 04 Aug 2026 17:15:04 GMT

Partner of woman killed by dangerous driver among those who say they are devastated at killers leaving jail early

When Calvin Buckley, whose pregnant partner was killed by a dangerous driver in 2023, secured a tougher sentence for the man who took her life, he felt some justice had been served. Now, under plans to release prisoners early to ease overcrowding, Adil Iqbal, who filmed himself speeding at 123mph before he crashed into 38-year-old Frankie Jules-Hough, may serve less time in prison than he would have under his original sentence.

“He could actually serve less time than he originally was going to before we appealed,” Buckley said. “We’ve fought for a tougher sentence. What is the point of having an actual sentence if the government can just reduce that?”

Victims and bereaved family members who fear perpetrators could be released early under government plans to free up prison space say they are deeply concerned at the prospect of dangerous offenders walking the streets.

Gemma Chappell, the great-aunt of Maya Chappell, who was shaken to death aged two by her mother’s boyfriend in 2022, said the early release scheme was further traumatising bereaved families.

Maya’s mother, Dana Carr, was sentenced to nine years in prison after being found guilty of child cruelty by neglect and allowing her child’s death, but Chappell has been told she is set to be released early under the scheme.

“I think it’s terrible. I think victims are not being heard. We should be allowed to grieve, we should be allowed to have our trauma,” she said.

Chappell said it was “ridiculous” that Carr had made no admission of guilt and applied to have her sentence reduced, which was denied, but was now set to be released early anyway due to overcrowding.

She said she welcomed Andy Burnham’s intervention to exempt rapists, serious child sexual abuse offenders and those convicted of grooming from the early release plans but said it didn’t go far enough.

“There’s still victims and families out there who remain deeply concerned about these dangerous offenders getting out early, and we’re one of them. Justice should always be about public safety and the victim’s voice first,” she told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme.

A former prison officer, Chappell said she wanted the government to invest more money in prison buildings instead. “Letting serious offenders out on to the street is not the answer,” she said. “We need some clarity on what’s going to happen if these offenders do get out because this affects our lifetime, not just the next couple of months.”

Buckley said he was devastated to find driving offenders would not be exempted from the plans. “To kill somebody and to have your [prison] sentence reduced is just not right. Our justice has been taken away,” he told BBC Breakfast.

“I understand there is a crisis, I agree that it needs to be addressed, but not at the expense of victims. For me it is another example of road victims not being treated the same as other offences.”

Iqbal was originally sentenced to 12 years for killing Jules-Hough and her unborn child, Neeve. This was increased to 15 years by the court of appeal under the unduly lenient sentence scheme.

Buckley said he was told Iqbal would serve a minimum of two-thirds of his original 12-year sentence – eight years – in prison. But under the new plans he could be eligible for release after half of his 15-year sentence, or seven and a half years.

The government has also been criticised for its decision not to exempt domestic abuse perpetrators from the early release scheme.

Alice Russell-Harris, the public affairs lead at Refuge, said the organisation was “deeply alarmed” and that the move would “put many domestic abuse survivors at risk”.

She said releasing domestic abusers early would “heighten survivors’ fears for their safety” and the charity was aware that perpetrators “frequently breach conditions to continue their campaign of abuse”.

The family of PC Andrew Harper, who was killed while responding to a report of a burglary in 2019, said they were devastated to learn two of the men jailed for his death would still be eligible for release.

Harper was killed after being dragged behind a car for a mile. Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers, who were passengers in the car and sentenced to 13 years for manslaughter, could apply for early release after serving half of their sentences.

“I count myself lucky though. There were other victims whose lives he had totally destroyed,” she added. She said she felt sick reading commentators who were defending the selection.

Bonehill-Paine, the creator of the viral Crewkerne Gazette series of AI clips, is due to stand for election to Somerset council next year.

He told the Guardian on Monday that he was an executive member of the Tories’ Yeovil branch, working as an events organiser, and has carried out counter-extremism work since he was released from prison.

Badenoch said on Tuesday that she was not recruiting neo-Nazis to the Conservative party and that Bonehill-Paine was certified by the Home Office to train police officers on antisemitism and on countering extremism.

She added: “Yes, he is somebody who had been previously convicted for this, but he is someone who has shown contrition for his crimes, has been rehabilitated and is spending every day working to solve the very problem which he knew he had caused previously.

“He’s going up and down the country training people and the Conservative party believes in second chances.”

But there was criticism from the Board of Deputies of British Jews, Labour and others who contrasted Badenoch’s support for Bonehill-Paine with the freezing out of centrist Tories. Former Tory minister Gavin Barwell last month lost the whip after warnings from Badenoch that supporters of policies such as targets for net zero were no longer welcome in the party while former defence secretary Grant Shapps was recently blocked from standing again for the party.

Karen Newman, vice-president of the Board of Deputies of British Jews, told HuffPost: “It beggars belief that any party would select as a candidate a multiply convicted felon and the founder of a far-right group called National British Resistance.”

“We have contacted the Conservative party to set out our concerns and call on them to rescind his selection and review their vetting processes.”

Bonehill-Paine re-emerged in recent years as the creator of the Crewkerne Gazette, a satirical online account, and has a conviction for assaulting a police officer and burglary of a police station. He was convicted in 2014 of malicious communications over an anti-Islam hoax that led to death threats against the owners of a pub in Leicester.

He was jailed in 2015 for more than three years after posting antisemitic material online ahead of a planned neo-Nazi rally. In 2016, he was found guilty of racially aggravated harassment of Berger, who is Jewish.

The abuse directed at her was cited by the Jewish Labour Movement, which described Bonehill-Paine’s selection by the Tories as “appalling”.

Bonehill-Paine has meanwhile hit back at Reform UK after its leader, Nigel Farage, joined in the criticism of the Conservatives. An image of an email in which Reform thanked him for applying to be a party candidate and informed him that he had passed vetting checks was shared on X by Bonehill-Paine.

He also provided evidence indicating that the chair of Reform’s Yeovil branch had written to him as recently as June to ask if he would like to meet to discuss the prospect of standing for the party.

A Reform UK spokesperson said: “There’s a reason why Mr Bonehill-Paine wasn’t selected as a Reform UK candidate. Meanwhile, while Kemi Badenoch claims to have a new generation of Tory candidates and says she supports the fight against antisemitism, she is selecting a convicted antisemite to stand for the Conservatives. The hypocrisy is breathtaking.”

Rod Liddle obituary

The Guardian Tue, 04 Aug 2026 16:44:21 GMT

Provocative journalist whose invective-laden columns targeting the liberal-left were laced with an ebullient humour

If the first rule of column writing is to be read and the second and third to be interesting and provocative, the journalist Rod Liddle, who has died aged 66 after a short illness, certainly met the bill.

His columns in the Sunday Times, the Spectator and the Sun, and his Saturday morning shows for Times Radio, gave his fans, mainly on the political right, all they needed to fulfil their prejudices, laced with a satirical edge and verve. He could fill the 2,500-seater London Palladium, as he once did for his conversational show.

A tousled and dishevelled figure, shirt flapping open, Liddle’s iconoclastic targets in recent years have included bureaucrats, politicians, “thought police”, campaigners for gay and trans rights and, above all and constantly, the supposed politically correct, liberal-left elite alleged to be undermining the stolid, respectable working classes, leaving them feeling left behind and ignored.

The columns regularly became boisterously laden with invective moderated by an ebullient, wrecking-ball humour and were the subject of regular complaints by those who did not see the joke.

Welsh nationalists were “miserable, seaweed munching, sheep bothering, pinch-faced hill tribes” and grievance groups indulged in “furious yapping”; others were waxen-skinned spaffgoblins. The alleged sacking of the old order had “left us fraught and clamorous, unhappy, isolated and averse”, never mind that some of his readers espousing such views were inflamed and confirmed in their opinions precisely by his prose.

The one person to whom he felt he owed an apology was the Labour politician Harriet Harman for a crude snub, saying that he had not thought how the remarks would affect her. Liddle was the first journalist to be censured for a blog by the Press Complaints Commission in 2010 after alleging that the majority of violent crime in London was carried out by “young men from the African-Caribbean community”.

It was an irony that some of his most ardent fans were among those he had mocked in regular columns for the Guardian for more than three years between 1999 and 2003. When in 2002 he had derided conservative members of the Countryside Alliance who had demonstrated against the Blair government as “angry ruddy-faced people”, going on to say “you may have forgotten why you voted Labour in 1997 but then you catch a glimpse”, he was condemned by the Telegraph and the Sun, which he would subsequently go on to write for.

Liddle was born in Sidcup, Kent, into a respectable, church-going family, the son of Margaret (nee Clee), who worked for the then Department of Health and Social Security, and Edwin, who came from a north-east family of railway workers but was himself an Inland Revenue clerk. They moved back up north when Liddle was eight to the Middlesbrough “select” suburb of Nunthorpe, a description that he later characteristically described as like saying “a select suburb of Mogadishu”.

He was educated at the Laurence Jackson comprehensive school and Prior Pursglove sixth form college, undergoing as he did so a rite of passage as a punk, a sartorial style that never completely left him, and briefly joining the Socialist Workers party. Canvassing for Labour at the 1983 general election, he claimed his appearance must have cost Labour 5,000 votes.

Liddle joined the South Wales Echo as a journalist, and then moved to London to study social psychology at the London School of Economics and worked as a researcher for the Labour party before joining the BBC as a trainee producer.

In 1998 he was made editor of the Today programme on Radio 4 and became perhaps the first to be widely known beyond the corporation. He undoubtedly made the previously rather cosy programme sound more aggressive and competitive, with more use of investigative journalism, and increased its audience figures accordingly.

It was under his watch in 2003 that the BBC was engulfed in a furious row with the Blair government over allegations that a dossier alleging that the Iraqi government was preparing weapons of mass destruction had been “sexed up” as a pretext in advance of the Iraq war – a story that led to the suicide of the weapons expert David Kelly, who had been the unwitting source of the reporter Andrew Gilligan.

Liddle defended the programme and the BBC vigorously in columns for the Guardian against the government and other newspaper attacks, reserving deepest scorn for Peter Mandelson, whose briefings he claimed had heightened the row.

It was Liddle’s increasingly outspoken columns for the paper that goaded the corporation into requiring that he either gave them up or left the BBC. Choosing the latter course, he soon found himself in demand by the Sunday Times and others for his pugnacious commentaries, delivered professionally on time and to length. A novel and books of his writing followed, including Selfish Whining Monkeys in 2014 and The Great Betrayal (2019), stating why in his view the Brexit referendum vote had been undermined by, naturally, the liberal elite and politicians.

While at the BBC in 1993, Liddle began a relationship with Rachel Royce, a reporter, whom he married in a ceremony in Malaysia in 2004. The relationship had already produced two children, Tyler and Wilder, but Liddle left the honeymoon early to his wife’s fury when she discovered he had done so to continue his affair with Alicia Monckton, a receptionist at the Spectator magazine who was half his age. Following the divorce from Royce, Liddle married Monckton in 2008 and the couple had a daughter, Emmeline.

Alicia and the three children survive him.

Roderick Edwin Liddle, columnist and broadcaster, born 1 April 1960; died 2 August 2026

The disgraced former BBC presenter Huw Edwards has been criticised after entering a Welsh poetry competition under a pseudonym.
