Edwards was given a six-month suspended sentence in September 2024 for accessing indecent images of children as young as seven.

In a Substack post on Sunday, Edwards wrote that he had entered the poem to a competition run by the National Eisteddfod of Wales festival on the theme of adnabod, meaning “knowing”. He describes the poem as a tribute to his late father, who was a historian of the National Eisteddfod.

Entrants to the Eisteddfod poetry competition are required to submit under a pseudonym, with winners’ identities only revealed upon announcement. Edwards entered the poem under the pseudonym “Y Gelyn”, meaning “The Enemy” in English. The former BBC journalist Martin Huws was announced as this year’s winner of the competition, receiving £750, for a poem about abuse.

Cracroft, who has spoken publicly about being sexually assaulted as a child, also called on the competition’s organisers to review rules regarding entrants using a pen name.

“We have a process in place which ensures nobody, including the judges, know beforehand who has competed,” said the National Eisteddfod in a statement. “After each Eisteddfod, we have a period of appraisal to ensure our processes are appropriate – this year will be no exception.”

Cracroft said it was “far too soon for him [Edwards] to try and redeem himself”.

In his Substack post, Edwards wrote that “one of the most distressing episodes in 2024 was seeing the nature of my relationship with my father wilfully misrepresented by the media”.

In reports cited in sentencing remarks by the chief magistrate, Paul Goldspring, consultant psychiatrist Michael Isaac wrote that Edwards’s father was “perceived as behaving monstrously within the family” and that the former BBC presenter’s relationship with his father was “probably damaging psychologically”.

“The poisonous narrative encouraged by the press two years ago needed correcting,” Edwards wrote in a statement reported by the BBC. “There was no way on earth I was going to win the competition and I knew that.”

On Cracroft’s remarks, he added: “This wasn’t a poem for the sickeningly self-righteous Welsh speakers – [Cracroft] amongst them – who take advantage of every opportunity to speak unthinkingly on every subject under the sun. She and her type are far too willing to ignore the damaging effects of mental ill health. In that, they are loyal to the heritage of London’s tabloid papers.”

The National Eisteddfod of Wales did not respond to a request for comment from the Guardian.

Skip the run: here are six joint-friendly cardio alternatives suggested by experts

The Guardian Tue, 04 Aug 2026 16:07:18 GMT

Whether you’re nursing a joint, have an existing condition or just don’t feel like running, these exercises help get your cardio in

The runner’s high might be contagious. In 2024, fitness tracking app Strava recorded a 59% increase in users attending social running events and run clubs globally. Applications for London’s marathon have increased 40% since 2024, while New York City’s received about 20% more applicants this year. Overall, an estimated 56 million Americans regularly run on a treadmill and 51 million jog, according to a report from the Sports and Fitness Industry Association.

But running has a reputation for being rough on our joints. There is some good news for those chasing the high: one 2023 study found little relationship between recreational running and arthritis of the hip or knee, and another suggests that the impact of running causes cartilage to adapt, fortify and thicken over time.

However, for those with existing joint issues, other cardio activities may be better alternatives. Here’s what experts say about running, joint health and good alternatives.

Running is a full body activity, but some areas are more affected by it than others.

“Most people come in with knee issues,” said Lauren Borowski, a primary care sports medicine specialist at NYU Langone’s Sports Medicine Center. Pain in the hips, ankles, feet and low back are also common.

“When running, you’re essentially landing in a single leg squat, and it’s a lot of repetitive pressure. It’s three to four times your body weight in every step,” Borowski said. “When the muscles are not ready to receive the extra weight, [the impact goes] more directly to the bones and the cartilage.”

“Unhealthy” joints can show up as a variety of things. Injuries such as a torn meniscus in the knee, hamstring strains, ankle sprains, Achilles tendinitis, shin splints, plantar fasciitis and stress fractures can make running painful. So can “osteoporosis or osteoarthritis, where the bone tissue is starting to break down”, said Dr M Claire Coopes-Meske at Good Reps Physical Therapy.

With conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis or arthritis related to inflammatory bowel disease, there is “a lot of known inflammation that’s attacking [the] cartilage”, Borowski said. Broken down cartilage further exposes the bone to stress.

Some pains are legitimate cause for concern and need attention from a healthcare provider. Alexis Colvin, orthopedic surgeon at Mount Sinai hospital and the chief medical officer of the US Open, recommends seeing a doctor sooner rather than later “if the knee is swollen or the pain is really persistent even after a day or two and it’s affecting their regular activity” – or if you are constantly taking painkillers to try to mitigate the pain.

Motion is healing and essential for healthy joints, said Coopes-Meske. “Any time we’re moving a joint, [synovial] fluids are released into the joint space that provide nutrition and lubricate the joint.”

Additionally, diversifying your exercise is essential for general health. Borowski recommends focusing on four categories: strength training, for the muscles; cardio respiratory exercise, which strengthens the heart and lungs; balance work; and mobility and flexibility training.

Sign up to Well Actually

Practical advice, expert insights and answers to your questions about how to live a good life

after newsletter promotion

If the impact of running is inhibitive for you, experts recommend the alternatives below to help you dodge physical stress on your bones and cartilage:

Cycling: If the knee cannot withstand the impact of running, biking is an option. “It’s a really great tool for range of motion,” Borowski said. Cycling stimulates the production of synovial fluids and allows for a range of leg extension. Coopes-Meske pointed out that people can adjust the resistance, speed and distance to vary workload. Increasing these measures requires more from muscles without the additional stress of impact on the joints.

Rowing: Rowing is also great for those who are looking to avoid joint impact but may not be ready for weight bearing exercises. It offers a greater range of motion than cycling, depending on how much your knee can bend. If your range is limited, modifications are available. For instance, on a rowing machine, you can adjust how much your knees are bent in the starting position and how much you straighten them when driving your seat back, making for a shorter stroke.

“The intensity, resistance and speed can also be adjusted based on their capabilities as well,” Coopes-Meske said. Rowing requires a lot of work from the hips, core and upper body, so its benefits go beyond the legs.

Swimming: For those with bone or cartilage issues that experience a lot of swelling, swimming is a great cardio option, said Coopes-Meske. It’s a full body workout and puts minimal stress on the joints. It’s excellent for building lung capacity and heart strength, and there’s an added bonus for swollen joints: “The hydrostatic pressure from the water can help push the swelling out of that area,” she said.

It doesn’t do much for bones or muscles, or from a strength standpoint, because water doesn’t provide much resistance, said Borowski: “But it’s great for mobility and range of motion of those joints.”

Incline walking: Incline walking reduces load on the joints while increasing heart rate. Unlike swimming, cycling and using the rowing machine, walking is a load-bearing exercise because you’re supporting your bodyweight against gravity while on your feet. “We still want to load those bone tissues, because the body starts to rebuild those areas and help build up the bone as well,” Coopes-Meske said.

Load-bearing exercises are important because the physical stress stimulates bone-forming cells to produce new bone tissue. This increases their density, which can slow age-related bone density loss and help with osteoporosis. “We still want to load those bone tissues, because the body starts to rebuild those areas and help build up the bone as well,” Coopes-Meske said.

Walking, however, avoids the harsh impact of running, and doing it at an incline gets your heart rate up quicker. Depending on whether you are using a treadmill or walking outdoors, you can also adjust the speed and incline depending on your symptoms, capabilities and the terrain.

Rollerblading, ice skating or cross-country skiing: Booted activities such as rollerblading, ice skating and cross-country skiing can be good alternatives for those with injured or weak ankles. “The boots come up much higher on your ankle, providing extra support,” said Coopes-Meske. Running and walking both involve heel strikes – the initial contact your heel makes with the ground. These activities eliminate the impact from heel strikes and focus on continuous gliding motion. They are great for strengthening the glute muscles, hamstrings and quadriceps, and deliver a full body workout with minimal stress on the knees and ankles.

Other options: As long as you are diversifying your movement and covering the four buckets Borowski referenced, many cardio alternatives are suitable. For instance, Latin, hip hop, house or ballroom dance classes and Zumba. (Skip ballet, which can involve high-impact leaping.) Be mindful of how much jumping is involved in any of these options, but there are typically lower-impact modifications for these movements. They are a great way to get your cardio in, mix it up and have fun.

Social care is for us all, and we all must fund it

The Guardian Tue, 04 Aug 2026 16:02:26 GMT

Readers respond to Polly Toynbee’s article on the new prime minister’s commitment to a fair system

Polly Toynbee (Battles loom over social care, but this fight must be won. At last, we have a PM who believes that, 29 July) is right that reforming England’s broken social care system will require winning the “attention, hearts and minds” of a public that knows little about it. Yet one of the biggest barriers to reform is that social care itself remains widely misunderstood, and public debate often reinforces narrow assumptions about who uses it.

Social care is too often equated with care homes and dementia services for older people. While these are vital, they are one part of a wider system. Demand has grown fastest among working-age disabled adults who are largely missing from the public and political narrative. As such, the assertion by Polly Toynbee that “the old must pay for the old” is incorrect. Social care is relied on by people of all ages.

Public debate not only misunderstands who uses social care, it often overlooks what social care makes possible. Social care should enable people to live independently, sustain relationships, take part in education and employment, and contribute to their communities. At its best, it is not simply about meeting needs but about creating the conditions for people to live full and meaningful lives.

Most people will need care, provide care, or both, during their lives. Only when society understands the scope, value and reach of social care will meaningful reform become politically possible. Dr Louise LawsonLecturer in social policy, University of Glasgow

Polly Toynbee asks: “Why do we endure this barely regulated, barely inspected patchwork of confusion” that constitutes Britain’s social care “system”? There are two main reasons. First, care provision has been regarded by governments as a domestic responsibility, overwhelmingly women’s work.

This patriarchal assumption was built into the welfare state from birth. The strain that this has placed on generations of, again mainly women, has been documented. Yet, the state has held firm in believing that providing support risks the family giving up caring. Research, including my own, has shown this assumption to be entirely false.

Second, we live in a deeply ageist society. Ageism “others” older people and diminishes their worth. Ageism allows the endless annual toll of cold-related deaths, and now heat-related ones.

This scandal has persisted long enough, but now there is a prime minister who appears to understand why social care is so important and why it is in such a parlous state. Alan WalkerProfessor of social policy and social gerontology, University of Sheffield

I’m in my 70s and my one concern is being able to pay for care that I may need as I get older. I live in a modest house and have a small amount of savings, so I know that this money could soon run out if I ever needed care later in life. I would love to have the peace of mind knowing that I would get care even if it meant paying a percentage of my estate on death or increased taxes.

It would salve so many worries for people who don’t want to be a burden on their children and to know that they can at least pass on some inheritance. If for some reason you don’t need care then you’ll have been lucky, but at the moment it’s so unfair that your care depends on wealth, where you live and the type of illness you have. I really hope Andy Burnham gets this sorted. Janet TouheyNewark, Nottinghamshire

North Sea oil is a litmus test for Burnham

The Guardian Tue, 04 Aug 2026 15:58:03 GMT

John Barstow says oil expansion is a necessity, while David Parker wonders if the prime minister will protect the planet or the fossil fuel industry

North Sea oil expansion is a necessity (Burnham risks first revolt as PM over apparent support for North Sea drilling, 31 July). I state this as an environmentalist – not despite. Oil is a feedstock, not mere fuel. Oil is necessary for the day-to-day maintenance of wind turbines, nuclear plants and rail. Hence oil is part and parcel of supply chains for green tech. A domestic oil base brings such supply chains closer. This also underscores the case for approval of coking coal extraction in Cumbria. Green tech needs high-grade steel and high-grade steel needs coking coal.

There are much better ways of helping the environment, such as more tree planting and stopping plastic waste being dumped into our seas. The carbon sink factor would be helped. A major expansion of the UK’s North Sea oil sector will make a more cohesive UK, complete with more jobs in Scotland and the north of England, including in supply manufacturing chains.

On these grounds, the full approval of North Sea oil expansion is an absolute litmus test of Andy Burnham’s credibility given his talk of reindustrialising. John BarstowFittleworth, West Sussex

Burnham’s avowed pragmatism appears to be disappointingly deficient as far as North Sea oil is concerned. His pragmatic antennae should be telling him that new drilling will bring insignificant gain in exchange for a considerable dent in the renewed optimism and the support which he has so far generated.

Rightly or wrongly, he will be perceived to have bowed to the oil and gas lobby, which is intent on burning the planet. He is reported as saying: “The question isn’t whether Britain will still be using oil and gas, the question is where does it come from.” Wrong. The question is which side is our prime minister on and seen to be on: the planet’s or that of the fossil fuel industry?David ParkerHolmfirth, West Yorkshire

Scrapping foreign doctors scheme will hurt the NHS

The Guardian Tue, 04 Aug 2026 15:54:07 GMT

The move is regressive and removes a successful route for international collaboration, including education and research, writes Dr Peter Trewby

The decision to abolish the medical training initiative (MTI) scheme (Medical colleges condemn scrapping of NHS placements for overseas doctors, 31 July) risks reversing years of progress in medical diplomacy and repeating earlier mistakes in the UK’s treatment of international medical graduates (IMGs).

In the early 2000s, in response to perceived workforce shortages, the government actively recruited IMGs and established a new GMC exam centre to process applicants at scale. Thousands came to the UK, but the number of available posts was insufficient. The government responded by ending the permit-free visa, which had allowed IMGs to work in the UK, so doctors could now only apply for posts when no UK graduate had applied, regardless of relative merits. International exchanges built over decades ended abruptly.

Following strong lobbying by the medical royal colleges, the MTI scheme was introduced to allow suitably qualified doctors to come to the UK for a maximum of two years before returning home. The scheme benefited the UK, the NHS, international graduates and UK trainees, while also serving as an effective example of UK soft power.

Abolishing the scheme removes a successful route for international collaboration, including education and research, and risks signalling again that nationality takes precedence over merit. For an NHS that prides itself on its inclusivity, this is a serious regression. Dr Peter TrewbyRetired consultant physician and former director, international medical graduates, Royal College of Physicians

UK Sport withdraws funding from GB Snowsport for next Olympic cycle amid governance review

The Guardian Tue, 04 Aug 2026 15:34:15 GMT

Organisation has lost second chair in three years

UK Sport commits record £33m funding for winter sports

UK Sport has withdrawn all funding from GB Snowsport for the next Olympic cycle, after commissioning an independent review into the organisation’s governance.

The news comes just six months after Team GB recorded their most successful Winter Olympics at Milano-Cortina and at the same time as record levels of funding were confirmed for British winter sport and parasport athletes before the Alpes 2030 Games.

UK Sport has guaranteed £12.5m to fund coaches and athletes across ski and snowboard events, and their Paralympic equivalents, over the next four years. This is the largest share of a total pool of £33m for winter sports, ahead of the £10.1m guaranteed to bobsleigh and skeleton. But while UK Sport said it wanted to assure athletes of “our full commitment to them ahead of Alpes 2030”, a new funding mechanism outside of GB Snowsport is yet to be confirmed, with an announcement expected before the end of the year.

“The UK Sport Board has decided not to route the investment for snowsport through GB Snowsport once funding for the Milan Cortina cycle ends,” a statement from the funding body said. “UK Sport has written today to all funded snowsport athletes to make them aware of this decision, to affirm our full commitment to them ahead of Alpes 2030 and to commit to continue paying athletes grants directly into the new cycle whilst we address these challenges. Separately, UK Sport will be commissioning an independent review into the governance of GB Snowsport.”

GB Snowsport has changed chair twice in the past three years, with Michael Osterlin – a non-executive director at the organisation – currently operating in the role in an interim capacity. The body said it was “disappointed” at the funding decision and while they promised to continue to work with UK Sport on governance matters, “we reserve the right to keep all options open to ensure that the achievements of the past four years are not lost as we approach another European Games.”

In a statement released to the Guardian, GB Snowsport also said it had already completed another independent review into governance within the organisation. “We have recently concluded an independent governance review funded by UK Sport, which has confirmed that our governance standards remain strong and appropriate,” it said. “We look forward to engaging fully and robustly in any new review, which we are confident will reach the same conclusions.”

UK Sport also confirmed the creation of a “specialist, multisport performance delivery organisation”, to be known as Sport Org, which will take over the running of elite programmes in certain sports. The curling and wheelchair curling programme is already operated by Sport Org and it has been announced that the British Bobsleigh and Skeleton Association will transfer its programmes to the new vehicle before Utah 2034. In 2022 Joanna Poulton resigned as the BBSA chair over plans to create an organisation along the lines of Sport Org, calling it “laughable” and “naive”.

The director of performance and people at UK Sport, Dr Kate Baker, said: “Competition across Olympic and Paralympic winter sport is only getting stronger, which is why it’s more important than ever that we invest where we can have the biggest impact. It is also why we are not afraid of driving the change needed to give our athletes the very best chance of success. The investments we are announcing today, alongside the reform we are driving in the system, will enable us to do exactly that.”

In further funding news Ice Hockey UK is to receive £445,000 to help support the sport’s planned transition into a more commercially sustainable form. UK Sport says this is the first funding of its kind in the country.

Elon Musk’s X latest to block Saudi dissident accounts inside kingdom

The Guardian Tue, 04 Aug 2026 15:20:21 GMT

Exclusive: More than 60 accounts on X have been made unavailable in Saudi Arabia, after similar action on Snapchat and Facebook

Elon Musk’s X has become the latest major US social media company to block the accounts of Saudi Arabian dissidents so they are no longer visible inside the kingdom, following orders from Saudi authorities.

Earlier this year, the Guardian reported that platforms including Snapchat and Meta’s Facebook and Instagram had blocked dissidents’ accounts over allegations by Saudi authorities that they were violating local law.

At the time, X, formerly Twitter, said it had notified users that it had not taken any action following requests by Saudi authorities, and it “strongly believes in defending and respecting the voice of our users”.

However, since mid-July more than 60 accounts on the platform have been made unavailable in Saudi Arabia through geoblocking, which prevents users inside the kingdom from viewing the content, according to the London-based human rights organisation ALQST.

Those affected include Yahya Assiri, a Saudi human rights activist who runs ALQST, and Abdullah Alaoudh, a US-based activist and vocal critic of Saudi human rights violations. Others affected include exiled activists, Saudi academics and independent media.

Alaoudh, a senior policy adviser for Gulf issues at the American Committee for Middle East Rights, said: “I think it’s horrible because we were fighting tyrants back home and now we’re fighting tyrants and their cronies here where we are in exile.

“It’s censorship – and what’s even worse is that they did not say we violated X’s rules or Meta’s rules.”

Account holders received emails from X informing them that their content had been withheld in the kingdom “in order to comply with X’s obligations under Saudi Arabia’s local laws”.

A Saudi decree attached to the letters and seen by the Guardian said the accounts had transmitted material that “infringes on public order, religious values, public morals or the sanctity of private life”.

Abdullah Aljuraywi, a monitoring and campaigns officer at ALQST, whose X account was also blocked inside the kingdom, said: “The news was sadly not very surprising, given that the authorities have a long history of silencing criticism at home and treating Saudis who speak out from abroad, especially those still connected to people inside the country, as a threat.

“What is even more concerning is that technology companies have helped enable this suppression, instead of protecting the freedom of speech they often say they support.”

ALQST has called on X, Meta, Snapchat and YouTube to restore access to the accounts and provide transparency over how the decisions were reached.

Meta previously told the Guardian that when it received reports of content violating local law but not the company’s own community standards, the company may restrict the content’s availability in the country where it was alleged to be unlawful.

X and the Saudi embassy in London have been approached for comment.

Other accounts targeted include those of Ghanem al-Masarir, a prominent Saudi satirist. Earlier this year a British court ordered Saudi Arabia to pay him £3m in damages after his iPhones were hacked and he was physically attacked outside Harrods in central London.

In May, al-Masarir was notified by YouTube that two of his accounts, with more than 800,000 subscribers combined, would be blocked in the kingdom after legal complaints made from a “government entity”. YouTube did not respond to a request for comment.

The same month, X emailed al-Masarir informing him of the request from Saudi authorities alleging that his account violated Saudi law, with an attached decree. By July, the company had notified al-Masarir that his content had been withheld in the kingdom to comply with local laws.

“I’m not surprised that Saudi has asked to block, but I’m surprised Elon Musk has listened,” al-Masarir said. He predicted “other authoritarian countries around the world” would follow suit.

No smut, no swearing, wrong-feet wellies and a silly hat: the gentle comedy world of Jimmy Cricket

The Guardian Tue, 04 Aug 2026 14:46:29 GMT

Having cut his teeth in the holiday camps of the north, the comic bestrode 80s TV with his unthreatening brand of fun, being knighted by the pope in 2015 Jimmy Cricket, comedian known for his ‘And there’s more!’ catchphrase, dies aged 80

After the comedian Jimmy Cricket chose the catchphrase, “And there’s more!” he may have reflected that the words would one day have a poignant irony. As has now happened after his death, aged 80.

The stage name was adopted by James Joseph Mulgrew, from Cookstown in Northern Ireland, when he worked as an entertainer at the Butlin’s and Pontins holiday camps from the 1960s at a time when these summer resort venues were an academy for UK entertainers.

Both Jimmy and Jiminy Cricket were rooted in polite euphemisms for the expletive “Jesus Christ!”, but Mulgrew, a committed churchgoer and carefully clean comic, is unlikely to have been motivated by the oath. Whether deliberately or by luck, his chosen pseudonym was likely to pique the interest of fans of Disney’s Pinocchio (in which Jiminy Cricket is a key character), those interested in orthopteran insects in general and lovers of the greatest summer game. The Irish climate and distraction of more historically Irish sports might have restricted the resonance of that reference back home but it proved useful to schedulers in Britain. Jimmy’s Cricket Team was the title of his successful BBC Radio 2 series from 1990, making the return to wireless writing of Morecambe & Wise’s greatest writer, Eddie Braben.

At that time, BBC Radio was tapping into the peak of Mulgrew’s public popularity, encouraged by his biggest television visibility, from 1985-88, on an ITV show titled after his catchphrase, And There’s More. The words perfectly suited a show featuring short sketches, songs and standup. Fronted by Mulgrew as Cricket, the 24 episodes included regular appearances by comedy actors Nicholas Smith (Are You Being Served?) and Joan Sims (Carry On) and guest slots for Hazel O’Connor, singing, and Rory Bremner, impersonating.

As Cricket, he wore a stage costume of too-short formal trousers (possibly a homage to the similarly attired Max Wall), funny hats and Wellingtons on the wrong foot. That – alongside the somewhat silly professional moniker – led some wrongly to assume that he was a children’s entertainer.

It was not, though, entirely misleading. He aimed at adults the sort of material that classified him as what used to be called a “family entertainer” – no smut, no swearing and little songs in which his retained native accent allowed him to rhyme “faffing” with “laughing”.

The purity and implied puritanism of his comedy was perhaps rooted in a Roman Catholic upbringing in Northern Ireland in the 1950s, a creed and era noted for their censoriousness. The lasting impact of his upbringing was also evident in many references in his routines to letters from his “Mammy”. Though uncontroversial at the time, one aspect of the act – many gags relating to “Irish logic” – might now be regarded as offensive, although, in common with Jewish comedians, Mulgrew would have claimed a birthright to explore stereotypes within his own tribe.

Though the hold of the faith diminished for many of his Ulster generation, Mulgrew remained practising, receiving in 2015 a papal knighthood, Catholicism’s highest honour, from Pope Francis. The citation mentioned the recipient’s charitable work; although the Argentinian pontiff was something of a joker himself, the honour is unlikely to have been for comedy. (Mulvey’s Northern Irish peer, Frank Carson, though rather less scrupulously clean mouthed, had received the same honour from Pope John Paul II, creating an intriguing trend among Northern Irish jokers of that generation.)

The highest profile period of Mulgrew/Cricket’s career overlapped with the so-called Troubles in Northern Ireland, its associated atrocities often featuring in the headlines of news bulletins abutting his TV and radio appearances. The performer, though, was wary of sectarianism – holiday camp performers largely targeted those unlikely to be paying customers – and, in turn, didn’t suffer much bigotry, although, as with Carson, few impressionists could resist a go at the Ulster brogue.

“Always let your conscience be your guide,” sings Jiminy Cricket in Pinocchio and that was the credo of his near namesake during a career in which he aimed to provide unthreatening fun – and succeeded.

What if older people refuse help outside the family? This is the taboo that could wreck care reform

The Guardian Tue, 04 Aug 2026 14:13:01 GMT

Many fear losing their independence if they agree to care workers looking after them. Any social care review must take this on board

Emily Kenway is the author of Who Cares: the Hidden Crisis of Caregiving and How We Solve It

Lisa* has used her local glazier so many times that he gives her a discount. For months, when care workers arrived at her mum’s home, they would find the front door locked and the elderly woman – who has dementia – resolute in her determination to bar their entry. Often, the only solution was to break the glass in the front door. When I met Lisa, who was a participant in a research project I ran, her mother had finally accepted help, but it had taken years of frustration and smashed glass. Unlike Lisa, Lily* never got to acceptance. After two years spent trying to persuade her elderly father to accept social care, she lied. He thinks the people who visit twice a day are nurses, legally required to dispense his dementia medication.

Experiences like these are common among people caring for ageing parents. They present an uncomfortable challenge for those who, like our new prime minister, Andy Burnham, wish to fix our care system. Many people are like Lisa and Lily: they are providing eldercare not because of the lack of social care, but because their ageing relatives will not accept external help, or at least not without a years-long fight.

Numerous studies have shown that people with dementia are prone to refuse medical and wider forms of care. More broadly, we know that people’s preferences for treatment shift over time and as their conditions change: what your loved one thinks they’ll want in the future isn’t necessarily what they’ll accept when that future comes. There is a lag between ageing parents developing care needs and accepting external forms of help, and it’s in that lag that family members step in. There isn’t enough formal evidence of this problem – too few studies ask why people receive the type of care they do, rather than assume it’s due to absent alternatives. But in one of the few studies to pose this question, published in the Journal of Nursing Management in 2007, “frail older people” attributed their reluctance to their fear of losing independence, and the humiliation and embarrassment they felt at the idea of being deemed needy.

It is an understandable fear. In our culture, we vilify vulnerability and valorise independence. You only need to look around at the paltry nods to accessibility in our public spaces or the degrading assessments of people seeking to claim disability benefits. For people who have lived their lives independently and able-bodied, the slip into dependency can be hard to accept. This is why Lily’s father finds nurses more tolerable than care workers: he doesn’t want to need care, but medicine – with its connotations of formalisation and expertise – is more acceptable. My mother was the same; after a lifetime being able-bodied, cancer took her mobility. But the notion of a rota of workers trooping into her home was unconscionable; they would be a physical affirmation of her frailty. Nobody wants to need care, so why are we assuming everyone will take it up?

There are more granular reasons for refusal too. In the same research in which I worked with Lisa and Lily, Malik*, a British Muslim, explained why his family would not use external care: “It’s a cultural thing, it’s also a religious thing … responsibility for the parents just lives within the family.” Numerous reports have shown that Black and minority ethnic people are less likely to use formal services – this appears to be partly because of community norms that locate responsibility for care within the family, and also because services may lack culturally appropriate options. And lest we forget, the state is not considered a friend by all: past experiences of discrimination may reduce the uptake of services.

Last year, I raised this issue at an event packed with thinktankers and policy advisers working to fix our care system. In response, an attender asked, “What’s the risk of saying this?” She meant that talking about refusal of social care risks undermining the political case for its improvement. We may inadvertently strengthen rightwing arguments that care is a familial concern (by which they mean female family members should do it all for free), rather than something to be funded by government. In contrast, the political left locates care as a state responsibility, transferring it into the paid labour market (albeit still usually performed by women, for almost-free).

My heart sank as the people around her concurred – the prevailing feeling in the room was that good progressives should not talk about this problem in case we undermine long-fought campaigns to make social care a political priority. And, of course, many thousands of people are absolutely desperate for adult social care – according to the Association of Directors of Adult Social Services, at least 400,000 people are on waiting lists in England alone. But I saw in my mind the innumerable family carers I have met like Lisa, Lily and Malik. I saw the carers’ groups in which people have talked of their loved ones’ refusals. What does it mean if we allow political discomfort to get in the way of truth? And the truth of eldercare is that ageing parents will often refuse support even when they need it, at least for a while.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

There is some evidence that improving social care is actually part of the solution to its refusal: a study examining preferences in countries in the OECD found that “older adults in countries with greater national expenditure on old age support … showed a stronger preference for formal care”. Nobody wants to deal with bad service, and social care is no different. This bodes well, but alone it will not be enough. We need to undo people’s view of dependency as a source of shame. This requires a culture shift. I don’t know how we achieve it, but centring the principles of the disability justice movement is a good place to start. This movement has worked indefatigably to show that people are worthy beyond their productivity, and that interdependence is a fundamental of existence rather than a personal failing. Too few of us have imbibed this wisdom, and the consequences are being played out in households everywhere; we must change that for future generations.

Culture change takes time, time in which thousands of people like Lisa will continue to struggle with their ageing relatives’ refusals of support. Any realistic package of reforms must acknowledge this situation, providing improved rights and resources for family carers alongside reforms to social care. Time will tell if the government will face this reality, or whether some things remain too inconvenient to acknowledge.

Emily Kenway is a social policy doctoral researcher at the University of Edinburgh and the author of Who Cares: the Hidden Crisis of Caregiving and How We Solve It

*All names have been changed

The best microwaves in the UK for every kitchen and budget – tested

The Guardian Tue, 04 Aug 2026 14:00:02 GMT

They’re perfect for time-poor cooks, but which deserves your counter space? From combi models to smart designs, here’s what our expert recommends

The best air fryers

The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

If you’re at a restaurant and hear a ping a couple of minutes before your meal arrives at your table, it’s unlikely to be a good sign. But microwave ovens are a brilliant tool in the home kitchen. They’re fearsomely fast at heating up – or even cooking – food when you’re time-poor and lacking the energy to make something wholesome after a hard day at work. And in hot weather, cooking by microwave isn’t just quick: it also won’t warm your home.

The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

Microwaves work best for heating food with a high water content (they make the water molecules in food vibrate to create heat). However, before testing, I asked around to find out what people use theirs for most, with a view to using this information to shape my tests. I learned a few things – like lots of people eat mug cakes. Who knew? And that wheat bags are a popular alternative to hot-water bottles. But the majority of folk use their microwave for reheating cold cuppas, defrosting frozen batch-cooked meals, warming food, popping microwave popcorn – and, of course, cooking jacket potatoes more quickly. I used these insights to shape my testing.

Ease of use is important, too. Most of us only ever use a few buttons on repeat, often having to reach for the instructions if we want to use some of the smarter functionality these appliances now come with – some can even air-fry.

Microwaving can be healthy and fast, and it uses less energy than an oven. So, if you want to discover the best microwaves for your needs, read on.

Best microwave overallPanasonic NN-CD88 4-in-1 combi with air fry

Best budget microwaveSalter DuoWave 2-in-1

Best microwave for controlsLG MH6565CPS NeoChef

I’m an award-winning consumer technology journalist who’s been reviewing gadgets for almost 30 years. I live in a terrace house with my children and several pets, meaning there were plenty of mouths for the extra food I was making while testing these microwaves. The humans got a lot of jacket potatoes and beans; the animals helped with the rest … which is how I discovered that hens love poppadoms!

I selected 10 microwave ovens from leading brands at various price points. The models differed in capacity and features but were similar in other ways. They all had a dial and buttons for control on a panel on the right-hand side. They all opened to the left, other than the Samsung Combi microwave, where the door opens downwards. And they all had a one-metre power cable at the rear that came from the top right (looking front on).

I used each model to prepare the same set of foods. I made microwave popcorn, cooked jacket potatoes (200 to 250g each), and heated up 150g of baked beans.

Next, I used each microwave to heat 250ml of chilled (starting at 9C) tap water for two minutes, using a digital thermometer to check its temperature after heating. I also used the defrost settings on a 500g block of ice in each microwave for 10 minutes, weighing how much ice was left. Finally, I cooked poppadoms to evaluate a microwave oven’s ability to cook evenly, and frozen oven chips in those models that come with an air-frying feature.

None of the food I made went to waste, with the chickens happily eating any leftover popcorn and – surprisingly – the poppadoms, and the dog eating everything else.

With testing done and dusted, any models that weren’t collected by the manufacturers were donated to Furnishing Futures, a charity that fully furnishes social housing for survivors of domestic abuse.

This microwave is huge, arriving with the biggest capacity on test. The turntable sits on a roller with six wheels, rather than the usual three, and the controls are a dial with a button at its centre, plus six clearly labelled buttons. Helpfully, the display features scrolling text, so you always know what you’re doing, and you’ll find a list of all the programmes inside the door, so you never need to consult the instructions to make full use of it.

Why we love itPerformance was excellent: the microwave cooked popcorn fast, the poppadoms evenly, heated my mug of water to 75C and defrosted the ice well. I used a special programme to cook the jacket potato, which took 15 minutes but was well worth the wait. In fact, the Panasonic was the only microwave on test to produce a jacket potato that could have passed for oven-baked.

This model also offers grill, convection oven and air-fryer cooking – personally, I think those last two are the same thing. Again, though, performance impressed. It comes with a circular rack, a crisper tray and a wire basket, which I used to air-fry frozen chips to perfection.

If you want a microwave that does it all and gives you extra cooking capacity – essentially, an extra shelf’s worth of oven – this is the one to buy.

It’s a shame that … fingerprints show on the brushed stainless steel finish.

Dimensions: 56 x 45 x 34cm (WDH) Power: 1,000W (1,300W grill)Capacity: 34l Turntable diameter: 36cm Other cooking options: oven, grill, air fryer

The “duo” in the name refers to the fact that this microwave doubles as an air fryer. And it performed brilliantly on all fronts. If you don’t have the worktop space or the budget for the Panasonic, the Salter is a great buy.

Microwaving is on a standard glass turntable, but you air-fry on a full-width, rectangular roasting tray that slides into the unit like a shelf, with a rectangular mesh basket that sits on top of this tray.

Why we love itIt’s clever. Most microwaves have a jacket potato programme that takes five minutes, but that’s never quite enough: I experimented and found 5mins 20secs was the optimum time. The Salter automatically went for 5mins 20secs and cooked it perfectly.

It’s quick, too, heating my mug of water to an impressive 73C and cooking two poppadoms quickly and evenly. I used the basket to air-fry frozen oven chips, and they were ready within 15 minutes.

Controls are intuitive, with a button in the middle of the dial. It was easy to figure out how to defrost, and I could do so by time or weight.

It’s a shame that … there isn’t a list of all the programmes inside the door.

The cooking area is impressive, too: the turntable sits on a roller ring with six wheels, rather than the usual three, so it doesn’t wobble. It comes with a circular rack and a crisper tray, too.

Why we love itThe look is high-end and performance impressed, too. My mug of water was heated to 72C, and the 14-minute programme for the jacket potato gave decent results. The “healthy fry” setting did a great job of frozen oven chips as well – cooking them to perfection in 15mins 30secs, without the need to turn them midway.

It’s a shame that … I couldn’t find a setting to defrost by time, so I had to do it by weight. Nevertheless, it worked well, defrosting more than half my ice in 10 minutes. Also, its alerts are a bit musical, which you’ll either love or loathe.

It didn’t make the final cut because … cooking performance was so-so. My water heated to only 66C; it was slow to cook a jacket potato, and air-frying chips was a 19-minute programme – slower than most dedicated air fryers and closer to an oven.

Dimensions: 52 x 52 x 33cm (WDH); power: 900W (1,500W grill); capacity: 32l; turntable diameter: 34cm; other cooking options: grill, oven, air fryer, steam

Best for: a larger flatbed

The flatbed design means this model has more usable space than a microwave with a turntable. For example, I could fit in three poppadoms without any overlapping, which is good for a mid-size microwave. However, they cooked unevenly: I had to flip them over and give them another minute.

It did a good job of heating baked beans, but it was slow to cook the jacket potato and the popcorn.

It didn’t make the final cut because … I hated the controls. It is a truth universally acknowledged that all microwaves should have a button you can bash for 30-second increments. But this one does 30 seconds, a minute, then goes up in minutes (to a maximum of 10 minutes).

Best for: a mid-price combi microwave

This is a combi: a microwave, grill and oven that can combine cooking styles. However, performance was a mixed bag. It turned out a jacket potato in 6mins 30secs – which, although no replacement for an oven-cooked spud, was better than a microwaved one. It heated my mug of water to 76C, but defrosted less than 20% of my ice.

I was a fan of its controls, though: a dial with a button in the middle, plus six clearly labelled buttons.

It didn’t make the final cut because … I found it confusing; sometimes it would keep cooking, but the timer didn’t go down. Plus, defrosting yielded disappointing results.

Dimensions: 48 x 44 x 28cm (WDH); power: 900W (1,950W grill, 1,950W oven); capacity: 25l; turntable diameter: 27cm; other cooking options: grill, oven

Best for: a flatbed microwave on a budget

Doing away with a turntable means flatbed microwaves can fit in more food. For example, this one is compact but can accommodate a large 30cm dinner plate. On the downside, flatbed microwaves often struggle to cook evenly, and this model was no exception in my tests. I could fit two (and even three at a squeeze) poppadoms at a time, but while they were fully cooked at the centre, the sides were underdone.

The microwave was powerful, though, heating my mug of water to an impressive 72C.

It didn’t make the final cut because … it looks classy but the controls proved annoying. There’s no button in the middle of the dial and I had to read the manual to look up programmes.

Dimensions: 47 x 38 x 30cm (WDH); power: 800W; capacity: 23l; turntable: 33 x 31cm (flatbed) ; other cooking options: none

Best for: price

At RRP, this was the cheapest microwave tested – but you get what you pay for. The styling is simple but old-fashioned. Overall, it looks pretty basic.

When it comes to performance, while my mug of water was heated to only 64C, more than 60% of the ice was defrosted in just 10 minutes.

Capacity is small, though: it could cope with only one poppadom and couldn’t accommodate my 30cm dinner plates. Also, it has eight preset programmes, but they’re not listed conveniently on the appliance itself, so you’ll be reaching for the instructions.

It didn’t make the final cut because … I liked it, but I think it’s worth spending a bit more on the Salter.

Dimensions: 45 x 35 x 26cm (WDH); power: 800W; capacity: 20l; turntable diameter: 26cm; other cooking options: none

The room inside a microwave is usually measured in litres, but that’s the total volume, right up to the corners. I’ve included turntable diameter, so you can measure your dinner plates to see if they’ll fit. Some microwaves have a flatbed design, with no turntable. While you can fit more into these models, cooking can be uneven.

A microwave is a valuable tool in the kitchen, if you have the worktop space for it. If space is tight, look for one that’s shallow enough that you can make good use of the space in front of it to prepare food.

Microwaves are best at heating, reheating and defrosting food with a high water content. They’re great for reheating everything from batch-cooked meals to a forgotten cuppa.

Models that feature oven capabilities or air frying are great because they offer valuable extra cooking space, but only if you have the worktop space. It’s like having an extra shelf’s worth of oven – perfect when you’re cooking for lots of people.

Microwave power is measured in watts – this is a measure of cooking power, rather than electrical draw. The models on test range from 800W to 1,000W. They will all cook your dinner, but the higher-power appliances will do it faster. This shouldn’t use more electricity overall (and, therefore, money and carbon) as they use more per minute but take less time.

Larger microwaves sometimes offer grill, oven and air fryer modes – or all three. I consider air fryers and small convection (fan) ovens to be the same thing: they cook food by circulating hot air, and they’re faster than ovens thanks to their small size.

Combi cooking is when one of these styles and microwave cooking are combined for the best of both worlds. For example, you can cook a crispy-skinned jacket potato in less than 20 minutes.

Some microwaves also come with a set of plastic dishes for steam cooking. This works well, but do remember that you’ll need to find space in your kitchen to stow any accessories. Some people also prefer to avoid microwaving in plastic where possible.

Google Earth’s potential disinformation nightmare

The Guardian Tue, 04 Aug 2026 13:42:26 GMT

A new feature briefly allowed Google Earth users to overlay AI-generated images on locations of their choosing

This was originally published in TechScape, a newsletter about how technology shapes our lives. Sign up to receive it here.

Hello, and welcome to TechScape. This week we’ll be discussing a regrettable decision by Google Earth, the dramatic fall of the “Nostradamus of AI”, and what happens when AI agents go rogue.

Last Thursday, Google announced that users of its satellite-imagery software, Google Earth, could create AI-generated images to overlay on any location they looked up. The tool could be used to “help students visualize the past”, “create professional real estate plans” to envision the final result, or “give your favorite place a makeover”, Google suggested in its announcement. Nearly immediately, users began testing the limits of the feature. Turns out there weren’t many.

Henk van Ess, an AI researcher and investigator, posted images he created showing refugees near the Mexican border. He also said he “planted a nuclear plant in Iran”. “What on earth is Google doing?” Van Ess posted on X. Another image he generated showed a crater from a bomb near a fake hospital he created in Gaza. We tested the feature too. The process just required choosing a location, clicking “create image” and entering a prompt. We chose to show “refugees swarming New York”. The image it created was not ultra-realistic, but it was still troubling.

Satellite imagery has become widely used by journalists, researchers and investigators to shed light on the breadth and realities of global crises, especially in places that are otherwise inaccessible. The utility of satellite images first became apparent in 2020, after BuzzFeed News won a Pulitzer for a series that exposed the location and expansion of China’s Uyghur detention camps. The imagery captured, for the first time, factories within the walls of the camp. The journalists worked with satellite firm Planet Labs, which is backed by Google and acquired satellite startup Terra Bella from the tech giant in 2017.

The use of satellite imagery to better understand and uncover global crises really took off in the last two years as reporters and the world sought to better understand the mass destruction Israel has wrought on Gaza. Satellite imagery of Gaza before and after Israel’s years-long rampage on the 365 sq km strip shows cities completely leveled. Satellite imagery was also used to expose the human toll of the crisis in Sudan. Images captured from space in November 2025 showed stains that resembled blood and what researchers believed were human bodies scattered near the besieged city of El Fasher, which was under siege by paramilitary fighters from the Rapid Support Forces.

So a feature that allows you to “transform” satellite imagery, as Google described it, is a potential disinformation nightmare. Satellite imagery lends a degree of authority, authenticity and veracity to claims and has been used as a mechanism to better understand inaccessible global events. It feels more indisputable than images captured by humans on the ground, which face more public skepticism – even when they’re real – as AI-generated images proliferate. Enabling anyone to create any image overlaid on satellite photos of real places may make it impossible to suss out the truth.

Unsurprisingly, Google rolled back the feature so it can create more guardrails, meaning they may bring the feature back. “We know that people uniquely trust Google Earth for a reliable view of the world,” the company wrote. “We’ve seen geospatial professionals using this feature for a range of useful purposes, however we’ve also seen people sharing screenshots of generated imagery that appear to violate our policies.”

The popular podcaster Tim Ferriss once called Leopold Aschenbrenner “the Nostradamus of AI”, saying that the 24-year-old investor and his theories on the future of artificial intelligence were “as close to clairvoyant as you could possibly be”. But that lore hasn’t been borne out.

Last week, Aschenbrenner saw his multibillion-dollar hedge fund decimated as his many investments withered. By Thursday, the fund had no choice but to sell the majority of its public holdings to a rival.

Aschenbrenner isn’t a household name, but he is well-known in Silicon Valley circles. When he graduated college, in 2021, he started working for the now defamed crypto exchange FTX. When the exchange collapsed, he joined OpenAI. Aschenbrenner was later fired from OpenAI for reportedly leaking sensitive information to the husband of an Anthropic executive, according to the Wall Street Journal. At that point, in 2024, Aschenbrenner wrote a 165-page essay called Situational Awareness: the Decade Ahead, which catapulted him toward fame in the tech world.

The essay laid out his theories on AI, saying that the technology had set in motion “extraordinary techno-capital acceleration” and that “before long, the world will wake up”. As his essay gained momentum, Aschenbrenner collected prominent Silicon Valley investors for his hedge fund, also called Situational Awareness. The fund grew exorbitantly.

Situational Awareness didn’t adhere to the usual cautions of Wall Street, however. Instead, it took the gamble of borrowing money to buy stocks, a strategy that doesn’t have a safety net when stocks go south. And, as AI stocks took a downturn this past month – with doubts of the technology’s potential swirling – the hedge fund was forced to pay back skittish lenders. Situational Awareness sold off its investments in a fire sale with its billions now dissipated.

Sign up to TechScape

A weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our lives

after newsletter promotion

Over the past several weeks, Anthropic and OpenAI have revealed that their artificial intelligence models carried out unauthorized hacking operations against outside organizations. The hacks took place during their tests of yet-to-be released AI models, which were supposed to happen within isolated, controlled environments.

In OpenAI’s case, an autonomous AI agent carried out a days-long hack in early July against Hugging Face, a developer platform that hosts AI models. It also hacked a customer of the AI startup Modal Labs. Anthropic similarly revealed last week that its AI models had hacked into three undisclosed organizations during a cybersecurity test, in part because human error gave it access to the public internet during the test.

The reports of rogue AI agents breaking out of their testing sandboxes to carry out attacks have, unsurprisingly, drawn huge amounts of tech and media attention amid heightened cybersecurity concerns and distrust of the industry. They have also divided tech experts over whether these hacks are as consequential as they seem and how to stop them in the future.

One of the longstanding problems of AI development is that models can act in unpredictable ways when directed to complete a task. An AI instructed to win a racing game may not solely try to drive fast to succeed, for instance. It may also look for loopholes in the game or shortcuts in the course. This is a well-known phenomenon that is usually described as models “cheating” or “lying” during testing.

OpenAI’s hack of Hugging Face was an extreme example of this type of behavior and one that highlights how advancements in AI have exacerbated these unsolved problems. Models that go rogue to achieve their goals are now powerful enough that the unintended consequences can be much more damaging and far-reaching than finding a glitch in a video game.

While cybersecurity experts agree that AI has become incredibly capable at finding security vulnerabilities, some also cautioned that OpenAI’s hacking incident fit into one of the company’s well-worn marketing narratives – that its technology was scarily powerful and therefore exceedingly valuable. Others, meanwhile, described it as a wake-up call about the threat of AI as a cybersecurity nightmare, with the technology rapidly gaining new capabilities.

Regardless of whether the hacking incidents mark a new frontier or merely play into industry talking points, they highlight the lack of coherent policy and industry standards surrounding the technology. As AI experts Bruce Schneier and Barath Raghavan argued for the Guardian, the industry has been focused on whether AI can reach a goal without enough scrutiny of how it gets there:

Dozens of benchmarks and leaderboards tell us how well these AI models write code, perform logical reasoning, and pass standardized legal and medical exams. But there is nothing that scores whether a system does what you actually meant. We need to develop a measure for this, test it regularly, and push for improvement. We’re not going to have trustworthy AI agents without it.

Jerusalem’s most important Muslim religious site facing ‘imminent’ threat of Israeli takeover, says Jordan

The Guardian Tue, 04 Aug 2026 13:15:34 GMT

Country convenes emergency meeting of ministers from Arab and Islamic world, fearing such a move could ‘trigger a religious conflict’

Middle East crisis live – latest updates

Jordan is convening an emergency meeting of foreign ministers from the Arab and Islamic world over what it says is an “imminent” threat of an Israeli takeover of the most important Muslim site in Jerusalem, with the potential to “trigger a religious conflict”.

The meeting on Wednesday – and the Jordanian warning – follow an escalating pattern of government-backed incursions by Jewish religious extremists on the compound around al-Aqsa mosque and Dome of the Rock, in violation of a status quo treaty overseen by Jordan’s Hashemite monarchy, by which only Muslims can pray at the site.

On 23 July, more than 2,000 Israelis from the religious right – mostly settlers led by the national security minister, Itamar Ben Gvir – stormed the area, known to Jews as the Temple Mount. They prayed and performed rituals all around the compound in what Jordanian officials said was the worst violation in modern history.

Amman has also been alarmed at a recent recruitment drive for religious Jews for a special Temple Mount police unit, and is braced for more direct challenges to traditional Jordanian custodianship by extremist Israeli leaders in the major Jewish holidays in September. This year, those holidays will come amid an intense election campaign, in which the far-right coalition of the prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, will be fighting for survival.

“This is a constant threat, a dangerous threat that we’re trying to counter in every tool that we have possible,” Jordan’s foreign minister, Ayman Safadi, told the Guardian. “We warn that tampering with the status quo … could trigger a religious conflict that will reverberate beyond Palestine and Jordan into the whole Muslim world.”

Safadi, who will host Wednesday’s emergency meeting, bringing together his counterparts from Arab League countries, as well as Turkey, Indonesia, Malaysia and Pakistan, said it was “something that the whole international community should be aware of. Jerusalem is a tinderbox.

“We’re trying to explain the danger. We’re protesting legally. We are trying to create awareness of the imminent danger in the continuation of those Israeli measures.”

Jordan’s custodianship of al-Aqsa compound dates back to Ottoman times, and the status quo encompassing the city’s religious sites was enshrined in the 1878 Treaty of Berlin. The Hashemite kingdom’s oversight in Jerusalem was expanded to cover Christian holy sites in the 20th century, and its custodianship was reaffirmed after the 1967 war, and in the 1994 Israeli-Jordanian peace treaty.

Infringement by Jewish extremists triggered riots in the British Mandate period between the world wars, and a 2000 visit to the compound by the rightwing leader Ariel Sharon, soon to become the Israeli prime minister, ignited more than four years of violence in the second intifada.

Jordan is uniquely vulnerable to the impact of Israel’s broader ethnic cleansing campaign in the West Bank, which Amman fears may also escalate dramatically as the October elections loom. There is anxiety over what the Israeli government might do in the three months before the vote, as radical elements seek to change the geography of the region in ways which could be difficult to reverse.

For Amman, the worst-case scenario is an attempt at the mass deportation of Palestinians from the West Bank, which would destabilise Jordan in several ways, including economic costs, the political impact of an influx of an angry, dispossessed population, and threats to the country’s delicate demographic balance.

“Our position that this is a red line that we will not allow to be crossed. We have made that known to everybody that we will do whatever it takes to prevent any attempt at Israeli displacement of Palestinians into Jordan,” Safadi said. “Not only will that be a violation of international law and of the right of the Palestinians to stay on their land, but that will also be a tremendous escalation.”

Jordanians descended from previous waves of Palestinian refugees already represent more than half of Jordan’s 11.5-million population, and the country’s original residents, the “East Bankers”, are wary of what they see as a further dilution of national identity.

Israel has already refused to renew a 2021 water agreement under which it shared 100m cubic metres a year to its parched neighbour, one of the most water-scarce countries in the world. It reverted to the 50m cubic metres originally agreed in the 1994 treaty, which falls far short of the needs of a much bigger population than the Jordan of 32 years ago.

The Israeli government reportedly halved the water supply in retaliation for criticism from the Jordanian government of the mass killing of Palestinian civilians by Israel in the Gaza war, and officials have hinted that the taps could be turned back on if the criticism ended.

The Israeli government’s provocative actions in Jerusalem and the West Bank and over water raise the political cost to the monarchy of maintaining normal relations with its western neighbour.

“Anti-normalisation sentiment here has grown even larger than before due to the Zionist state’s plans of annexation of the West Bank, the denial of Jordan’s share in the water agreement and also the daily challenges to the custodianship at al-Aqsa mosque,” said Dima Tahboub, a member of parliament and spokesperson for Jordan’s Islamist Umma party. “Every day there is penetration by settlers into al-Aqsa mosque and at the same time, [Palestinian] Jerusalemites are prevented from entering the mosque.”

Tahboub’s party is Jordan’s biggest political bloc, known as the Islamic Action Front (IAF) until earlier this year when it was ordered to adopt a less ideological name. Its rise has largely been driven by events on the other side of the River Jordan, and the Gaza war helped it win more than 22% of the available seats.

The surge in political Islam came as a shock to the monarchy, which slowed down its plans for political reform and the transfer of more power to parliament as a result. The Muslim Brotherhood movement was outlawed last year and IAF, which operates as its political arm, had its offices raided. It has, however, been allowed to continue as a party, under the name of Umma, which means “community” or “nation”.

Tahboub said there was more the government could be doing to rally international support to resist Israel’s encroachments.

“I think more pressure can be exerted. The issue is not being put to the table with the force that it needs,” she said, while stressing that the Umma party stood together with the Jordanian government in the face of its adversaries, and that it understood the limitations imposed by geography and economics which have left it significantly dependent on the US for its economic and security needs.

Unlike other Gulf monarchies, Jordan has not allowed the US its own military bases on its territory, but there is a US presence on Jordanian bases, which has grown significantly since the start of the US war with Iran. Amman has sought to play down the presence of US forces, planes and other equipment, but that has been made harder by repeated successful Iranian airstrikes, which have killed three Americans and injured scores at the Muwaffaq Salti base in the eastern desert.

For decades the US military presence has been seen as a security guarantee for Jordan, but it has also proved to be a political liability, especially as the Jordanian air force has found itself serving as Israel’s first line of defence shooting down Iranian drones and missiles heading towards Tel Aviv.

Last month, several hundred prominent figures from politics, the law and Jordanian cultural life signed an open letter calling for the withdrawal of US forces, in a rare direct challenge to the government.

The letter said: “We maintain that their presence exposes Jordan to security, political, and economic risks that serve no national interest and that it increases the likelihood of our country being dragged into a regional conflict to which it is not a party.”

Asking Anthony Fauci for medical advice then calling for him to be jailed? Katie Miller is the latest Maga hypocrite

The Guardian Tue, 04 Aug 2026 13:07:09 GMT

The vocal vaccine sceptic and wife of Trump’s deputy chief of staff turned to the former US science adviser when she was worried about Covid. Now, she’s claiming it was a cunning plan

You should keep your friends close, your enemies closer, and Stephen and Katie Miller as far away from your general vicinity as humanly possible. Many people will not need to be told this. Stephen Miller, the White House deputy chief of staff, is famous for masterminding the first Trump administration’s family separation policy and Muslim ban. His wife, Katie, is similarly enthusiastic about mass deportation and has reportedly said she didn’t feel compassion for families separated at the border. Stephen met Katie when they were both working in government, but she has since left politics to start a podcast. Now she asks guests such as JD Vance important questions such as: is a hotdog a sandwich?

While I may not need to inform you that the Millers are bad news, it seems Dr Anthony Fauci is only just getting the memo. The former top US government science adviser, who helped guide the country’s Covid-19 response, was forced to appear at a US Senate committee hearing last week. Senator Rand Paul of Kentucky framed the hearing as an investigation into the origins of the pandemic. Really, however, it was an opportunity for Republicans to harass Fauci, who is widely loathed among the Maga base. He has become such a target of vitriol that Biden preemptively pardoned Fauci before leaving office in case he was prosecuted by the Trump administration.

While the Millers were not directly involved in the Fauci hearing, they did make an interesting cameo. Paul released more than 1,000 pages of Fauci’s diary from 2019 to 2022, which revealed that Fauci regularly talked to Katie, then a communications aide to vice-president Mike Pence, about her health concerns.

“I am calling katie frequently to check on her couple time per day,” Fauci wrote in notes dated 9 May 2020. “She is very anxious about getting very ill since she is 10 weeks pregnant. Tonight she had an anxiety reaction. I calmed her over the phone.”

Fauci seemed to like Katie, who he described as “tough, smart, but great”, and she seemed on good terms with him. Fauci also sent the Millers a baby gift and, per his diary, the couple called him to say thank you. “We had a nice discussion about life after Trump,” he wrote in December 2020.

I don’t think any more gifts are going to be exchanged, however, because Katie has thrown Fauci under the bus. It’s very embarrassing for a Maga bigwig like her – someone who has amplified vaccine-sceptic views and publicly called for Fauci to be jailed – to be revealed as having privately asked him for medical advice. Katie has tried to explain away the relationship by insisting that she had simply been feigning friendship as part of a cunning plan. Katie told the political news website Notus that she’d been cordial with Fauci so that he “did not leak against me or my husband”. She added that she understood “how to manage somebody like him”. Some of the information about her seems to have been redacted. Notus reports that the original Fauci journal entries released “mentioned Katie Miller 56 times, while the redacted document mentioned her 37 times”.

After the diary entries became public, Katie attacked Fauci on social media and accused him of being fame-hungry. “Every man who has a journal is a narcissist,” she wrote on X on Thursday. “Dr Fauci was neither my friend nor my doctor, but a work colleague who weaponised my pregnancy and child for his gain to aggrandise himself. As they say, keep your friends close and your enemies closer … this man should be in prison.”

Katie isn’t entirely wrong about Fauci enjoying fame. His journal entries contain cringeworthy details about flattering press coverage and celebs fawning over him. Julia Roberts, he wrote, “said that every time she sees me her throat gets dry and she gets nervous”. Barbra Streisand apparently also chatted to Fauci about vaccines. “Had great call with Barbra Streisand,” he wrote in February 2021. “I told her that I work listening to her songs on Alexa. She really did not know what Alexa was. I accidentally butt called her later in the evening …”

Still, this was a private journal, and we’ve all been embarrassing in private haven’t we? Plus, if Roberts was gasping over me, you best believe I’d be telling dear diary. Fauci getting carried away by his sudden fame is understandable; there is no vaccine for being cringe. One day, however, I hope there will be a cure for the harm people like the Millers have inflicted on the body politic.

Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist

The hill I will die on: You should be legally obliged to play Mr Brightside at your wedding

The Guardian Tue, 04 Aug 2026 13:00:00 GMT

Sure, it’s about jealousy, infidelity and paranoia, but the Killers’ biggest hit is a dancefloor banger: any marriage that starts without it is guaranteed to end in divorce

I’ve been to two weddings where the bride and groom refused to play the Killers’ pop-rock hit Mr Brightside, and both ended in divorce. Well, not yet or anything – but I’m sure it’s coming. How happy can a couple really be if they’re not willing to play the biggest banger to ever bang moments after their hearts have been bound together as one? There are some things that should never be missing from a wedding unless you outright detest your guests. Canapes, yes. Cake, sure. And the opportunity to scream, “Comin’ out of my cage and I’ve been doin’ just fine” next to someone’s Auntie Debs? Undoubtedly.

Why should a song about jealousy, paranoia and infidelity pump through the speakers on your special day? Because everyone knows it. Mr Brightside is the third most sold and streamed song in the UK, and it’s the longest-charting single in this country’s history, even though the Killers are (somehow) American. Unlike much else these days, the track transcends borders. In 2025, YouGov asked more than 1,000 Americans which songs they knew all the words to, and Mr Brightside came in 15th place. The songs above it included The Star-Spangled Banner, Happy Birthday and Jingle Bells.

Four years ago, my husband and I fought over our wedding playlist because he (I possibly unfairly believed) wanted to look cool and cultured, and I wanted to serve up a cheeseboard of belter after belter. In the end, our elderly Sicilian DJ forged his own path, playing The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air theme tune twice in quick succession, to my husband’s consternation and my utter delight. Was that DJ simply confused by our shared language barrier? No. He knew something, I think, that so many couples refuse to accept: your wedding playlist is not about you. Your wedding day is, sure. The dress, the venue, the food, the poems – they can all be a careful curation of your tastes. But the playlist belongs to the people. And the people demand to dance.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

Dancing Queen. Come On Eileen. Jolene. Many failsafe wedding staples unite the generations by ending in an emotive “een”. But another way to be sure a song will set fire to the dancefloor is to ask yourself a very simple question: can my guests do a series of impassioned hand gestures as they scream-sing? Mr Brightside encourages listeners to not only touch their chests, but also take a drag of a phantom cigarette. The song allows us to bring a little finger-and-thumb-shaped phone to our ears twice – once to call an imaginary cab and once to answer the phone to destiny.

This, in the end, is all that most of us come to a wedding to do. And as the track comes to a close, we can heed its final call to open up our eager eyes. Because in that moment, we’re all Mr Brightside.

Amelia Tait is a freelance features writer and the author of Lily Tripp: Diary of an Accidental Time Traveller
