A rail nightmare: what it’s like on England’s busiest commuter-only train

The Guardian Tue, 04 Aug 2026 11:00:49 GMT

This evening service from London to Crewe is hot, sweaty and heaving with people, many having to stand or sit in the gangways

The 5.46pm train from London Euston to Crewe is the low point of Nikhil Patel’s week. “I’ve never gotten a seat. I always stand up even when I get here early,” says the 22-year-old, struggling to keep his balance while the gangway underneath sways from side to side.

Painfully for Patel, who is commuting back and forth to the capital for a computer science internship, it’s the first leg of a three-hour journey home to Walsall. He grabs the back of a chair to remain steady but says he’s just thankful that the train has left on time – and that it’s even on the move at all.

“There’s been a couple of times where everyone’s boarded and then the train’s been cancelled and we all had to get off,” he says. On another occasion, his journey home took five hours because this service was delayed, meaning he missed a connecting train.

This rush-hour service, operated by London Northwestern Railway (LNR), is the busiest commuter-only journey in England and Wales, according to figures by the Department for Transport.

Overall, it’s the second busiest commute, the No 1 being a morning Thameslink service from Bedford to Three Bridges – which passes through three international hubs: St Pancras International, and Luton and Gatwick airports.

We decided to join commuters getting the packed, two-hour-plus service on Thursday evening. According to the DfT, the service had a load factor – how many people are on a train compared with its maximum capacity – of 170% when the analysis was carried out last autumn. LNR says the number of seats on the service has increased from 460 to 812 since the data was gathered.

There is the familiar scrum moving towards the train after the platform is announced, an infamous tradition at Euston station. At first it seems as if this crop of commuters has lucked out, as it isn’t overly busy. But as the clock approaches 5.46pm, the carriages begin to heave with people.

Some fan themselves to keep the summer heat at bay. When the train is finally on the move, most gangways are cluttered with unlucky commuters unable to snag a seat. Some stand but others sit, bearing the rough and tumble of the shifting metal surface underneath.

Among them is Daniel Garrill, 23, who regularly gets this service. “I know I’m going to be sitting in some dodgy spot,” the data analyst says, having never got a seat during the week.

He travels between London and Manchester at least twice a week, meaning he has to bring a suitcase – which is tricky because there’s “nowhere to put your bag either”. He has to keep fiddling with his luggage to ensure it doesn’t escape down the carriage.

On the other side of the gangway is Akshay Vaghela, 31, who is commuting to Rugby. He says he is forced to stand half the time, and more often than not is “resigned to finding a seat on the floor”. This train is particularly busy because it is cheaper than the shorter Avanti service also heading to Crewe.

“I’ve gotten used to it because I know what booking this service means. It’s a free-for-all for the seats, otherwise you’re standing,” he says. Despite the train being kitted out with air conditioning, Vaghela says it’s still “stuffy, hot and sweaty” because there are so many people on it. “Unless you’ve got water, you’re struggling until you get home,” he says.

There is a chance things might not stay this way. Andy Burnham, newly installed as prime minister, has had rail operators in his sights for a while, making headlines for calling out poor performers while mayor of Greater Manchester.

He has previously said nationalising railways is a “no brainer” and launched the Bee Network as mayor, which brought privatised bus and tram networks into the local government’s control and capped fares at £2. Rail services across Greater Manchester will start to join the network by the end of the year.

He faced a rude reminder of the state of our railways last month. After his election as MP for Makerfield, he took a 10.54am Avanti West Coast train from Manchester to Euston. The service was delayed by 21 minutes, making him eligible to claim compensation.

The transport secretary, Heidi Alexander, has also faced a bumpy train journey, saying she sat on the floor of a packed service from London Paddington to her constituency in Swindon.

Sign up to Headlines UK

Get the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morning

after newsletter promotion

Burnham hinted in May that there could be a swifter move towards rail renationalisation – a number of operators were brought under state control while Keir Starmer was prime minister – saying it would “reduce train fares and make them affordable to people again”.

Vaghela is optimistic that Burnham will enforce some change. He says “priority routes like this one which connect main parts of the country should be looked at”, especially because “everyone’s paying the same price and some people get seats and others don’t, there’s a disparity there”.

As we advance further down the carriages, we squeeze past commuters packed together by the platform doors, sidestep buggies and grab on to windows, poles or even fellow passengers to avoid tumbling to the floor.

Standing among a group of commuters in a packed gangway is retiree Andy Simms, 65. He has a lucky escape, only having to bear the service for half an hour. He’s getting off at the first stop: Milton Keynes Central.

Simms isn’t too bothered about the packed train. “It’s fine but busy,” he says, though he admits: “If you’re doing this every day it must be very annoying, especially if you’re paying for a season ticket.”

Overall, he thinks trains are better than he remembers. “Things used to be a lot worse on trains back in my youth. It was scruffy, dirty and violent,” he says.

On the prospect of Burnham making changes to the rail system, he’d rather he keep his focus elsewhere. “I think social care is more important than train journeys. I’d rather he fix that than this,” he says, while holding on to a pole behind for balance.

An LNR spokesperson said: “Our services to and from Euston are extremely popular, which is why we have made a major £1bn investment in new trains to provide extra space for our customers.

“Since this data was gathered we have added hundreds of extra seats to this particular service, increasing its capacity by 77% and significantly reducing its load factor to provide more comfortable journeys for passengers.”

‘When you kill it, it doesn’t die’: the jellyfish that has cracked the secret of immortality

The Guardian Tue, 04 Aug 2026 11:00:47 GMT

Turritopsis dohrnii has the ability to turn back into a baby jellyfish and grow up all over again

Revealed: the top ten invertebrates of the year

Immortality is generally considered the realm of the gods or science fiction, a fantasy that’s actively pursued by tech entrepreneurs in macabre experiments that include injecting “young blood”, cryopreservation, or resurrection in an AI afterlife.

But one ethereal, thimble-shaped jellyfish has already cracked the code.

As associate professor Maria Pia Miglietta, a marine biologist at A&M University, explains, Turritopsis dohrnii has an incredible ability to cheat death.

“Turritopsis is unique, because when faced with unfavourable conditions – and I mean high temperature, physical cutting, starvation, chemicals in the water, you name it – when you try to kill the jellyfish, it doesn’t die.”

Most normal jellyfish start off life as larvae. They metamorphose into polyps (tiny, stationary soft bodies) that bud off swimming medusas, which grow up to become adult jellies. Eventually, after reproducing, most will stop swimming, crumble a little and then die.

But the immortal jellyfish escapes that fate. It reverts to a juvenile form, and starts its life cycle again.

The process is called “cellular transdifferentiation”, Miglietta says. The jellyfish looks like it’s dying and sinks to the bottom. Then – like a butterfly returning to a caterpillar – it shrinks into a ball, and within 24 to 48 hours, buds off a new polyp with the same identical genome, she says.

It’s one of “nature’s coolest tricks”, says Guardian reader Raquel López-Aragón. “When this jellyfish gets old or gets hurt, instead of just dying like most animals, it transforms itself back into a baby jellyfish and grows up all over again. It can do this as many times as it wants, which means theoretically it never has to die from getting old, it just keeps hitting the reset button on its life.”

In the lab, where Miglietta studies them, these jellies can theoretically live for ever. However, for some in the wild, getting eaten may eventually end that dream run.

Globally, there are eight accepted species of Turritopsis – but (so far) only one holds the key to eternal life.

Immortal jellyfish are only a few millimetres in size. But, if you know what to look for, they can be found in many places, from the Mediterranean sea, to the Atlantic, from the coast of Japan to Panama and Brazil.

As another reader remarks, the immortal jellyfish does “exactly what it says on the tin”. “They have the very enviable ability to simply turn back into a juvenile at any sign of stress, which is something that I’m sure we all wish extended to humans.”

With their delicate bodies and veil of tentacles, Dr Lisa-ann Gershwin, a biologist specialising in jellyfish, describes Turritopsis as “exquisite” and “the most beautiful little creature”. But what makes them remarkable is their capacity for reincarnation.

Since ancient times, humans have speculated about eternal life, she says, it’s one of the things that unites us all.

“It’s so hardwired in humans to not want to die. And I think the drive that we have to survive, and the absurdity of that being in a jellyfish – the juxtaposition of those two just entertains me to no end.”

We launched a war on nature. Now we are in a climate war zone

The Guardian Tue, 04 Aug 2026 10:00:47 GMT

Summer is not what it once was. We have been robbed of one of life’s great joys

Far beyond the fires raging across Europe and North America, the smoke, dangerous to breathe, hangs in the air, dimming the view, changing the very color of sunlight into something grimly unsettling.

An estimated 20,000 are said to have died in the extreme heat in Europe earlier this year, and heat is climate change’s quiet killer, compared with the dramatic violence of death by fire or flood. In eastern Washington, 600 homes have just burned down, and in both Europe and North America, firefighters have died in the effort to contain the climate-fueled firestorms.

Once, across much of the the world’s temperate zones, we looked forward to summer as a time of delights, from summer’s bounty of fruits, long days, warmth, school holidays, activities like camping and swimming, travel and adventure. Now many of us dread it.

Summer was the sweet season celebrated in poetry and song, often pictured as a gentle goddess; now it is too often a threat and a misery. All this makes me think of Bill McKibben’s 2011 book Eaarth, a proposal that we can understand climate change as equivalent to moving to a more perilous, unwelcoming planet than the gentle, stable one we evolved over the 12,000 years since the last ice age.

I know that there are parts of the world where summer was already harsh, intense – 20 years ago, my friend Mark Klett, a photographer living near Phoenix, Arizona, joked: “Phoenix has two seasons: summer and hell,” summer being January and February; hell being the rest of the year.

But even in Phoenix, summer is now more intense; there, people get severe burns from falling down on superheated asphalt. It’s changed everywhere.

I’ve driven to New Mexico almost every summer since 1989. A few years ago, I found that I feared heat for the first time: the temperature in Needles, a California desert town on the Colorado River near the Arizona border, was going to be 116F (46.6C). I didn’t know if my car could survive temperatures like that, and I feared what survival would look like for me if the air-conditioned car broke down on the highway. (I managed it by staying on the edge of the Mojave Desert the night before and darting across the low desert to Flagstaff, which at 7,000ft elevation stays cooler, and pressing on to New Mexico the next day.)

I’m in New Mexico now, as I write, enjoying the beauties of its incomparable skies and summer thunderstorms, but 37 summers since I started coming, summer is not what it used to be. It’s hotter.

The monsoon rains are less reliable and often more violent when they come; one New Mexico town, Ruidoso, has over the past few years been beaten up repeatedly by flood and fire. Like so many westerners, I have too often breathed in the toxic smoke of burning forests, have followed the news of forests and towns being consumed by flames, have friends whose homes have been reduced to ash and rubble, have seen brick chimneys standing above the blackened ruins of a neighborhood.

As I hear about summer tourists sweltering miserably from Japan to Spain, I wonder if, going forward, travelers will shift peak vacation times to spring and fall, if schools will change when students have their holidays.

Keeping them indoors in air-conditioned spaces may be even a safety measure for those who lack such protection at home. Summer has too often, in too many places, become something to brace against, prepare for, and dread: the season of danger, heat, fire, misery. The New Yorker reports: “ A conflagration west of Bordeaux, described as four times the size of Paris, prompted the largest peacetime evacuation in the country’s history: 220,000 people.”

It’s as if we launched a war against nature, and that has turned place after place into something that resembles a war zone. The climate movement is a peace movement, a movement to end this war and its casualties.

We often talk about what climate change has wrecked in terms of what’s material, tangible, structures lost to fire, flood, or sea level rise, trees dying, species threatened, glaciers melting in warmer weather. But summer was an immaterial treasure and joy that belonged to all of us.

There have been youth-led lawsuits against the producers of climate chaos and the governments who’ve refused to act adequately – essentially for robbing them of their future. Robbing us all of the immeasurable joys of summer as it was is part of that theft. It’s not the main reason that climate action matters so much, but it’s a reminder that what we’re losing is not only the terms of our survival and our safety, but our freedom and pleasure.

Rebecca Solnit is a Guardian US columnist. Her newest book is The Beginning Comes After the End: Notes on a World of Change

The truth about blushing: why we do it, how we can resist it – and why it’s actually good for us

The Guardian Tue, 04 Aug 2026 09:00:17 GMT

Humans are the only animals whose faces redden with embarrassment. Should we see that as an affliction, or as a blessing?

‘Blushing is the most peculiar and most human of all expressions,” Charles Darwin once wrote, and he wasn’t wrong. Though certain species of bird pinken up as a means of communication, and uakari monkeys have red faces when in good health, we seem to be the only animal that flushes as a sign of embarrassment.

“It’s a very truthful signal,” says Prof Sophie Scott, the director of the Institute for Cognitive Neuroscience at University College London. “It’s not fakeable, and there aren’t many things that humans do that fall into that category. You can’t blush on command.”

You might, of course, hate it when it happens, but it’s a useful signal, one way or another. So what is it actually signalling? And is there any way to stop it?

To get the “Why does it happen?” question out of the way, blushing is caused by your sympathetic nervous system – the same one that kicks in when you’re stressed or frightened – triggering your fight-or-flight response. Your brain releases adrenaline, which widens the blood vessels in your face (known as vasodilation), increasing blood flow to the skin and producing a visible shift in colour.

“It’s more noticeable as a redness if your skin is pale, but everybody blushes,” says Scott. “In people who don’t have pale skin, it’s more a darkening of the skin, but your skin also does get hotter. So there’s this hall of mirrors effect: you know you’re blushing, other people know you’re blushing, and they know you know you’re blushing.” Which, of course, can make you blush even more. Other animals might exhibit involuntary physical reactions such as laughing, or screaming in terror, but blushing seems to be unique to us because it’s linked to our theory of mind: our ability to guess what other people are thinking.

This is important because we’re social animals: cooperation is what allowed us to survive and thrive when we were still hunting our food with pointed sticks. In early human societies, committing a faux pas, making a mistake or challenging a leader might have led to physical confrontation or expulsion from the group. It’s likely that blushing emerged as a way to signal recognition of rule-breaking, or genuine remorse: a way to de-escalate possibly deadly situations without any physically risky behaviour.

“It seems to be associated with increased trustworthiness,” says Scott. “When somebody blushes easily, you’re more likely to know if they’re lying to you, for instance – or even if you don’t, you think that you can. That bonding and closeness is also what helps us work in groups. We’re apex predators because we can work cooperatively and, usually, read each other’s intentions really clearly.”

Obviously, blushing can still be useful today for all of the reasons above. If we’ve dropped a clanger at work, it can be helpful to have an unfakeable signal that we genuinely regret it. But if we’re prone to blushing and hate it, is there anything we can do?

The short answer is very little. But it also might not be the disaster you think. Frequent blushers seem to view blushing more negatively than people who don’t blush all that much: if you’re aware that you blush a lot, it can create feelings of shame or self-awareness. If you’re an infrequent blusher, on the other hand – or you don’t tend to notice when you do it – then you might associate it with getting an unexpected compliment, being publicly recognised for an achievement or doing a bit of light-hearted flirting.

The good news is that, whatever it feels like, you might not actually be blushing much more than anyone else. “Our research indicated that when embarrassed, people who weren’t frightened of blushing blushed as much as people who were frightened of blushing – they just didn’t notice it so much,” says Prof Peter Drummond, the lead author on a study examining the gap between actual and perceived blushing. “When we brought this to their attention, they started to become more concerned about blushing. In this way, being worried that you might blush could actually trigger it in certain situations. However, it’s comforting to know that most people don’t even notice that others are blushing during social interactions because their attention is focused on speaking or thinking about what to say.”

If this alone isn’t a comfort, then cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT), which aims to reframe your feelings about blushing, is one option. Another is task concentration training (TCT), a form of therapy developed specifically for people whose anxiety is anchored to visible body sensations such as blushing, trembling or sweating. TCT argues that your attention is a finite resource, and so if you deliberately direct it to external data – the tone of someone’s voice, say, or what else is going on in the room – you’ll be less likely to focus on how red your face feels.

“The aim of TCT and CBT is to manage anxiety about blushing rather than the blushing response itself,” says Drummond. “Even so, given that being worried about blushing can become a self-fulfilling prophecy, reducing that anxiety can reduce how often we blush.”

Finally, it’s worth considering that, even if you hate it when you blush, there’s a decent chance that it’s doing you good overall. “I think of blushing as a ‘letting off steam’ response, as it shares the same physiological mechanism as flushing during exercise,” says Drummond. “Although we might feel hot and bothered when we blush, we generally feel better once we cool down. In fact, blushing might help dissipate unpleasant emotions such as anger, embarrassment and shame, just like flushing helps to dissipate heat generated during exercise.”

In other words, it’s showing other people you’re sincere while also helping to calm you down. Nothing at all to be ashamed of.

Ben Stokes rules out 2027 Ashes return but ambition is ‘to coach England one day’

The Guardian Tue, 04 Aug 2026 08:12:56 GMT

Captain also voices concern over Root’s return as captain

Stokes expresses surprise Brook was not made Test captain

Ben Stokes has trained his sights on becoming England head coach in the future and expressed concerns about Joe Root’s impending second stint as Test captain.

In his first interview since retiring from England duty in June – a two-hour chat with his former teammates Stuart Broad and Jos Buttler on the For The Love Of Cricket Podcast –Stokes again ruled out returning for next summer’s Ashes.

But the 35-year-old still has ambitions in the international arena, namely a possible move into coaching when he eventually calls time on his domestic career with Durham and any potential overseas franchise gigs in the coming winter.

Stokes said: “I’m doing my level three coaching now while I’m still playing because I want, when the day comes that I’m not playing any more, I’d love to be able to have all that stuff signed off and done.

“I know what I want to do in terms of staying within the game, which is to be a coach. And would I love to be coach of England one day? Absolutely. I just really like the idea of being, again, like, in some form of leadership away from playing.”

While England’s director of men’s cricket, Rob Key, has recently said the door would remain open for Stokes to make a dramatic return for next summer’s Ashes series at home, the all-rounder is currently insisting he is “definitely” retired.

One thing that might have tempted him back is his close friend Root having returned to the Test captaincy, under a new head coach in Stephen Fleming, after Key decided it was “too soon” for Harry Brook to step up.

Stokes signed off from his final Test at Trent Bridge insisting Brook, his vice-captain, should be his successor and has now reiterated the point.

The worry is that Root could once again find the job all-consuming to the detriment of his own game, while Stokes also disagreed with Brook not being asked to lead when he missed the second Test against New Zealand for disciplinary reasons.

Stokes said: “I think just if you think someone’s going to be a good captain or a good leader, then just give them it.

“Brooky was made vice-captain – I’m not there anymore, but even when I missed that Test match[against New Zealand], I was like, ‘he’s vice-captain?’

“I sort of understood the reasoning why they were saying it, but what message is that sending to him? He’s vice-captain, and the captain is not playing, but he’s not captain. And then the same again here [with the permanent role].”

On Root, who previously held the role from 2017 to early 2022 but struggled for results during the pandemic, Stokes added: “I love Rooty and I wish him nothing but success. I hope he achieves amazing things in his role as captain.

“He’s going to really enjoy working with [Fleming]. He’s a great man, I’ve worked with him before. I told Joe, I said my only worry is just you.

“And that’s all I really care about now, just because I have seen what he went through and how much he put himself through for someone.

“He’s just always put the team first, like he always comes second. And that’s just my only concern with it is just obviously knowing what he went through last time he was in charge of the team because I don’t want to see that ever happen again because I care for Joe a lot, but I wish him all the success in the world.”

Ceuta was a carnival of anti-migrant content for hateful opportunists on the right – and a lesson for the left

The Guardian Tue, 04 Aug 2026 08:00:16 GMT

It was framed as a perfect storm because nativists dearly wanted it to be. Looking on, progressives failed to meet the moment too

The live streams are still running, training their cameras on the beach at Ceuta, where nothing is happening. The self-styled citizen journalists are still pounding the streets, capturing their shaky smartphone footage. Zia Yusuf of Reform UK was out there at the weekend, wearing a crisp white shirt and smart tailored trousers, lest anyone confuse him with the other brown people there. The bad brown people.

Why was the migrant incursion at Ceuta, on the Spanish-Moroccan border, such a big story across the world? How did it manage to pique the interest of Donald Trump and Elon Musk, to feature on NBC’s Nightly News, not – shall we say – a programme massively predisposed to spotlighting news stories from continental Africa? What about it so exercised Europe’s heads of government? What made it an irresistible front-page story in the Daily Mail, the Daily Express and the Daily Telegraph?

Certainly not any kind of urgent or imminent threat to our own borders, much less the borders of the United States. The Spanish enclaves of Ceuta and Melilla operate under special exemptions from the Schengen area, rendering it almost impossible for an undocumented migrant to reach mainland Spain, about 12 miles away across the Mediterranean. Once many of the migrants realised this, they duly left.

Nor any kind of humanitarian concern for those who drowned or were killed in the crowd crush. “About 48,000 of the up to 60,000 people who came into Ceuta from Morocco returned within a day. Still, the sudden influx created a crisis for Spain’s pro-immigration government. Nearly three dozen died.” So read a New York Times subheading on Friday. And once you fight your way past the tortured syntax, did you notice anything unusual there? First the integrity of the border, then the political ramifications, then the people who died: the hierarchy of rightwing immigration discourse expressed in three perfect sentences. The death toll has since risen to either 72 or 88 – authorities disagree on the number – and nobody seems over-fussed either way.

Rather, Ceuta functions as a kind of border porn for the global far right: a locus upon which to project their most vivid and apocalyptic fantasies. If the historian Mike Davis once described the US-Mexico border wall as “a political stage set”, then in the age of the deepfake and the troll-farm, Ceuta has proved a similarly fertile source of content: the border interface reimagined as digital theatre, mass migration as primetime television.

The rich irony here is that from a securitisation standpoint, Ceuta functions almost exactly as it was intended. A six metre-high barbed-wire fence, reinforced by watchtowers and a network of video cameras, separates it from Morocco. From Ceuta, an internal checkpoint guards the only ferry route to mainland Spain. The European Union has spent years, and hundreds of millions of euros, on developing partnerships with Morocco on border management.

None of which seemed to matter in the slightest as European leaders queued up to give the Pedro Sánchez government a ritual horse-whipping. Italy reintroduced air and sea border controls with Spain. Emmanuel Macron deployed mobile units to the Spanish border to strengthen controls. Giorgia Meloni – backed by Finland, Denmark and Czechia – has argued that Spain’s membership of the Schengen area should be suspended.

And of course these are primarily domestic politicians catering to a domestic market, ahead of an electoral cycle in which incumbents in France, Italy and Poland are being outflanked by nativist insurgents to their right. Sánchez himself faces the ballot box in 2027, an election in which his government can boast strong economic growth and which his rightwing opponents will therefore be desperate to turn into a referendum on immigration.

So that’s the political angle. But really the spectacle of Ceuta represents a more primal and guttural need, particularly in the English-speaking world, for the inflammatory anti-immigration crusade to be seen as well as spoken. The photos and footage coming out of the enclave in recent days, all shot from distance and almost never in closeup, are all geared towards a single end: to encourage the viewer to see these brown bodies as a single mass, each indistinguishable from the other, the accountants and surgeons from the bomb-makers and rapists, the living from the dead.

And so, by small degrees, the line between nationalism and pure-blood white supremacy blurs a little more. Indeed, the very idea that a single border crossing 1,000 miles and two seas away from us is somehow our urgent problem, only really makes sense in a worldview whose real distinction is not between “Britain” and “abroad” but between an imagined white Christian Europe and a savage brown other.

For all this, the right does not act alone. The palpable relief on many parts of the left as most of the original 60,000 migrants returned to Morocco spoke of a worrying acquiescence: a tacit acceptance of the dangerous trope of migration as a prima facie problem. Here’s a radical thought: what if migration is only a problem to those who want it to be? What if we started seeing the mass movement of people less as an existential threat and more as a simple inevitability of human existence? Nine years ago the great Gary Younge set out in the Guardian a utopian vision of open borders and no immigration controls. What happened to that sense of vision and idealism? When did border discourse, the conversation on why and how we move, become something to be feared and not embraced?

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

Whether Ceuta was an accidental security lapse or a deliberately engineered event is actually beside the point. The point is that as the global right grows in confidence, as the migration industrial complex thirsts for new content, new border porn, there will be more Ceutas in the future. People will keep migrating and die trying, and because this is good telly it will keep happening. “Today more than ever,” writes the sociologist Mimi Sheller in her book Mobility Justice, “these borderlands are soaked in the blood of white nationalism, ethnic profiling, and enforced death in the no man’s land.”

The endgame here is massacres, vigilante violence, not “stop the boats” but shoot the boats, the border reimagined as a computer-game war zone. The endgame is what the likes of Musk and his far-right meat puppets are already depicting: a world where zombie armies of “military-age males” invade our virgin turf, and the problem is not the forces that drove them from their homes, but your “suicidal empathy”, because these are not equal humans deserving equal treatment. These are the stakes. And frankly, when the next Ceuta happens, the left needs to think of a better response than simply being thankful they went home again.

Jonathan Liew is a Guardian columnist

After five brutal years of Taliban rule, Afghan women and girls need our help – and I have a plan

The Guardian Tue, 04 Aug 2026 06:00:14 GMT

Even in the face of appalling repression, girls yearn to fulfil their educational potential. We must set up a global fund to help them

Next weekmarks the fifth anniversary of the takeover of Afghanistan by the Taliban as US coalition troops were evacuated from the country. That’s five years for the terrorists to have consolidated their grip, so now is a good time to reflect on what the “coalition of the willing” left behind.

Through vindictive edict after edict, these five years have brought an ever-escalating repression of Afghan girls and women – with far too little done by any outside authority to speak up or stand up against the most egregious denial of girls’ rights in the world today.

Barely reported was the shocking massacre in June by troops who fired on a group of women’s rights protesters as they demonstrated against girls’ exclusion from education and the enforcement of strict dress codes. They were marching under the banner “Azadi”, meaning “freedom”. Two people, including a young boy, were shot dead and several were injured.

In the most medieval of ways, the Taliban are also imposing even harsher laws to legitimise child marriage and provide legal exemption for domestic violence perpetrated by husbands, including against school-age girls.

According to UN observers, these girls, often sold into marriage or forced to become child brides, are victims of a new form of crime: gender apartheid. Historians will look back and ask why it is that, after landing more than 1 million coalition troops, suffering more than 3,500 deaths and 23,000 injuries and spending in excess of $1tn, we have been unable to prevent the Taliban destroying the most basic of rights. But perhaps more important, and with the Taliban entrenched in Kabul and religious leaders regularly sending out instructions from Kandahar, the question for now is: what can we do immediately to improve the lives of girls and women?

Can we help them fulfil their potential? Globally, the proportion of women aged 20-24 who were married before 18 has declined over the past decade, and Unicef suggests at least 25m child marriages that could have involved school-age brides have been prevented. Yet an estimated 12 million girls under 18 are still married off each year when they could be at school.

The issue is acute in the Afghanistan the coalition left behind, where girls are banned from secondary schooling and Afghan women are banned from university, public sector employment and even work with NGOs and charities. They are forbidden to travel or to enter many public places, from parks to restaurants, unless accompanied. And with the Taliban confident that they can act with impunity, a dozen recent anti-girl, anti-women injunctions are tightening their grip. In one recent case, a 15-year-old Afghan girl is reported to have been killed, along with her mother, by a Taliban official after he tried to abduct her for a forced marriage.

It is appalling, and it does speak to the particular brutality of the Taliban. Pakistan’s Sindh province, by contrast, has enacted one of the strongest legal frameworks in the developing world against child marriage, criminalising marriage under 18 and introducing penalties for those who facilitate it.

Bangladesh, too, has enacted new laws. A stronger birth registration system has made it harder to conceal a girl’s age, closing off a common pathway into early marriage. At the same time, programmes providing small-scale financial support to poor families have enabled girls to remain in education. Save the Children reports that in one programme in Bangladesh, the offer of financial support helped more than 1,000 girls stay in school and avoid early marriage. Child marriage is not simply a cultural practice, as often portrayed. It is also driven by poverty, as much as weak enforcement of the law.

There are “child marriage-free zones” in parts of Pakistan and Bangladesh, where young people come together to support any school friend who is being married off against her will. Young people become known as “wedding busters” because of their willingness to intervene. With assistance and will, so much is possible.

It is no accident that the Taliban have focused so much attention not just on denying women rights but specifically on denying them an education, because they know, as we do, that schooling is the most potent enabler. Across the world, it is the single most powerful protection against early marriage. Organisations such as Girls Not Brides have established that every additional year a girl spends in secondary education significantly reduces the likelihood that she will be married as a child.

If we could open the doors to quality schooling, ensure girls had access to safe spaces and provide financial support for their families, tens of thousands more could get that education. Even in Afghanistan, that is no pipe dream. Through Unicef and Education Cannot Wait, and with secret, on-the-ground support, girls are learning in unconventional ways: often online, sometimes in underground schools or in family homes, unseen by the authorities.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

But there is so much more to be done, not least because thousands of girls have had to leave the country to obtain schooling, and with tension rising between Afghanistan and Pakistan, one favoured route out of the country is fast closing.

Britain’s home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, has announced that under the new immigration and asylum bill, there will be two routes under a refugee resettlement scheme for students that could help girls get the education they have been denied. The first is through recognised charities sponsoring girls coming to the UK. The second is through colleges and universities offering scholarships.

That’s good, but we must go further. I believe a fund must now be set up in support of Afghan girls who are threatened with being married off against their will. It should offer them bursaries to continue their education, if necessary outside their home country. And as UN special envoy for education, I am happy to work with any charity or educational institution that wants to assist girls in defence of their human rights.

It may be a small gesture, but five years after they were condemned to Taliban rule, isn’t it time to truly support all the girls who risk their freedom and their lives for an education, and the hope of a meaningful existence? They yearn for things we take for granted. It is our moral duty to help them.

Gordon Brown is the UN’s special envoy for global education and was UK prime minister from 2007 to 2010

‘They’re not alone’: Chris Hoy on his ambition to stop men dying of prostate cancer

The Guardian Tue, 04 Aug 2026 05:00:13 GMT

Cycling legend on living with a stage 4 diagnosis, fundraising with Miguel Induráin and why Andy Burnham could be key to his ambition of helping others

Sir Chris Hoy arrives a couple of minutes late and the apologies roll from him. I don’t have a chance to tell the six‑time Olympic sprint cycling champion that waiting an hour for a star interviewee is more common. Hoy is already deep into a story about how he and his wife, Sarra, were walking here when an unknown man stopped him on the street in Glasgow.

The stranger had recently been diagnosed with prostate cancer and he wanted to share what had happened to him and, I suspect, find new strength by talking to a compassionate public figure. Hoy has lived a full life with stage 4 cancer for nearly three years. He has also worked tirelessly to highlight the fact that prostate cancer affects more men in this country than any other cancer while, at the same time, to offer a tangible sense of hope when there is horror for men, and their families, after a terminal diagnosis.

Hearing a discreet account of this encounter, it sounds as if the 50‑year‑old Hoy helped the man at a raw and vulnerable moment. “It’s so isolating when you get a cancer diagnosis,” Hoy says. “You’re suddenly on borrowed time. You’re observing the world and not living in it – because it’s for other people. But then you realise you’re not special and it’s very common, sadly. I want to make sure that anyone in a similar situation will realise they’re not alone.

“I also want to raise awareness that 10,000 men a year get the news that they have stage 4 prostate cancer. A lot of it comes down to a lack of awareness so we need to get men to understand the risk.”

In September 2023, Hoy saw his physiotherapist about a nagging pain in his shoulder. Without any other symptoms he assumed he had strained a muscle while lifting weights. The physio sent him for a scan, which identified a tumour in his shoulder. Two days later, a second scan brought shattering news. The primary cancer was in his prostate and had spread to his pelvis, hip, spine, ribs and shoulder. “Just like that,” Hoy wrote in his memoir, “I learn how I die.”

His life-expectancy was said to be between two and four years. I ask Hoy how he is feeling now. “I’m doing really well, thank you,” he says. “As well as can be expected, really.”

How often is he tested? “On average, between every three and six months. But if there’s an area of activity you might have it more frequently. You have blood tests regularly and there’re periods where you’re in and out of the hospital. The regular blood tests are horrible because it’s like the clock is ticking. At some point that afternoon or the next day, you’ll get that email.

“I remember when I was about to walk on stage for a talk. It was one of these ‘An Evening With …’ events. It had sold out and I was just about to go out in front of a packed audience. I shouldn’t have done it, but I checked my phone and the results were there. The PSA [prostate-specific antigen] had gone back up. It was like: ‘Oh God.’ And then: ‘Put your phone down, put a smile on and do it.’”

Hoy makes a grimace before smiling more wryly. “In a way the concentration of being on stage helped.”

When did this happen? “Probably last summer. Even the Tour de 4 [the charity bike ride in Scotland which Hoy led for the first time in September last year] was difficult. The treatment at that point had started to fail so I was changing to a different treatment. Only with hindsight do you realise [the difficulties].

“For me, the worst is when you walk into the consultant’s room. You’re immediately trying to read their body language. Is it good news? Is it bad news? Let’s get to the punchline. So it’s why I’ve switched to Zoom for these meetings about my results. You can switch it off and you’re in your sanctuary, your home. You don’t have to be in the hospital, walking past strangers, having that long drive home.”

He seems able to live in the moment better than most people, but does the fact that he is approaching the end of his third year of a supposedly limited life‑expectancy play on his mind? “A little, but not really because these are average statistics you get in the very early days. You have to remember the people outliving those statistics can’t be added to the data yet.

“But not everybody is as lucky as me to respond to treatment. Sadly, you have people like Dermot Murnaghan [the television journalist who died from prostate cancer last month]. I’d been confident and hopeful he and I would do the Tour de 4 for many years to come. So that was a big blow, a huge shock when I got the message from his family saying the time was coming.”

Hoy continues to live with real vitality – even if he endured a serious accident on his mountain bike in November. He was racing down a trail in south Wales when, at speed, he misjudged a steep jump. Hoy still shudders at the memory.

He was warned that if surgery was unsuccessful his leg might have to be amputated, but Hoy plays down the situation now. “It’s shocking at the time, but they have to tell you what could happen from a legal perspective. It wasn’t a little fracture of the leg. It was a full reconstruction of the tibial plateau. A friend of mine who’s a doctor saw the X-rays and said: ‘Oh. That’s the kind of X-ray you’ll see when someone’s parachute hasn’t deployed.”

Hoy describes his post-op recovery as “a miserable, incredibly difficult time”, saying: “I was keeping my head above water and everything was going OK and then you have this freak accident. You have a lot of time sat around thinking, which you don’t want to be doing.”

He looks down at his right leg and says: “It’s just metalwork from here [just below his knee] down to here [near the ankle]. It’s not what I needed and yet the irony is that mountain biking gives me so much physically, mentally and socially. Being out in the fresh air and being in the moment is so good for me.”

A new fortnightly newsletter covering the intersection of sport and the climate crisis

after newsletter promotion

Hoy was soon back on his bike and last month, despite another injury to his “good” leg, he cycled across Spain with riders including his teenage hero Miguel Induráin, a five-time Tour de France winner. “I was on holiday in Greece and feeling great. I had this big charity ride across Spain coming up, coast-to-coast, with Miguel and others. Amazing. I was sitting cross-legged on a paddle board with my son for quite a long time, just watching the sunrise.

“When I stepped off the paddleboard, my weight shifted, and there was sharp pain: ‘Oh. That didn’t feel good.” It was a torn meniscus and there was this little piece floating about in the knee.

“It was four days before I went out to Spain but so many people were coming I couldn’t say: ‘I’ve got a knee injury, I’m not coming.’ I thought I’ll take my bike and see what I can do. I was hobbling through the airport using my carry-on case as a crutch, thinking: ‘This is ridiculous, I can’t even walk.’ But on the bike you never fully extend your knee. So, tentatively, I was like: ‘This doesn’t feel too bad.’ And long story short, I managed to get through the week and we raised £200,000 and had an amazing experience.”

He somehow rode alongside the mighty Induráin with a torn meniscus? “Yes. He’s not your average 62-year-old. He still does these crazy 10-hour rides and he’s as fit as a butcher’s dog. It was a huge honour to be with him.”

Such drive, against all odds, stands in stark contrast to the laxity that epitomises the failure of successive governments to take coherent action against prostate cancer. “I can’t see how the government are not coming up with some form of proactive decision,” he says. “They say that the risk of testing every man, and the number of men who would have elevated PSA levels, would then lead to too many being unnecessarily treated, and then having to deal with the consequences of surgery or treatment. To me, that’s a treatment issue, not a screening issue … I don’t know why we don’t [have a screening system]. It just doesn’t make sense.”

Hoy has other pressing concerns. Sarra was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis two months after he heard he had stage 4 cancer. But, worrying about him, she kept the news from her husband for almost a month. “She’s incredible,” Hoy says. “She’s receiving treatment and doing really well. Sarra took up cycling to do the Tour de 4 and she’s physically fitter than she’s ever been. She’s adamant that [MS] won’t get in the way. She’s doing all she can to support me and the family.”

How are their children, 11‑year‑old Callum and eight‑year‑old Chloe? “Kids’ concept of time is very different to ours and they know how to live in the moment. They were more concerned when I broke my leg than about my cancer diagnosis, because they could see me in pain. I was unable to get up.

“Cancer is an abstract concept for kids and we’ve tried not to allow it to change family life too much. They understand the situation but, equally, they’re living in the here and now.”

Next month, with Tour de 4, he and Sarra hope to raise even more than the £3.1m they made last year for cancer research. Hoy is inspired by the rapid progress being made in medical science in terms of treating, and potentially, finding a cure for the disease. “From what I’ve been told by people at the forefront of new treatments, this is the most exciting time for prostate cancer drug development in the last 25 years. They’ve seen a real upturn in new treatments and new therapies.”

This additional source of hope means Hoy is still full of ambition. He has just completed work as a pundit for TNT at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, where the cycling was held at the velodrome named after him.

“I also have ambitions to help decision-makers do something proactive. A change of prime minister, with Andy Burnham, might help. I’ve met him a couple of times and he’s good friends with [the former GB cyclist] Chris Boardman. I would love to speak to Andy and see what he thinks we could do.

“I have all kinds of goals and the biggest are raising as much money as we can for these amazing charities, changing perceptions of what is possible during a stage 4 diagnosis and also trying to one day have some proactive gateway to screen men – so less men die of prostate cancer as a result of my diagnosis. That would be quite something.”

This article was amended on 4 August 2026. An earlier version said prostate cancer had the highest mortality rate of any disease in the UK; in fact, it is the most common form of cancer in men. Also, France does not have a screening program as an earlier quote said. This reference has been removed.

‘The war leaked into every lesson’: learning Ukrainian in a country under siege

The Guardian Tue, 04 Aug 2026 04:00:12 GMT

Soon after my first visit to Ukraine four years ago, I began language lessons. It taught me more than I ever expected

Almost as soon as I returned from my first reporting trip to Ukraine, in October 2022, I decided to start Ukrainian lessons. Not as an act of solidarity, exactly, but as a marker that I was committed to returning. I wanted to know some Ukrainian in order to feel less helpless, to edge towards a better understanding of what I was reporting, and to be more courteous to those whom I encountered. And I hoped, in time, to be able to pull myself through a piece of poetry in the original.

I began meeting Olha, my teacher, by weekly video call later that autumn. She was in Ivano-Frankivsk, her home town in the far west of Ukraine, I was in London. With endless patience and humour, she led me by the hand through the unfamiliar letters of her language, those elegant, sensuous shapes of the Cyrillic alphabet.

I have not yet fully internalised them, as I have the Roman alphabet, whose shapes are so much part of me that I don’t see them any more. The unfamiliarity of Cyrillic characters, by contrast, allows me to enjoy the exhilarating ski-slope swoop of the Л (l), the generous expanses of the Ю (yu), and the majestic architecture of the Ж (zh), which spreads out its arms and legs like candelabra. (Enjoy, please, the extravagant double Ж in Запоріжжя – Zaporizhzhia – which has a particularly graceful etymology: it means “beyond the rapids”.) And, though I shrink from trying either to write or decode the curlicued Ukrainian cursive, just forming these letters is a joy for the hand: the twin sweep of a З (z) and the harsh angles of a Д (d), which I like to write as a triangle with a pair of sharp, inward-facing tails dangling from it.

Then there is the special category of Cyrillic letters reserved only for the Ukrainian language. You may see, for example, on a Ukrainian necklace or bracelet, or on a T-shirt, the letter Ї – like our letter I, surmounted by a diaeresis. The character, which expresses the sound “yi” – as in Kyiv (Київ) – is absent from the Russian variant of the alphabet, and thus operates as a subtle signifier of allegiance. In occupied Mariupol, in 2022, the letter Ї was seen scrawled in chalk on the ­streets – a single letter as an act of defiance. I enjoy the fact that in the transliteration of my surname, Гіґґінс, there is another Ukrainian-only letter, Ґ, which, from its jaunty upturned serif, one can tell is the rare hard g, most commonly employed for loan words; it was removed from the alphabet in Stalin-era reforms, and formally given back a place in the Ukrainian alphabet after the fall of the Soviet Union and Ukrainian independence in 1991.

There is a text artwork that I love, by the sculptor Nathan Coley, installed in a library in Edinburgh, which consists of the sentence: The Basic Material is Not the Word but the Letter. I often think of it when navigating a forest of Cyrillic signs. Thick accumulations of Ukrainian consonants conspire against my tongue and my memory: airless crushes of them, like the compressed folds of a concertina. I cannot tell you how many repetitions it took to memorise незважаючи на (nezvazhayuchy na) – “despite” in Ukrainian. It seemed important to master this phrase. How else could I say, “despite the war”? Emblematic of the many sound collisions in Ukrainian is the magnificent single letter Щ, expressed in English as “shch” – as in “fresh cheese” , as one of my grammar books puts it. After much deliberation, I have only come up with one word in English (with the exception of those we have borrowed, such as borshch) that contains this fricative-affricative alliance: “pushchair”. Four whole letters in English for a single pair of glorious, fat loops in Ukrainian.

I had studied classics at university, and recklessly, perhaps arrogantly, felt that I needn’t be defeated by a tricky language. I knew, at least, what I was getting into with Ukrainian nouns, which, like those in Latin and Greek, come in three genders – masculine, feminine and neuter – and are inflected, meaning their endings change depending on what role they perform in a sentence. Even so, I feel that seven case endings, which is one more than Latin, and two more than Greek, is a lot. Their usage is almost baroque in its excess: I have a kind of stunned respect for a language in which some numbers – but by no means all, and for no perceptible reason – demand to be followed by the genitive case. One says п’ятдесят доларів (pyatdesyat dolariv), meaning $50, the genitive case; but п’ятдесят два долари (pyatdesyat dva dolary), $52, using the ordinary nominative. On the other hand, $51 has yet another ending, because the crucial extra dollar bill you have added to your 50 means that it is, according to the Ukrainian language, a singular, however hard you may protest that you are, in fact, clutching a fistful of dollars.

I had heard rumours of the perils of Ukrainian “verbs of motion”, which turned out to be more than well founded. Speakers of Slavonic languages describe movement at a level of subtlety that, to an anglophone, seems absolutely bewildering. Ukrainian has two basic verbs where we have one to express the idea of “to go” – the first used for travelling on foot and the second for travelling by some form of transport. Both of those, in turn, come in different forms depending on whether you are moving in one direction only, or going there and back again. That is true for other verbs of motion, right down to, say, the verb to crawl. Is your baby moving across the floor in one direction? Or is she planning on taking an indirect route, or perhaps undertaking this journey regularly? Answer these questions before selecting your verb form!

Learning Ukrainian, it turned out, was more than a side-interest, an extracurricular activity. It forced me to look at myself in entirely new ways. In my 50s – treading the pleasant plateau of knowing broadly how to do my job after all these years – it was confronting to be back at the bottom rung of knowledge, out of my depth. There would be moments – when Olha was speaking to me, or when I was trying to keep up with what Ukrainian friends were saying, or even during a seemingly predictable encounter in a cafe – when I would feel an unfamiliar, blind panic rising to engulf me. It would start out well, I would be clinging on to comprehension, and then there would be a block, a word or phrase I would snag on, or an unexpected conversational current – and I would lose my grip. I recognised the feeling from only one other area of my life: playing chamber music. When you lose your place in a Beethoven quartet, say, and everyone else is moving onwards at speed, you can feel stranded, as if you are watching the vessel of the music slip into the distance without you. The redeeming fact is that attempting to speak even terrible Ukrainian in Ukraine is met, in my experience, with a response on a scale set between courteous acceptance and ecstatic (and undeserved) gratitude.

But my new language was also the language of war. From the very first, the experience was quite unlike that of studying Italian, the only other modern language in which I can claim any kind of proficiency – a language, for the learner, full of the pleasures of ordering cappuccino and gelato, for asking directions to the duomo, and exclaiming over the splendour of il paese più bello del mondo – the most beautiful country in the world. The very first sentences in Ukrainian that I read – when Olha introduced herself – were coloured by her wistfulness for a life that war had forced her to leave behind: До війни я жила в Києві. Я дуже люблю це місто і хочу знову там жити. “Before the war I lived in Kyiv. I love this city very much and want to live there again.”

It would be wrong to suggest that every lesson was filled with darkness. We laughed a lot. Olha often steered us towards a world of red wine and ice-cream, of opera and music and reading. The Ukrainian delight in the consumption of delicious food (a constant pleasure, thanks to the excellence of produce grown in the чорнозем, or chornozem, the fertile black earth) was present in our lessons. Soon I learned the words смачний (smachnyi), tasty, and смачного! (smachnoho!), bon appetit! – lip-smackingly onomatopoeic vocabulary, full of the joy of the Ukrainian table. But the war leaked into every lesson. Indefinite pronouns were explained to me via the example Ніхто не любить Путіна – “No one likes Putin”. The impersonal expressions communicating necessity, треба and потрібно (treba and potribno), were illustrated via a speech made on the eve of war by Valerii Zaluzhnyi, then commander-in-chief of the Ukrainian armed forces, about the urgent need to be equipped for battle. Треба готуватися до війни – “We must prepare for war.” Нам треба мати ресурси, потрібно 300 танків – “We need to have resources, we need 300 tanks.”

My vocabulary grew to include the words for drone and rocket, explosion, bomb shelter and air-raid alarm. There is a Telegram channel that is commonly consulted when an air-raid alert goes off in Ukraine, as it provides details on whether there are drones on the way, or ballistic missiles, and their direction of travel. For ease I switched this channel to English, using an automatic translate function. With every new siren, it leapt into life, asking, “Why the anxiety?” It took me a while to figure out that the word used for air-raid alarm, тривога (tryvoha) also means “anxiety” in Ukrainian. (The English word “alarm” behaves similarly, being both the mechanism that produces the sound, and the feeling it engenders.) But still, every time I checked it I imagined it was asking me, yet again, a sarcastic question about my state of mind.

As Christmas 2022 arrived, Olha and I read a speech of Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s that contained a nice example of the compound future tense formed by an auxiliary verb and the infinitive: Ми будемо співати колядки – голосніше ніж генератор. “We are going to sing carols – louder than a generator.” The noisy chugging of generators side by side on a pavement, servicing a row of shops during a blackout, would become a familiar music to me. In the same speech, the president also provided an introduction to impersonal adverbial constructions suggesting a state or condition. Нам може бути темно, холодно і складно. Але нам більше не страшно. “It may be dark, cold and difficult for us, but we are no longer afraid.” That winter truly was dark. Even in far-western Ivano-­Frankivsk, Olya was affected by Russian attacks on power infrastructure designed to freeze Ukraine into submission. Blackouts meant the cancellation of several lessons.

In time a kind of intimacy sprang up between us: there is something vulnerable-making about learning a language, when your normal ease of expression crumbles and you have to start again like a child acquiring speech for the first time, but oh, so much more slowly. You open yourself up to being and sounding foolish as you reach for ways to say what you mean. You build fragile little linguistic structures, and they collapse time and time again. You want to cry like a child with frustration. Olha – younger than me by a good 15 years – reassured me like an encouraging parent.

Soon I was speaking excitedly of plans for another reporting trip. Olha’s notes recorded our dialogue. У які міста ти будеш їхати? Я буду їхати у Київ, у Ізюм, у Харків і теж яхочу їхати у Херсон. “What cities are you going to go to?” “I am going to go to Kyiv, Izium and Kharkiv, and I want to go to Kherson, too.” Olha must have asked what my partner thought of all this – an extremely good question. I offered the truthful although carelessly incomplete reply, Мій чоловік розуміє, як це важливо для мене. “My partner understands how important this is to me.”

When I returned from that trip – it had been my first time to eastern Ukraine and to territories recently clawed back from Russian occupation – Olha asked for my impressions. I described seeing зруйновані вулиці, мости, будинки – “destroyed streets, bridges, buildings”. Це було дуже стресово для тебе? “Was it very stressful for you?” she asked. Another good question. Було стресово бачити міста зруйновані. “It was stressful to see destroyed towns,” I replied, evasively, perhaps enjoying wrapping my tongue around the word зруйновані – zruynovani, ruined. At that moment I lacked either sufficient insight into my own emotions, or the linguistic skill to explain precisely how stressful this trip had in fact been. It was a world away from any kind of journalism I had done before: the mass grave site; the hours with the grieving parents of a killed son; the sorrow of it all.

In Lviv, a couple of months ago, I attended an intensive language programme. I put great hope into this course, as if it were not a series of lessons but rather a magical linguistic wand that would offer me the gift of tongues. When we arrived – the 20-odd students, an eclectic group of mainly Americans, some with Ukrainian roots, some at university, some volunteering for the Ukrainian cause in one way or another – we were given a written test and an interview. On the basis of this, I was placed in what became understood as the “top class”. I spent two weeks in this class, with three excellent female classmates, taught by a gentle and learned teacher, having my sense of myself as a competent person systematically undone. No English was uttered in these classes, as we discussed such subjects as the wartime rifts in Ukrainian society and were tasked with preparing presentations to the assembled staff and student body – something I would shudder to do even in English.

Every evening, I went home to my flat fighting the urge to weep, convinced that there had been an error and I was simultaneously “holding everyone up” and “letting the side down”. One of the Americans – a level-headed economist who, when she finished her course, was told she held the record for speed of learning – gently pointed out that we had been placed in our classes based on our scores in a test. Perhaps, she offered, my response was gendered? Would many men be flailing around in quite this level of self-doubt? I despairingly messaged a colleague and friend who’d learned Russian as a teenager, who briskly informed me that he had cheated an aptitude test in his youth precisely to be in a confounding top class; that he had observed at work that I was a very competitive person; and that I should sit back and enjoy the sensation of not being the best at something.

I had not expected to be recalibrating my relationship with myself, or to be confronting the gap between my own and others’ perceptions of myself, in this way. There were other moments of inner tumult, too – the day we discussed Victoria Amelina in class: a Ukrainian novelist who had become a friend, and who died of her injuries after a Russian cruise missile targeted a pizza restaurant she had just sat down in. Or the morning we were asked to read out our favourite Ukrainian poem. I chose a very recent work: My Day, by poet and film-maker Iryna Tsilyk. It anatomises the peculiar state of being that engulfs people living behind the lines, where incompatible experiences (sheltering in the corridor from an air raid, making pancakes for your son’s breakfast, attending a funeral, dithering over whether to buy zinfandel or pinot noir in a supermarket aisle) are crammed together in bizarre and uncomfortable proximity. I read it aloud, as directed, fairly competently until the line “I cried in the park” (Плакала в парку – plakala v parku), at which point I felt a surging desire to cry myself. Natalya, our teacher, gently took over the reading. It wasn’t just me feeling overwhelmed at times. You don’t turn up in wartime Ukraine for an intensive language course just for the hell of it.

I try not to envy the young. There are many reasons not to. But I did come to envy brains that could more readily absorb, memorise and parrot languages than mine. Ukrainian vocabulary is, to me, truly difficult to remember. It is an Indo-European language, which helps up to a point – it shares deep roots with English, such that some basic words are familiar (such as мати, сестра, maty, sestra – mother, sister). But it is a much more distant relation than, say, German, or the Romance languages. In Italian, for example, the verb “to use” is usare. Fine, done. In Ukrainian, the verb “to use” is використовувати, vykorystovuvaty. No apparent connection to English, an absolute pain to memorise, seven syllables.

And yet, while ordinary, everyday words such as the verb “to use” seemed almost unconquerable, somehow I found it easy to memorise words and phrases in two distinct categories: pointlessly poetic, or plain rude. For my own satisfaction, for example, I made an English translation of Tsilyk’s My Day. It contains a line about the sound of distant rockets; the noise is described as шелест (shelest), a word that describes the whisper of leaves in the wind. I spent ages puzzling over how to translate the word in the context of her poem, since, though I could see that a very distant rocket might make a kind of shivering sound like a wind-shaken tree, the English word “rustling” felt wrong, and I couldn’t imagine rockets doing it (I settled on “eerie thrum” in the end, although I’m not entirely satisfied with it). Of course, that left me with a perfect recall of the Ukrainian word for “rustling” – but what good was this piece of knowledge, when I couldn’t even remember the verb “to use”? My friend Mariana cheerfully informed me that the word, in verb form, appeared in an older famous poem, by Pavlo Tychyna, dating from 1911: Ви знаєте, як липа шелестить / У місячні весняні ночі? (“You know how the linden rustles / On moonlit nights in spring?”). I memorised it with ease. I suppose it might come in handy sometime, if I’m ever passing a lime tree with a Ukrainian on a breezy May evening.

In 2025, I visited the Kharkiv studio of the artist Pavlo Makov. He was finishing a work – a large, bright drawing in pastels – of a very battered-looking, ordinary plant. A weed, many people would say, but it is not a weed: it is a humble and in its way rather handsome plant, which also grows in Britain and the US, with oval leaves and modest flowers on little spikes, often seen on verges and in the cracks in the pavement. I confess I did not know the English word for it, until I sent a photo to my brother, a botanist: it is the common plantain. (Not to be confused with the fruit, a different species altogether.) In Ukrainian, Makov told me, it is called подорожник, podorozhnyk – because it lives along (по, po) the road (дорога, doroha). The drawing was, he told me, a kind of portrait of himself and other Ukrainians, who – battered but alive, ragged but tough – are metaphorically living by the road, just a rocket or drone strike away from losing a home and being displaced. Подорожник is also known as a healing plant in Ukraine – you pick a leaf and press it against a scratch or a sting. Now, every time I see this inconspicuous little plant in England – something I couldn’t name in my own language before I could in Ukrainian – I am tugged back to Kharkiv, my mind filled with thoughts of lives full of instability, but pursued with a kind of rooting toughness.

As for the bad words – yes, I can swear like a Mykolaiv dockworker, and have a repertoire of disreputable phrases, many of them learned on long car journeys on reporting trips. On one occasion, I was in the car with two much younger female colleagues. We were looking at some photos. I regret to inform you of the occasional low level of chat among us, but one of these photos was of a good-looking young man, with a hipster moustache. Finding a boyfriend, for many of my female Ukrainian friends, presents certain difficulties: men are absent, at the front, on the whole. But I’m always keeping half an eye open for them. Just in case. As we appraised this particular image, one of us giggled and uttered the phrase усики – пропуск в трусики (usyky – propusk v trusyky) which I suppose, loosely translated, means, “a ’tache is a pass to your panties”. Utterly memorable, nicely rhyming in Ukrainian, it stuck at once. Not entirely useless, either, if you decouple the vocabulary from the particular phrase: пропуск, propusk, could be your pass for a festival or workplace, or the gap left on a form for you to fill in your information. Tрусики, trusyky, is a perfectly respectable word for underwear. As a phrase used in its entirety (judiciously, of course, in the right company), it causes Ukrainian men to finger their upper lips nervously and Ukrainian women to erupt in laughter.

Even when I was not working on Ukrainian stories, and was immersed in writing about culture in the UK or the US, that act of plugging away, however slowly, at Ukrainian kept a thread of connection with the country, and with my friends there. Though, at times, it would have been easier to forget about Ukraine, because the memories could be so painful: the rescue workers gently easing a corpse from the ruins of the smashed Kyiv apartment building; the crumpling face of the mother who had lost her son; the young artist with the radiant eyes who was haunted by guilt after a brother soldier had been killed beside him. Through all of this, it was impossible to forget that, though I wasn’t learning Ukrainian to make any kind of political point, the Ukrainian language itself was deeply concerned with the war.

The Russian president, Vladimir Putin, repeatedly claimed that the invasion, or special military operation as he initially called it, had been mounted in order to rescue Russian speakers in Ukraine from a repressive state. This seemed especially ironic given that the Russian military bombed and killed thousands of civilians in, for example, Mariupol, a largely russophone city. In the wake of the invasion, and Putin’s propaganda, many Ukrainians have switched away from the Russian language (including the president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy). New Ukrainian-language bookshops have blossomed, despite the war, on the streets of Kyiv and other cities. “People began to understand that the Russians came here to kill people simply because they were Ukrainian,” Bohdana Laiuk, an editor and cultural manager, now Ukraine’s deputy minister for culture, told me. “So people are asking: what does it actually mean to be Ukrainian? Literary culture gives us the place to understand who we are.” Since the Maidan protests of 2013-14, and especially since 2022, embracing the Ukrainian language has, for many, been an active, personal act of decolonisation.

But the politics of language are also a matter for passionate debate. “If you are ever short of conversation at a Ukrainian party,” joked Olha once, “just ask about language.” I remember witnessing an argument between two friends. One, much more positive about Russian-speaking Ukrainians, was an academic based in western Ukraine. The other was a Ukrainian-speaker from the Kharkiv region, who remembered being bullied as a child for speaking his own language in the big Russified city, and who argued that the Ukrainian language should be protected by strong legal frameworks.

Artist Pavlo Makov, who was born in 1958, took a different view again. Although he was born into a Russian family, his father insisted he should be able to speak Ukrainian. So he grew up bilingual, loving Ukrainian-language children’s books and comics. “Being a citizen of Ukraine means much more to me than the fact that I am ethnically Russian,” he said. But “we should maintain our knowledge of Russian”, he argued: Ukrainians needed to understand the country across its eastern border. For him, it was a complex and personal matter. “Russian is the language of the enemy, yes – but it was also the language of my mum.”

I talked to friends who had stopped using the Russian language. It takes years to set aside the language of your mum. Even if you speak your chosen language perfectly, you might think in the old language, or dream in the old language, and when that is all past, there are still things that may persist in the old language – memories of the books you read when you were little, for example. One of my friends, writer and cultural manager Sasha Dovzhyk, wrote a remarkable essay about her rejection of Russian. “My mother tongue tastes like ashes,” she wrote. “I felt the taste of my mother tongue most acutely while driving through Borodianka, Bucha and Irpin two months after these Ukrainian towns in the Kyiv region were liberated by the Ukrainian army from the Russians’ ‘brotherly’ embrace.” Her rage and horror turned inwards, into her own body, into the very words she had first formed as a baby on her mother’s lap. “Russian,” she wrote, “is my mother tongue and liberation means ripping it out of my throat.”

You think about time a lot when you are learning a language. How much time do I have to devote to this pursuit? How much time will it take me to get where I want to be, linguistically? The curious thing was that the horizon of desire kept receding into the distance, and likewise, the time it might take me to get there also moved into the barely perceptible future. When I first started Ukrainian, I wanted only to be able to read road signs, exchange pleasantries and order coffee, but soon my desires stretched – from booking a pedicure on the phone, say, to understanding my friends so that they didn’t always feel the need to switch to English. At the same time, I had to keep revising my short-term expectations downwards, making peace with the fact that, after four years, I was still only OK at Ukrainian, and often stumbled over basics.

One day, early in 2026, I went to a gallery in London showing a work called Repeat After Me, by the Ukrainian artists’ collective Open Group. I had first seen this work in 2024 in Lviv, then later that year at the Venice Biennale. The work is a video installation, with screens on which Ukrainian refugees imitate the sounds of war, and then invite visitors to “repeat after me”, karaoke-style. On one screen, Svitlana, from the Luhansk region, re-created the sound of a Ka-52 Alligator – a Russian attack helicopter designed to take out tanks and infrastructure. Antonina came next, singing the mournful, gut-clenching wail of the air-raid siren. Iryna imitated a T-80 tank, while Boris, from Mariupol, mimicked the keeeeen-thunk sound of aerial bombing. “Repeat after me,” he said, “so you’ll remember.”

This was also the language of war, a new unwritten dialect of violence that Ukrainians had learned and absorbed not out of choice, but because they needed to – so you could hear the direction the Shahed drone was moving in, or differentiate between the outgoing crump of air defence and the sharp blast of incoming explosions. At the gallery opening I chatted with one of the artists, Anton Varga, who complimented me on my Ukrainian – so much improved, he said, since the last time he’d heard it. I thanked him. But it was not because of my diligence, I realised. It was just that time had passed. Even a lazy student – or to be kinder to myself, a time-poor student – will get somewhere after four years. My progress, I understood, was just a clock – a clock that marked the painful pace of war.

This is an adapted extract from Ukrainian Lessons: Art in a Time of War by Charlotte Higgins, published on 20 August. To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop. com
