Inside the Oval Office Showdown Between Trump and Jeanine Pirro

The New York Times August 04, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

Jeanine Pirro, the U. S. attorney for the District of Columbia, told President Trump that his interior secretary, Doug Burgum, had misled him with a self-serving cover story for his own mistakes.

By Tyler PagerGlenn Thrush and Katie Rogers

Tyler Pager and Katie Rogers cover the White House. Glenn Thrush covers the Justice Department. They reported from Washington.

Jeanine Pirro had had it up to here with Doug Burgum. The famously voluble U. S. attorney for the District of Columbia strode into the Oval Office late Monday with her future on the line and the interior secretary, whom she privately called an incompetent liar, in her cross hairs.

A few hours earlier — in front of the cameras, from the Resolute Desk — President Trump had accused Ms. Pirro, an ally and friend from New York going back decades, of “folding like an umbrella” and “choking” after she withdrew charges against a man accused of destroying the lining of his beloved but shoddily renovated Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.

Why was he so angry at her? Because Ms. Pirro had dared to publicly demolish one of his most cherished narratives, promoted by Mr. Burgum, that vandals — and not a contractor hired by the Interior Department to do a rushed job — had defaced a Washington landmark.

Mr. Trump raged against Ms. Pirro in private on Monday. Then he raged a little to reporters. Rumors she would be fired burbled through West Wing. Then he raged a little bit more before hosting a high-drama, face-to-face meeting with Ms. Pirro at the White House worthy of two decorated veterans of confrontational reality TV.

Mr. Burgum had been invited too, so Ms. Pirro came prepared. She entered the White House from the West Executive driveway in a bright red blazer that matched her fight-back mood, schlepping a white box containing evidence, plus a black box with documents, on wheels.

Waiting for her in the Oval Office, along with the president: Mr. Trump’s chief of staff, Susie Wiles, and David Warrington, the White House counsel.

After about an hour of intense back-and-forth, Ms. Pirro emerged with her job intact, for now.

During the meeting, Ms. Pirro, her voice raised at times, directly confronted Mr. Burgum, accusing him of misleading the president. She made the case that Mr. Burgum had promoted a self-serving cover story to conceal his own missteps.

Mr. Burgum spoke less, but did his best to defend himself, according to a person briefed on the exchange requesting anonymity to discuss internal conversations.

Mr. Trump seemed considerably less angry by day’s end, the person said.

Spokespeople for the White House, Ms. Pirro and Mr. Burgum did not respond to requests for comment.

This account, based on interviews with several people with knowledge of the events, demonstrated a core truth of Mr. Trump’s second term: Anyone willing to contradict the president is in trouble, even if the dissenter happens to be a family friend who has faithfully executed his prosecutorial agenda over the years.

The saga began on July 2, when a fired-up Ms. Pirro appeared before members of the news the media to announce that her office had indicted David Hearn, 67, a former Olympic canoeist, on a single count of felony vandalism after he had been observed damaging the pool lining.

“This is not only a priority for the president, but for myself,” Ms. Pirro said, adding: “We will prove beyond a reasonable doubt that Hearn willfully destroyed property.”

She did not. Last Friday, Ms. Pirro beat a humbling prosecutorial retreat in a 20-page court filing, admitting that her fast-track July indictment of the three-time Olympian had been based on false assumptions and incomplete evidence.

The document amounted to an indictment of sorts of Mr. Burgum; the contractor hired to repair the pool, Atlantic Industrial Coatings; and U. S. Park Police officials.

Ms. Pirro’s filing suggested that Mr. Burgum had committed the twofold sin of failing to competently oversee the renovation, then prodding Mr. Trump to accept the vandals-did-it story. Ms. Pirro said that her staff had relied almost exclusively on claims by Interior Department officials that extensive damage to the lining was caused by Mr. Hearn and other vandals who were observed tugging at or removing pieces of material from the wall.

After reviewing thousands of pages of evidence, she concluded the department had rushed and “botched” the renovation, and that bad information from Park Police officials had led her to cite “tremendous evidence” against Mr. Hearn that did not exist.

The whole episode had a vaguely comic air (why would the leader of the free world, juggling war and a wobbly economy, fixate on a pool liner?). But consequences for Mr. Hearn were anything but. The felony charge carried a maximum 10-year prison term, based on an assessment by Ms. Pirro’s team that the damage inflicted amounted to more than $1,000.

Ms. Pirro knew full well that her U-turn could infuriate Mr. Trump, but decided to cram her filing with enough evidence to decisively disprove Mr. Burgum’s claims.

She gave the White House a heads-up last week before filing the motion to dismiss the charge against Mr. Hearn in federal court, although it was not clear if Mr. Trump was briefed, according to people familiar with the situation who requested anonymity to discuss internal deliberations.

Ominous signals from Mr. Trump began to emerge on Saturday morning, a day after Ms. Pirro filed her motion.

“I disagree 100 percent with Jeanine Pirro,” Mr. Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social. “I don’t know what she was thinking? To me, it was a pure case of VANDALISM.” He added, “There may have been some contractor difficulty, but the major damage was caused by VANDALS!”

Mr. Burgum took to social media to defend himself soon afterward. His staff “provided the U. S. attorney’s office expert and eyewitness testimony to the damage done by vandals and provided every piece of evidence they asked for in the requested time line detailing each area of damage at the pool,” he wrote.

Mr. Trump seems at first to have taken Mr. Burgum’s side, and grew steadily angrier at Ms. Pirro as the weekend ground on.

By mid-Monday, he pounced when asked a Pirro question at a press availability in the Oval Office, saying he was disappointed and accusing Ms. Pirro of being too afraid to present the case to the judge in the Hearn case.

Notably, he did not answer a question from a reporter about Ms. Pirro’s future employment.

Why Ms. Pirro, who knows Mr. Trump’s personality and trigger points better than almost anyone outside his family, was willing to risk the president’s wrath remains somewhat unclear.

After reviewing thousands of pages of evidence over the past few weeks — much of it from Mr. Hearn’s defense team — Ms. Pirro determined the Hearn indictment needed to be rescinded before it was thrown out of court, according to two people close to the situation.

Her critics have questioned whether her motive was nearly so straightforward or altruistic.

They suggest that Ms. Pirro’s decision to withdraw the indictment was self-protective: She might be trying to head off disciplinary action that could result if grand jury testimony or other internal materials are made public. Mr. Hearn’s lawyers said she was guilty of what she had accused Mr. Burgum of doing — rushing to take an action to appease her boss — and that she had ample access, before indicting Mr. Hearn, to evidence showing that the damage had been caused by the contractor.

The contractor, Atlantic Industrial Coatings, has not responded to queries about the case, but a June 21 statement on the company’s website says there are “some areas” of the pool that require repairs.

Ms. Pirro, who rose to prominence in the jostling New York City tabloid market alongside Mr. Trump, has also demonstrated a greater sense of independence than many other senior department officials, whose careers have been entirely made (and can be unmade) by Mr. Trump.

She left a far higher-paying job at Fox News to take over the U. S. attorney job, is lukewarm on Washington, and has told friends (some of them skeptical) that she sees her current post as a capstone, not a steppingstone, and does not fear a “you’re fired” moment.

Yet, by all accounts, Ms. Pirro offered a spirited defense of herself on Friday, and appears determined to win her battle with Mr. Burgum and, eventually, win back Mr. Trump.

David A. Fahrenthold and Maxine Joselow contributed reporting.

Tyler Pager is a White House correspondent for The Times, covering President Trump and his administration.

Glenn Thrush covers the Department of Justice for The Times and has also written about gun violence, civil rights and conditions in the country’s jails and prisons.

Katie Rogers is a White House correspondent for The Times, reporting on President Trump.

Connections Coach

His frozen-in-time anthems, odes to going with the flow, are the soundtrack to a summer of “hopecore.”

Credit...

Supported by

By John Hendrickson

As the house lights crept up, Jack Johnson ambled — does he move at any other speed? — down the center aisle of a Manhattan movie theater.

It was a rainy Monday night, and “SURFILMUSIC,” a documentary about the singer-songwriter’s enviously low-cortisol life, had just screened at Angelika Film Center. At 51, Johnson hovers an inch or two below the rarefied air of household-name status. His catalog of unassuming beach pop is a staple at many a white-walled brunch spot where drinks come in Mason jars. “Banana Pancakes,” his song about, among other things, the tyranny of getting out of bed, has more than 750 million streams on Spotify. He is the soundtrack for a Sunday drive in a sensible hybrid vehicle, and, these days, his original devotees are, like him, navigating the turns of midlife. Surprisingly (or not), some of their kids have become Jack Johnson fans, too.

Facing the Angelika crowd, he flashed a smile as he scanned the room for questions. A young guy raised his hand. His wedding day was approaching, he said, and he was curious if Jack and his wife, Kim, had any relationship advice. Also, he wanted Jack to know that he and his fiancée had picked one of Jack’s songs for their first dance.

Also: that Jack was invited to their wedding.

Also, could Jack sing it for them?

This hyper-familiarity, a collapsing of distance, is nothing new for Johnson. (Millions of people love Oasis; it’s difficult to imagine someone trying that move with Liam Gallagher.) Two and a half decades into his career, Johnson emanates the energy of an old buddy who never moved away. He is not edgy, nor is he prone to provocation. Rather, he represents a challenge to the laws of time and physics: What if everything pleasant just stayed the same forever?

The morning after the film screening, Johnson shuffled into the lobby at the Gansevoort, a hotel in the Meatpacking District. Though he carries an almost anonymous presence, he was approached for an autograph the moment he stepped onto the sidewalk. He sat with his hands in his lap and shoulders sinking into his athletic frame, and, over many cups of coffee, was exceedingly polite with the wait staff. He is the type of star who, even during his run of four consecutive platinum albums in the 2000s, preferred to hop in the front seat when being driven.

This Johnsonian simplicity, or the performance of it, has lately become aspirational. “Jack Johnson summer” — the movie, a companion soundtrack, a tour — is cruising along with a rather simple philosophy: Count the ways you can touch grass.

Over the past couple of months on social media, a meme has bubbled up: “Before you try to spike my cortisol, just know that I’m having a Jack Johnson summer.”

The phrase accompanies all manner of bucolic images: waking up in a tent, biking with pals, sparking up at a municipal golf course. Bennett Artman, a Gen-Z content creator who leads biking expeditions and posts, uploaded his own “Jack Johnson summer” montage (grilling burgers, drinking a Coors) as part of a larger effort to counter “rage bait” with “hopecore” videos, which he’s noticed have grown in popularity.

In a clip encompassing a grab-bag of ills that Johnson can soothe, a different user issued a joking proclamation: “Let’s Jackmaxx! Let’s dopaminemaxx to some Jack! Iran, Israel, Russia, North Korea, U. S. A. — sit in a circle, bonfire on the beach, toes in the sand, Jackmaxxing. DNA spinal tap of Jack. Of happiness.”

Though (mostly) a joke, the viral video captures something real: Legions of people feel trapped in a cesspool of stress, anxiety, anger, declining mental health, diminishing attention spans made worse by the pandemic and, more recently, a feeling of being pummeled by A. I. slop.

Meanwhile, Johnson is off catching waves, noodling tunes, teaching kids about sustainability and compost. If you wondered where he went, he’s been here the whole time. Does he think the rest of us are nuts? Could life really be as simple as unobtrusive tones and a plethora of vitamin D?

At his screening, after a few audience questions, Johnson picked up an acoustic guitar and played “Holes to Heaven,” a musical memoir of a surf trip, followed by “Better Together,” which he dedicated to the soon-to-be newlyweds. He held eye contact with the couple while he strummed and sang. They beamed.

He reflected on the interaction the next morning. “They didn’t have their phones out, they were both leaning in and listening, and I was so happy for that,” he said. He finds it “interesting” how many wedding invitations he gets.

That, and, well, the number of parents who tell him they use his music to put their kids to sleep. He has decided to take the latter as a compliment.

In one of the first scenes of the documentary, Johnson appears in an office chair. It’s a jarring sight, like seeing King Charles in a Pizza Hut. When pressed about it, he lightly scoffed at his perceived image. “Somebody told me about that term,” Johnson said, referring to “Jackmaxxing.” He smiled, but made it clear he wasn’t keen on being reduced to a caricature.

“This idea of what I am, the barefoot guy on the beach,” he began: “A lot of that is true, but I’m very much a guy who’s raising teenage kids in the modern world, and I totally understand the pros and cons of social media and the world that we’re living in,” he said.

Though Johnson himself is not a slave to the algorithm — his team handles his social accounts — he insists that he’s also not Rip Van Winkle. He sees Instagram Reels and memes via texts from his friends. He and Kim haven’t set restrictions for their children, and have instead given them a mantra: Try to produce more than you’re consuming.

In late June, Jack Johnson’s “Jack Johnson summer” included an afternoon in Asbury Park, a night on the water at Jones Beach, and a stop at the waveless yet serene Saratoga Performing Arts Center, where teens roamed in baggy jeans and earth tone tees.

For the bulk of Johnson’s career, his wife and kids have accompanied him on tour. Kim left her teaching job to become one of his managers. Sitting backstage in Saratoga, she emphasized that her husband was far from an aloof rock star.

“I think he’s one of the most grounded people I’ve known in my life, and he helps ground me so much,” she said. “But I don’t want to say he’s totally disconnected from the world.”

She described Jack as well-read, someone who likes to talk politics and current affairs, a guy who often plays devil’s advocate when chopping it up in conversation.

Johnson can be surprisingly dry and self-deprecating. At the film screening, he waxed about growing up on the North Shore of Oahu, ensconced in the unhurried rhythm of the ocean. “I kind of blame that for why my songs are so slow and boring,” he said.

When he’s home in Hawaii, he says he can easily go weeks without picking up a guitar, but he must get in the water.

Were it not for a surfing accident at age 17 that left him with a head injury and broken front teeth, Kim said, he probably would have pursued a pro surfing career. During his recovery, he was briefly on the path of a “straight” life, and his dad wanted him to become an actuary. At University of California, Santa Barbara, he studied math before eventually switching to film. But the surf accident also increased his interest in songwriting.

Throughout much of his 20s, though, music was still a hobby, and Johnson saw the world through a camera lens. He developed a close relationship with the filmmaker Emmett Malloy, collaborating on a pair of surf docs, “Thicker Than Water” and “The September Sessions.” (Malloy also directed the new film.) When Malloy became an in-demand music video director, he brought along Johnson as a secondary cameraman on shoots for bands like Blink-182, Foo Fighters and Limp Bizkit. When working on the video for Limp Bizkit’s “Break Stuff,” Malloy recalls, the rap-rocker Fred Durst expressed interest in signing Johnson.

“I mean, it would have been a whole different trip,” Malloy said with a chuckle.

In “SURFILMUSIC,” the singer-songwriter Ben Harper, one of Johnson’s mentors, crystallizes something that many people seem to miss about his friend: “It takes a great deal of intensity to actually sound simple and pure.”

Malloy, when describing Johnson, brought up Andy Samberg’s sendup of him on “Saturday Night Live.” In one sketch, Samberg-as-Johnson, host of “The Mellow Show,” throws out non sequiturs: “Cargo shorts! Ultimate Frisbee!” “Vegan cookies!” In another, Samberg does an ad for “J. J. Casuals,” shoes that look like bare feet.

The “mellow man” thing, Malloy said, is an incomplete picture.

“He’s a sweet guy to everyone, and he’s very caring,” Malloy said, “but I will say the big, big surprise is that he’s easily the most competitive person I know.”

Out in the ocean, in the surfing lineup fighting for a wave, for a magazine cover image, Johnson could be relentless. “You have to be kind of gnarly,” he said. “And that’s in Jack.”

Backstage in Saratoga, Johnson and his bandmates warmed up in a rehearsal room dotted with black and white photos of Pete Seeger, Tina Turner, and other stars who had graced the venue. Zach Gill, his piano player and old college friend, offered up hot toddies. Johnson eventually took the stage in the same thing he’d been wearing all day: a mustard yellow tee, faded jeans, and flip-flops.

Fans bopped and swayed and threw their arms around each other. When Johnson arrived at his hit “Sitting, Waiting, Wishing,” he instead sang a few bars of Turner’s “What’s Love Got To Do With It.” He covered Sublime’s druggy ’90s anthem “Badfish,” and his guitar sounded, rather pleasingly, like liquid. A cool breeze blew through the Saratoga pines. Suddenly, everyone was Jackmaxxing.

Though the crowd spanned generations, from middle schoolers to Gen-Xers like Johnson, a huge swath of attendees appeared to be in the prime of their teen years. A trio of skater-looking dudes passed a joint. Some guys stood in circles in bright polos while eyeing circles of girls in cowboy boots and denim skirts.

A 16-year-old named Sam wandered the grounds with a couple friends. He’d been listening to Johnson his whole life, he said, and, like several teens interviewed, discovered him through the music he wrote for a “Curious George” reboot. One track for that movie, “Upside Down,” became one of Johnson’s biggest songs.

A 17-year-old, Gianna, said her dad used to play Johnson’s music while he made breakfast. Many others had found him through TikTok, where users did household chores to Johnson’s song “Washing Dishes,” or picked up a friend and spun them around to the tune of “Upside Down.”

As the night drew to a close, the backing band left the stage, and Johnson took requests for an acoustic set. He played “Constellations,” a song that nods to his late father’s love of stargazing. Though his dad died in 2009, Johnson can still toggle between referring to him in the past and present tense.

“My dad is a sweetheart, but he was a very eccentric guy,” Johnson said over coffee. Jeff Johnson, was, in his son’s telling, someone who could fix anything, who could sail by the stars. Johnson found it harder to sing in front of his dad than his mom. “He wasn’t a gruff guy, but he wasn’t the quickest to give out compliments,” Johnson said. One night in the early 2000s, during a run when Johnson’s shows started to become larger, Jeff asked his son if fame was what he really wanted. It was a question he never forgot.

Johnson is still chasing something. “I don’t pretend to have any kind of big answers for anybody,” he said. “I think every once in a while, if I’m lucky, I’ll get at a feeling that we all have. But I don’t have any big solutions for the problem.”

Instead, as he puts it in the film, he focuses on “moments that feel a little more slow motion,” or “like salt on the skin at the end of the day.” Sometimes, when popping out for a surf session on tour, he intentionally won’t wash off afterward, as an attempt to hold onto the feeling while onstage.

It is, perhaps, the purest form of Jackmaxxing: to ride a consciousness-obliterating sensation longer than it actually lasts. But if that’s not your thing, you and your buds could always just throw on some Jack Johnson.

After Midtown Building Buckles, Violations Are Found at Many Other Sites

The New York Times August 04, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

New York City officials conducted inspections at 180 construction sites. None of the violations posed an immediate danger to the public, they said.

By Mihir ZaveriPatrick McGeehan and Arfa Momin

A sweeping review of 180 construction sites across New York City involving firms connected to the redevelopment of a Midtown high-rise that became dangerously unstable last month found dozens of violations, though none posed an immediate danger to the public, city officials said. Inspectors also shut down some work at several of the sites.

The findings were released in an email on Tuesday, as part of the city’s continuing response to the Midtown building that buckled on July 7 at 235 East 42nd Street, a high-profile conversion of the former Pfizer headquarters to apartments.

Each of the 180 sites targeted in the review was associated with a developer of the Midtown project, MetroLoft; two subcontractors, Barone Steel and Northeast Specialist Group; or a third-party inspection firm, Domani Inspection Services, that was supposed to be overseeing structural work.

Andrew Rudansky, a spokesman with the Buildings Department, said the agency had issued more than 60 violations, and fully or partially shut down work at 19 sites. He said that most of the violations had been issued “for site safety issues that posed a hazard to the workers on site, failing to follow the design drawings and plans, or for administrative issues.”

Only 24 of the 180 sites were office-to-residential conversion projects. The others included a new three-story development in Williamsburg, Brooklyn; a six-story apartment complex in Lower Manhattan; and a 36-story residential tower in Chelsea near the High Line.

Mr. Rudansky said inspectors “did not find any hazardous structural issues that posed an imminent danger to public safety during this sweep.”

A spokesman for MetroLoft declined to comment. Northeast, Barone and Domani did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Among the problems discovered in the review:

The construction of a 20-story residential building in Gramercy Park involving concrete work on the third floor did not align with the project plans;

A wall made of masonry on the roof of a new two-story building in Queens was temporarily being braced by wood and rebar without engineering plans;

Construction work was being performed on a Saturday without a special allowance to work on the weekend.

A spokesman for Mayor Zohran Mamdani referred questions about the review to the Buildings Department.

The episode at the old Pfizer building last month involved the buckling of two steel columns on the 21st floor, prompting the evacuation of thousands and sending construction crews and city officials scrambling to stabilize the building. An analysis by The New York Times of publicly available engineering plans and photographs of the building showed that the columns appeared not to be properly reinforced.

The city is continuing its investigation into what went wrong.

But the episode has raised questions about the safety of other conversion projects.

City leaders have repeatedly sought to quell those concerns, and Mr. Rudansky said on Tuesday that there was “no evidence to suggest that the structural failing at 235 East 42nd Street is in any way inherent to office-to-residential conversion projects.”

An investigation by The Times found that several firms, including MetroLoft and Domani, had brushes with the Buildings Department in the past.

The investigation into the columns’ failure at the Pfizer building will involve “a massive review of construction documents and reports held by the developer and construction team, interviews with witnesses and responsible parties, a hands-on sweep of the entire construction site and review of available video and photo evidence,” according to the Buildings Department.

City inspectors had previously moved to fully or partially shut down work at three other conversion projects. Mr. Rudansky said none of those were connected to the review.

One was at 222 Broadway, a 30-plus-story office building being converted to luxury housing in Lower Manhattan, over issues with a horizontal concrete beam on the roof that had cracked and been repaired. The Buildings Department had conducted an inspection based on a tip, and work remained on hold there on Tuesday.

After conducting a routine inspection, the department also partially shut down work at 77 Water Street over issues it found during an inspection on July 11, including equipment that was being used without proper certification. Work was allowed to resume a few days later.

Some steel work at another high-rise conversion project at 750 Third Avenue also remains on hold. That followed another routine inspection.

Mihir Zaveri covers housing in the New York City region for The Times.

Patrick McGeehan is a Times reporter who covers the economy of New York City and its airports and other transportation hubs.

Arfa Momin is a graphics reporter at The Times and a member of the 2026-27 Times Fellowship, a program for journalists early in their careers.

Trump’s Decade of Comebacks Might Be Over

The New York Times August 04, 2026

Advertisement

Newsletter

By Ross Douthat

Opinion Columnist

On Oct. 1, 2016, Jesse Farrar, then a freelance scribe for sites like Vice and Deadspin, issued a tweet that would define the next 10 years of American politics. I’ll reproduce it as a poem:

Well, I’d like to see ol Donny Trump wriggle his way out of THIS jam!

*Trump wriggles his way out of the jam easily*

Ah! Well. Nevertheless,

Three months out from the midterm election, five months into a stalemated (at best) war of choice with the Islamic Republic of Iran, we are back once again in the territory of Farrar’s first verse. Trump’s approval rating has reached a second-term nadir. His attempts to shake free of his unwise Middle Eastern war have been repeatedly frustrated by a counterparty in Tehran that doesn’t think it needs to take his deal. And the Trumpified Republican Party is in real danger of losing the Senate, with reddish seats from Iowa to Texas to Alaska increasingly vulnerable.

His health permitting, Trump is going to be president through 2028; in that bare sense he will presumably survive this moment as he has survived many times before.

But a true Trumpian “wriggles his way out” resolution requires Republicans to avoid catastrophe in November, to keep the Senate as they did in the 2018 midterms, and thereby preserve a certain freedom of movement for the president in the second half of his second term. It also requires him to remain popular enough — 40 percent approval would do it, 30 percent would not — to make people believe and behave as though an anointed heir might actually succeed him in the White House. There’s no room for even a modest Trumpian comeback if the entire political world spends the next two years positioning itself for an age of certain Democratic power and revenge.

So what might improve Trump’s position now? The obvious answer is the deal with the Iranians that the administration has been seeking and promising for months. (As of this writing, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is the latest administration official to suggest that it might be just a day or two away.)

One of Trump’s political strengths is his willingness to cut bait on an unsuccessful policy, to sell a walkback as a victory rather than doubling or trebling down. That’s what I’ve expected him to do with Iran ever since the initial regime change hopes disappeared, and since Americans never really bought into the case for war in the first place, even a bad deal should help the White House’s political position through the effect on gas prices alone. (You could see Trump’s poll numbers tick upward following the all-too-temporary truce that Vice President JD Vance negotiated in June.)

But the Iranian regime can see the midterms looming just as much as any American politico, and having held out this long they have strong incentives to hold out even longer, since every poll showing a Democratic candidate leading in Texas or Alaska is a new forcing mechanism for Trumpian concessions. So it’s quite possible that the administration will be required to choose between a truly desperate deal or no pre-midterm peace at all.

In that Middle Eastern scenario, Trump’s position at home could still theoretically be saved by the Democratic Party’s mix of radicalism and inertia — the rise of socialist and socialist-adjacent candidates and the failure of the party’s moderates to meaningfully adapt to the realities that drove its 2024 defeat.

Again and again, the folly of his domestic opponents has been crucial to Trump’s rebounds and escapes. Before the Iran war began, that was roughly what I expected to happen yet again in 2026: a collision between an unpopular president and an unpopular opposition party yielding a split decision, a Democratic House and a Republican Senate, rather than an anti-Trumpian landslide.

I still think the trajectory of the Democratic Party is carrying Democrats away from the political center, which all things being equal should put a limit on how many close elections they can win. But all things aren’t equal when the president’s approval ratings are sinking into the 30s. In that environment, you can win even with further-left candidates and also expand the map so that your unforced errors don’t matter as much. If you can’t win narrowly with a candidate like Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, you can lose narrowly with him and still pull off upsets in states like Ohio and Iowa where you have less polarizing nominees.

Then if we set aside Iranian conciliation and Democratic radicalism as saviors for the Trump administration’s political position, I’m not sure what remains.

Some unlooked-for crisis or debacle that reminds Americans of what they fear about progressivism? It’s hard to imagine what could have that effect when conservatives control every branch of government.

A sweeping, pandering reversal on tariffs by the president that cuts prices and sends the markets surging even higher? It’s hard to imagine Trump making that kind of concession to reality given everything we know about his second-term state of mind.

A speech announcing that the deep state is aware of the existence of extraterrestrial or nonhuman intelligence? The U. F. O. people are hoping for that before the midterms, but I’m not sure it would move his poll numbers in the Midwest.

Yes, it’s awfully hard to see how Donald Trump can wriggle out of this jam. And by the time November arrives, maybe I’ll summon enough courage to predict boldly that he won’t.

Francis Young on the problem of the gods.

Patrick Collison on pivoting to beauty.

Damian Thompson on how bishops reproduce.

An Invasive Mosquito Is Spreading With Alarming Speed, Threatening Africa’s Cities

The New York Times August 04, 2026

Global Health

The malaria-carrying mosquito is resistant to all insecticides. Scientists are scrambling to find ways to blunt the risk.

An Anopheles stephensi mosquito under a microscope in the lab of the parasitologist Mahaman Lamine in Niger. Credit... Mahaman Lamine

Supported by

By Stephanie Nolen

Stephanie Nolen interviewed entomologists in seven countries to report this article.

An invasive, malaria-carrying, insecticide-resistant mosquito that thrives in cities, where malaria has not been a major threat, has moved farther and faster across Africa than even pessimistic scientists had feared. And many public health experts believe it is too late to eliminate, or even contain, it.

A new genomic analysis of the mosquito, called Anopheles stephensi, using specimens collected from 10 countries, showed that those found in Africa had genetic resistance to all of the chemicals currently used in spraying campaigns and other mosquito-control efforts, meaning those insecticides will not kill it.

It is moving with terrifying efficiency and speed across flat, open, windy terrain, pushing westward to Ghana and south through Kenya, from its initial arrival on the continent in Djibouti in the Horn of Africa more than a decade ago.

“The last couple of years there’s less talk of, ‘We really need to contain this invasion,’ because everyone who knows what’s what realizes that genie is completely out of the bottle,” said Tristan Dennis, who studies vector genomics at the University of Queensland in Australia and who led the new analysis, published in the journal Science.

This mosquito alarms health experts because, unlike the species that historically spread malaria in Africa, it thrives in urban as well as rural areas, and is not deterred by dry seasons. This means that malaria, already one of the top killers in Africa, could become a grave problem in megacities such as Lagos and Kinshasa, each of which are home to about 20 million people.

“We’ve not had to worry about malaria in urban settings,” said Dr. Eric Ochomo, the head of entomology for the Kenya Medical Research Institute.

Much of the urban population has no immunity to malaria, and the parasite will make people gravely ill, he said. And when a stable population of stephensi is established, it transmits malaria all year, not just on the rainy season cycle most current malaria programs are structured to address.

“It’s going to really complicate our ability to manage malaria,” Dr. Ochomo said.

In most countries, stephensi is not yet established in populations big enough to detect whether it is affecting malaria rates. But in Djibouti and Ethiopia, the first countries it invaded, it is possible to see the risk it represents.

Before stephensi arrived in 2013, Djibouti was on the cusp of declaring malaria eradicated. In 2012, there were just 27 cases. A year after stephensi was found, cases shot up to nearly 1,700. Each year thereafter, the number crept up, and in 2020, there was an explosion: more than 70,000 cases.

In Dire Dawa, Ethiopia’s second-largest city, stephensi drove a surge of malaria cases in 2022, one that initially baffled health care workers who were not used to diagnosing or treating the disease.

The spread of stephensi is yet another setback in an already sputtering battle with mosquitoes in Africa. In 2024, there were nine million more malaria cases than in 2023. While the full 2025 data is not available yet, and will be less comprehensive due to health program funding cuts, there are clear signs that malaria is resurgent.

Teams of scientists have been working together, often against a backdrop of armed conflict and climate-driven displacement, to combine their bare-bones surveillance efforts and map the dimensions of the new threat.

Mahaman Lamine, a parasitologist in the city of Zinder in the West African nation Niger, trapped a pile of mosquitoes around ponds with a couple of students in 2024. In his university lab, he asked the students to identify the species for a biodiversity survey, and almost as an afterthought reminded them about stephensi, the invasive species that had been detected elsewhere in Africa. A short while later, his students mentioned that they had found some of those in their samples.

“I said, ‘No, no, no!’” Dr. Lamine recalled.

Stephensi had never been found in Niger. But Dr. Lamine rechecked the mosquitoes against one morphological key, and then another. They matched. Soon he dispatched a student on a bus to the city of Kano, across the border in Nigeria, carrying mosquito samples through an area with an armed insurgency to reach a lab that could do molecular confirmation.

The students were right: Anopheles stephensi had reached Niger.

The recently published genomic analysis showed that after arriving in Djibouti, the new African stephensi population split into three groups. One went into Ethiopia, then south into Kenya; one skipped from Djibouti over a narrow channel in the Red Sea and into Yemen; and one went into Sudan and from there headed across the Sahel to West Africa.

Other scientists have speculated that stephensi has been introduced from South Asia via ports in West Africa in separate incidents, but the genomic analysis provided a compelling case for how efficiently the mosquito had moved across the flat, windy Sahel, expanding its territory by as much as about 300 miles a year.

“We’ve never seen anything like this, this kind of spread. We never imagined a mosquito could spread this fast,” said Dr. Ochomo, who contributed mosquito samples to the study.

A few years ago, he expected stephensi to pose a threat only in Kenya’s very dry north. It has already been found moving steadily south and fanning out through different kinds of habitats.

Stephensi arrived in Africa in about 2013, likely on a ship from Pakistan or India. Researchers in Djibouti identified it as they were scrambling to explain a massive spike in malaria cases in a country that had been on the verge of eradicating the disease.

Everywhere it goes, stephensi encounters malaria-control programs trying to do more with shrinking budgets. The United States, the world’s largest funder of anti-malaria efforts, slashed its support at the start of the Trump administration. Malaria-control budgets were reduced by a third or more in most countries with a high malaria prevalence last year, compared to 2024.

“The first thing cut is surveillance,” Dr. Ochomo said. Yet without data on which mosquito is where, it is harder to make decisions about where to invest in interventions, such as bed net distribution. “If we could do really good surveillance, we could decide where to put the limited resources,” he said.

In Niger, Dr. Lamine is also struggling to continue to track the mosquito. “We do not have any funding, and we have only one very old microscope. But we try to do the work, because we love science,” he said.

Dr. Dennis said stephensi was benefiting from human interaction with the environment.

“They’ve come at a time when there’s massive fragility and instability, lots of displaced people, very little state control in some places, on a really rapidly urbanizing continent,” he said. “And they came armed to the teeth with defenses against the insecticides we can use.”

Scientists fear that stephensi has also reached other countries, including Chad, Somalia, Eritrea and South Sudan, nations that do not have the resources for national vector surveillance. “Nobody is looking,” Dr. Dennis said.

Scientists in Afghanistan, Pakistan, Yemen, Sudan, Ethiopia, Kenya, Iran, the United States and Saudi Arabia collaborated to do the genomic study, to home in on where the African stephensi population originated. Almoevery country had violent conflicts raging when the research began or descended into war over the four years of the work.

Hmooda Toto Kafy, a medical entomologist with the ministry of health in Sudan, contributed samples from his country, collecting the last of them just weeks before the civil war began. Dr. Kafy has been poised to start research on if and how stephensi is driving malaria transmission in the country. “But this is not easily done during the war,” he said.

Regions he hoped his team could surveil are inaccessible because of fighting, while staff members and students left as refugees. And the banking system is in disarray, so it is difficult to pay for supplies. All of it makes the already daunting prospect of hunting for a tiny mosquito in one of the world’s largest countries massively more complex.

In Yemen, Dr. Tarek Sultan Bin Hawail, a public health specialist, supervised a team that collected samples for the study, and shared ominous findings with researchers in Africa. His team found stephensi in the huge camps that ring the Yemeni capital Aden, housing people displaced by the country’s civil war. There were mosquito larvae in the water containers inside people’s homes and tents — living alongside another mosquito, Aedes aegypti, which carries dengue fever and other viruses.

Health workers at clinics overwhelmed with patients with fevers were treating patients with dengue, because malaria was not supposed to be in the area. Stephensi brought it.

Africa is home to nearly half the global total of displaced people; there are 15 million displaced by the war in Sudan alone.

When the global network of scientists had contributed samples, Dr. Dennis carried out the genomic analysis. His findings were bleak. “All of the resistance genes in the invasive population confer resistance to pretty much every insecticide we are using in vector control, so this is actually even worse news than we thought it was,” Dr. Dennis said.

Even with the growing body of evidence about how stephensi is moving and where, there are few signs of resources being shifted to meet it. “You can have these data that tell you a certain thing, but if there’s not the infrastructure to put a response into practice, then it doesn’t help much,” said Dr. Dennis.

Despite this, the scientists who study stephensi speak about the mosquito with grudging admiration.

Typically an invasive species struggles to establish itself in a new place, shrinking down to a small population with limited genetic diversity.

“The fact that this mosquito was able to lose a huge amount of genetic diversity and then still go on to occupy this vast swath of the continent,” Dr. Dennis said. “It took over Africa.”

Stephanie Nolen is a global health reporter for The Times.

Yes, the Show Has Drawn Raves. But Some of the Objects Are Not Real.

The New York Times August 04, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

When the New York Historical realized that sunlight in its new wing would potentially damage some items on display, it scrambled to reproduce or remove them.

By Robin Pogrebin

A Grover Cleveland campaign kerchief. A Betye Saar assemblage sculpture. A hand-lettered evening gown urging the passage of the long-stalled Equal Rights Amendment (E. R. A.). Posters by Norman Rockwell.

These were among the historical objects featured in the first show in the New York Historical’s new Tang Wing for American Democracy. Built at a steep cost of $175 million, it has been touted as an important expansion for the museum and a capstone to the architect Robert A. M. Stern’s career.

But, just one month since the show opened, none of those objects — several of which were called out in glowing reviews — are on display anymore.

Well, they still appear to be there. But look closely.

The wall labels quietly acknowledge that this object is actually a “reproduction” and that item is a “facsimile.”

This is because it was only as the exhibition — “Democracy Matters” — was about to open on June 18 that the museum fully reckoned with the fact that windows in the new gallery would shower sunshine on some very light-sensitive artworks.

The museum’s first response was to lower blackout shades on the large upper windows. But when Louise Mirrer, the director of the museum (formerly the New-York Historical Society), realized how much that undermined the wing’s soaring architecture, she insisted the shades be raised back up.

“I felt it was disrespectful of the architect’s final museum project,” Mirrer said in an interview. “We had to find a means that could accommodate both the architecture and the exhibition narrative — which we did.”

So, to protect the vulnerable works, the museum replaced 17 of them with reproductions and removed another three.

In one instance, a three-dimensional assemblage by Saar — “Extreme Times Call for Extreme Heroines” — featuring what the wall label describes as a “mammy caricature” with an assault rifle on a washboard topped by a clock — was replaced by a simple digital photograph of the work.

Rocky, Reconsidered: The sculpture is at the center of a show by the Philadelphia Museum of Art that explores the meaning of monuments.

Route 66 Turns 100: Exhibitions recall the history of the neon corridor that helped define the American road trip.

A New Museum Comes With a D. J.: The space in Indianapolis, housed in a former dairy barn, aims to upend expectations of what an art museum can be.

The Fisher Collection in a New Light: A Bay Area family made a deal with SFMOMA that called for exhibitions of the collection’s works every 10 years.

More on Museums: Artists and institutions are adapting to changing times.

In recent days, after The New York Times raised questions about the prevalence of reproductions in the show, the museum said it would remove the photograph because it did not adequately depict Saar’s assemblage.

Much of this has likely gone unnoticed by the many people who have visited and enjoyed the exhibition. The reproductions of Rockwell’s 1943 “Buy War Bonds” posters, for example, which were created by the museum’s digital printer, look strikingly like the images they replaced.

But museums — more so art museums than institutions that chronicle history — have long promoted themselves as places where visitors come in contact with authentic objects. Would patrons wait in long lines at the Louvre to see a reproduction of the “Mona Lisa?”

“What is real? What are visitors’ expectations? Are they evolving with younger generations who are often experiencing things digital first or replicas first?” Devon Akmon, chairman of the board for the American Alliance of Museums, said in an interview. “In a world where we’re seeing more and more things like artificial intelligence, do people want to see what they perceive as being the authentic piece? It’s a really interesting question that a lot of museums and a lot of scholars are trying to determine right now.”

It is certainly true that authenticity matters most in the art market, where the price for a painting thought to have been done by an associate of Rembrandt can soar by millions of dollars when it is re-attributed to the master himself. In such a setting, authenticity is not only a matter of visual aesthetics and visitor expectations, it is the essential foundation of financial value.

Gerhard Schlanzky, a 19-year veteran of the museum who worked on the “Democracy” show before stepping down as the creative director and director of exhibitions last month, was one of several current and former museum staff members who said they were disappointed by the changes.

“You come to see real things,” he said. “Otherwise people might just view them on their devices at home.”

In addition to the Saar, two other items removed from the show were the E. R. A. dress, worn by the Democratic New York congresswoman Carolyn B. Maloney to the 2021 Met Museum gala, and a mannequin in crocheted pink camouflage by the artist Olek that commemorates the 2017 Women’s March on Washington.

Informed by a reporter that their piece had been removed, Olek — who uses they/them pronouns — said in a WhatsApp message from Poland: “Art is safe in storage. But this is not what art is made for.”

Holland Cotter, in his New York Times review of “Democracy Matters,” written when the original works were still on view, cited the new wing’s “primary, high-ceilinged, light-flooded special exhibition gallery,” calling out in particular the Saar piece.

Schlanzky said he recently returned to see the show and was disappointed to find so many objects replaced or removed. “It sucked the life right out of it,” he said. “Particularly upsetting was the Betye Saar piece — to see something so dimensional and bright reduced to this not very good reproduction.”

This was especially distressing, Schlanzky said, given that Saar had just passed away, on July 26.

Alison Saar, one of the artist’s daughters, said in an interview that while she was “a little disappointed,” to hear about the situation, she gave “the museum the benefit of the doubt that this was done with the thought of preserving the artwork.”

“It’s unfortunate,” she said. “But you go down the hallway and can see a huge beautiful show of my mother’s dolls.” (An exhibition celebrating Saar’s 100th birthday featuring examples from the artist’s Black doll collection — a promised gift to the museum — is currently on view in another gallery.)

Schlanzky said Mirrer was aware of the light challenges early on. “The dialogue was always that if we were going to do an exhibition in that space, the windows had to be covered,” he said. “We never would have proposed light-sensitive objects if we knew the shades would be up.”

Mirrer said that, because she had been busy fund-raising for the $175 million project, she hadn’t paid sufficient attention to light issues in advance. She said her priority was to realize Stern’s vision of “a soaring, sweeping space that would invite the city in.”

The show’s curator, Wendy Nalani E. Ikemoto, who left the museum last month, said she had “no involvement in or advance knowledge of” Mirrer’s decision to raise the window shades and replace light-sensitive objects with reproductions. “I have documentation establishing that this decision was made after my departure,” Ikemoto said in an email.

David Nasaw, a historian who has frequently been a speaker at New York Historical, said authenticity is not essential to appreciating and learning from a historical object.

“When we go to Gettysburg battlefield or when we look at the Lincoln Memorial, we can’t see them exactly as the contemporaries saw them,” he said. “Paintings get dirty, buildings decay.

“A reproduction that we know captures the essence of the original artifact — that’s the second best,” he added. “If the only objects we can learn from are the originals, then the historians are lost and the history is lost.”

Robin Pogrebin, who has been a reporter for The Times for more than 30 years, covers arts and culture.

I’m Begging You: Never Write With A. I.

The New York Times August 04, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Bret Stephens

By Bret Stephens

Opinion Columnist

This column isn’t so much an argument as it is a plea: Don’t use artificial intelligence to help you write. Never let A. I. do your writing for you.

Don’t use it for school papers, work briefs, letters to your in-laws, speeches at your company gathering or emails (however perfunctory) to your colleagues or friends. Don’t let it organize your notes. Don’t let it suggest an opening sentence, a segue or a closing paragraph. Don’t ask it to write a first draft and pretend that editing that draft somehow makes it your own. It doesn’t.

Do none of these things not because they are unethical. Writing with A. I. is unethical when it’s a deception: when you pass off words, ideas and information as your own when they aren’t. An acknowledgment can largely address the problem. Do none of these things, either, because you might be able to learn to write better than an A. I. can. Pretty soon, if not already, you won’t, just as you can’t outrun a car or outplay a chess app.

The problem with writing with A. I. is that it’s mentally enfeebling — an escalator toward a result when you really need to make a daily habit of taking the stairs. As it becomes ubiquitous, it undermines not only our individual ability to write but also a society’s collective ability to reason, a culture’s inner capacity to create and everyone’s reason to care. We’re already reckoning with the well-documented decline of reading; A. I. is accelerating the decline of writing, ushering us further into what The Atlantic’s Rose Horowitch calls our “postliterate age.”

What, uniquely, does writing do? It compels thought. It compels thinking in ways that silent contemplation or spoken language rarely can. It compels us to subject our thinking to the effort of articulation, the rigor of grammar, the tests of intelligibility and coherence, the inspection of others. In doing so, it also enjoins us to be clear, logical and accurate — and accountable. People may easily forgive a word said in anger but not so easily one written in anger, precisely because the fact that it was written tells us that it was considered.

The considered word matters. It has staying power and moral weight. We use the expression “I want that in writing” not only so there’s no mistaking the exact words that have been agreed upon but also as proof that the words are meaningful in the first place.

But what happens when the words aren’t considered because they were written by (or with the help of) a machine?

Words become hollow. Imagine the father of the bride turning to A. I. to help him write his daughter’s wedding toast: What the A. I. can supply in eloquence it subtracts in effort and authenticity. Now imagine that the daughter learns that the speech was written by A. I.: Wouldn’t she be right to be disappointed, if not insulted?

Many would argue there’s a big difference between using A. I. for something as significant and personal as a wedding speech and the boring and frequently exhausting tasks of writing, say, routine office memos. But the intellectual muscle that’s exercised in everyday writing is the same one used for the writing that matters. We become better writers by the constant effort that mundane writing demands. We become better thinkers by investing into that writing a degree of attention we’d never give it if we relinquished the task to A. I. We become more creative when we learn how to put a personal stamp even on routine things, making them unmistakably our own.

These skills are now evaporating. A recent examination using A. I.-detection technology of 100 doctoral dissertations found that 56 percent of them contained “more than negligible” A. I.-generated writing and 19 percent had “more than 50 percent A. I.-generated text.” Anecdotal stories from college professors have a finger-in-the-dike feeling with regard to their efforts to hold back the flood of A. I.-generated student papers. It’s easy to treat the problem as one of mere cheating. But cheating doesn’t capture the real scope of the A. I. threat, which isn’t merely to academic integrity or personal betterment but also to democratic self-governance.

The link between broad-based literacy and the rise of democracy is well known: People who can read and write for themselves have, historically, also been good at choosing and advocating for themselves. What happens when the process goes into reverse? When people lack the patience to absorb arguments more than a few pages or sentences long? When they lack the ability to contradict those arguments because they’ve never honed, through daily practice, the most essential skill for clear thinking?

We’re already getting a taste of what this world looks like in President Trump’s social media posts and the sway they clearly exert over tens of millions of Americans. But that’s a reflection of where the country was a decade ago, in the pre-A. I. age. How much farther down the road are we now, with our even more diminished capacity to read, write and think?

The next time you’re tempted to just adopt an automated response for a text message or an email, don’t. Type out a response that’s your own. Think of it as an act of free will. Or a vote against Trump. What takes you a few additional seconds is an act of resistance against an ever-dumber world.

The Neonatal Doctor Crisis in a Country Desperate for Babies

The New York Times August 04, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

South Korea, which has one of the world’s lowest fertility rates, is in the throes of a breakdown in emergency care. It is particularly acute for at-risk newborns.

By Jin Yu Young

Reporting from Seoul

The baby started turning blue almost immediately after she was born in a small clinic last month in South Korea.

There was a neonatal intensive care unit a short drive away, but the specialist there had reportedly resigned recently after years of grueling 90-hour work weeks. Another did not have any free beds. So the clinic’s staff rushed the newborn, who was struggling to breathe, to a third hospital. That facility was 30 minutes away by car, and by the time she got there, she died.

The clinic later learned that the first NICU had been staffed by another specialist that night who could have treated the baby. But many in the medical community had assumed that the nearby facility had not filled the vacancy because of a growing shortage of specialists.

Her death, in the western city of Jeonju, detailed by lawmakers in parliament and local news media, was part of a bigger crisis in South Korea: a widening gap in emergency care. The shortage of neonatal doctors is particularly alarming because the country has been trying for years to increase its fertility rate, which is among the world’s lowest.

As the birthrate dropped below replacement level in the 1980s, South Korea has gone through profound changes. Thousands of schools have closed in recent decades. Over 40 percent of day care centers have shuttered in recent years. The number of pediatricians, delivery wards and neonatal physicians is plunging every year.

Now the country has 77 NICUs where 240 specialists are tasked with caring for some of the most vulnerable patients, according to the government and doctors groups. The shortage is the most acute outside the greater Seoul area, the country’s population center. Some hospitals outside the capital only have one specialist to care for over 30 babies at once, doctors say.

Neonatal doctors say that government measures to reverse the birthrate have done little to improve their working conditions — long hours, low pay and litigious patients. These concerns echo those from the wider medical community in South Korea and contributed to an 18-month walkout by thousands of doctors that ended last September. The future of the neonatal specialty is particularly dire: The number of residents working in NICUs has decreased by 94 percent in recent years, according to government data.

Young-Ah Youn is a teaching doctor at the neonatal department of Seoul St. Mary’s Hospital. She said that during her 16-year career as a physician, she has worked more 100-hour weeks than she can count, particularly during her early years as a junior faculty member. Now her department does not have any residents, raising questions about the future of the ward.

“Who would want to work here when there’s so little support or protection for us?” she said. The hospital relies on contract doctors or nurse practitioners to fill in staffing gaps.

Government efforts, doctors argue, have been focused on increasing the birthrate. Over the past two decades, South Korea has invested the equivalent of hundreds of billions of dollars in programs like cash stipends for new parents, egg freezing procedures for women and free wedding venues for soon-to-be spouses. But experts say the outlays have not tried to secure the medical infrastructure to provide adequate care for the nation’s youngest citizens.

There is still “an imbalance in incentives to ensure adequacy in trained medical specialists,” said Professor Tan Poh Lin, a pediatrics expert who teaches public policy at the National University of Singapore. She added that policy focus has been “overly oriented toward the family formation process.”

The Korean Society of Neonatology has described government policy that encourages people to have children while largely ignoring a lack of emergency medical care for newborns as a “paradox.” NICUs outside the Seoul metropolitan area, it said in a statement last month, are near “a state of catastrophe.”

The government has announced that it would increase fees for deliveries and high-risk procedures — a move designed to raise doctors’ pay. It also said that it would increase the number of dispatchers on call at the National Medical Center’s Central Mother and Child Medical Center to expedite emergency transfers.

Choi Han-seon spoke about her premature delivery and the importance of NICUs at a policy forum at the National Assembly in June. She needed surgery after a hemorrhage in the 20th week of her pregnancy. Her son was born three weeks later, only weighing about 1.4 pounds, and had a series of health complications like high blood pressure and a brain hemorrhage.

He was left with developmental disabilities, but survived after nearly five months in a NICU. Ms. Choi said, “NICUs are not an option, they are an essential service that saves the lives of babies.”

But if the number of neonatologists continues to dwindle in South Korea, that care may be at risk.

“I’ve worked tirelessly out of a sense of duty,” Professor Youn said. “But I fear that, if things continue this way, there will soon be no one left to care for these babies.”

Jin Yu Young is a reporter and researcher for The Times, based in Seoul, covering South Korea and international breaking news.

Family Demands Answers About Death of Immigrant Held at Detention Center

The New York Times August 04, 2026

U. S. Immigration Crackdown

Advertisement

Supported by

Edwin Lopez-Cornejo’s relatives said that federal officials who oversee Delaney Hall in Newark had refused to provide his medical records.

By Ana Ley and Mark Bonamo

Relatives of a Salvadoran immigrant who died after being held at a troubled detention center in Newark gathered outside a church on Tuesday pleading for answers about the circumstances that led to the man’s death.

Edwin Lopez-Cornejo, 41, was taken from the Delaney Hall detention center to University Hospital in Newark, where he was pronounced dead on Saturday. His family members appeared before news cameras on Tuesday to demand that state officials investigate Mr. Lopez-Cornejo’s death. They also called for the closure of Delaney Hall and for the release of detainees held there.

Mr. Lopez-Cornejo’s mother, Maria Cornejo, said in a phone interview on Tuesday morning that she did not understand why he had died and said that federal immigration officials had refused to provide his medical records to the family. Mr. Lopez-Cornejo is survived by a 12-year-old daughter, his mother said.

“The pain that I feel is irreparable,” Ms. Cornejo said. “His daughter is devastated.”

Family members, who stood on the steps of the church, held Ms. Cornejo by the arms as she approached the news cameras and placed their hands on her shoulder while she spoke to reporters and cried. When she was finished, she hugged her granddaughter.

Ms. Cornejo said that her son had been diagnosed with diabetes and epilepsy but that the conditions were managed for years with medication. She said she did not know if detention officials had been giving him his medication since he was arrested while walking to work on June 18 near his home in Plainfield, N. J., where he had a job in construction.

Neither the Department of Homeland Security nor the Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency, which oversee Delaney Hall, responded immediately to the family’s demands. Geo Group, the private contractor that operates Delaney Hall, did not reply to inquiries about Mr. Lopez-Cornejo’s death.

ICE officials had said on Monday that Mr. Lopez-Cornejo experienced a medical emergency at Delaney Hall and that employees “responded immediately and called 911 for emergency medical services.” The cause of his death was not known; Ms. Cornejo said that she was told autopsy results would take months.

While in custody, Mr. Lopez-Cornejo “received proper medical care and was seen by medical professionals,” ICE said on Monday in a statement.

“ICE is committed to ensuring that all those in custody reside in safe, secure and humane environments,” the agency statement said. “At no time during detention is a detained noncitizen denied emergency care.”

Mr. Lopez-Cornejo is the second Delaney Hall detainee to have died in the past eight months. His death renewed criticism of the federal detention center, where protesters have gathered for months to denounce what detainees have described as inhumane living conditions.

At least 53 people have died in immigration detention facilities since President Trump took office last year, according to a New York Times analysis of news releases from the federal government.

“His death was preventable, and his family deserves answers, accountability and justice,” Jorge Torres, the organizing director of the National Day Laborer Organizing Network, said in a statement. “Edwin is one of too many people whose lives have been cut short while in ICE custody or during immigration enforcement operations.”

Protesters gathered at the Delaney Hall gates on Monday evening to denounce Mr. Lopez-Cornejo’s death while lawmakers from Washington to New Jersey criticized federal immigration officials for restricting their ability to inspect the detention center, which members of Congress have the authority to inspect.

New Jersey’s attorney general, Jennifer Davenport, had sued the federal government in June to gain full access to Delaney Hall after immigration officials repeatedly blocked state inspectors from housing and medical units.

“You have all these stories that run counter to what the administration has been telling and selling and spinning to the American people,” Representative Rob Menendez, a New Jersey Democrat, said during a phone call with reporters Monday evening. “There is an erosion of support for this administration with respect to their immigration enforcement.”

In December, Jean Wilson Brutus, 41, died after a medical emergency at Delaney Hall, federal officials said at the time. The detention center had been reopened last year to accommodate President Trump’s expanding immigration crackdown.

Border Patrol officials said that Mr. Lopez-Cornejo had entered the United States illegally in 2006. An immigration judge had ordered him removed at that time, and he was deported to El Salvador two months later, according to federal officials. He entered the country illegally again later. He was detained at Delaney Hall pending removal from the United States.

Allison McCann contributed reporting.

Ana Ley is a Times reporter covering immigration in New York City.

Appeals Court Says E. P. A. Cannot Block Billions in Climate Grants

The New York Times August 04, 2026

The funds have been frozen since early in President Trump’s second term.

By Claire Brown

An appeals court on Tuesday handed a victory to a group of federal grant recipients that the Trump administration has prevented from spending billions of dollars in climate funding for over a year.

In a split decision, 10 judges on the U. S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit upheld an earlier injunction that said the Environmental Protection Agency could not terminate $20 billion in climate grants, and that the recipients should have access to the funds as their case proceeds.

If the E. P. A. does not appeal the decision to the Supreme Court in the next seven days, the judgment will effectively reinstate much of the Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund, a Biden-era “green bank” initiative that supports low-cost loans and investments for renewable energy projects across the country.

Brigit Hirsch, an E. P. A. spokeswoman, said the agency is reviewing the judgment and considering next steps. It could appeal to the high court and ask that the funds remain frozen in the meantime.

“It’s screamingly good news for the plaintiffs,” said Michael Gerrard, director of the Sabin Center for Climate Change Law at Columbia University, though he said the legal process could continue to drag on for a long time.

Last February, the E. P. A. administrator, Lee Zeldin, attempted to claw back $20 billion in climate grant funding that the Biden administration had awarded to eight nonprofit groups. Mr. Zeldin suggested the program was vulnerable to waste, fraud and abuse, citing a hidden-camera video released by the right-wing group Project Veritas in which a former E. P. A. staff member likened the outgoing administration’s spending to throwing “gold bars” off the Titanic.

Despite investigations by the agency’s inspector general, the Justice Department and the F. B. I., the government never substantiated these claims. Several of the nonprofits sued to force the money out, and in April 2025, U. S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan of the District of Columbia issued a preliminary injunction preventing the E. P. A. from canceling the grants and allowing the groups to access the money during the litigation. But the E. P. A. appealed that decision, and the program has been in limbo since.

“The practical effect of this is to eliminate that deep freeze,” said David A. Super, a professor at Georgetown Law.

The delay has taken a toll on the grant recipients, which relied on the funds for basic expenses like payroll and office rent. Beth Bafford, the chief executive of the lead plaintiff, Climate United, left the organization in March and was not replaced. Other groups have laid workers off. Power Forward Communities, which received $2 billion in grants, was down to two employees earlier this year.

On Tuesday, the nonprofit plaintiffs celebrated the judgment. Representatives for Justice Climate Fund and the Coalition for Green Capital said they were looking forward to moving forward with their work.

“Today, the D. C. Circuit Court judges affirmed what we have always known: E. P. A. took actions to unlawfully freeze and dismantle the National Clean Investment Fund grant program,” Climate United said in a statement. “Despite efforts to harm the awardees with false allegations and misinformation, there remains no legal basis for terminating our grant award and clawing back funds that were already disbursed in our bank accounts.”

If the E. P. A. does not appeal to the Supreme Court, the case will proceed in federal court, either moving to trial or summary judgment. The grant recipients will be able to access their funds in the meantime.

Claire Brown covers climate change for The Times and writes for the Climate Forward newsletter.

The S&P 500 rose 1.8 percent, pushing past its previous peak at the start of June and capping a big turnaround from a recent sell off in technology stocks.

Source: LSEG.

Jacqueline Gu and Karl Russell/The New York Times

By Joe Rennison and Aruni Soni

The S&P 500 rallied to a record high on Tuesday, led by a recovery in tech stocks and bolstered by signs that a peace deal between Iran and the United States might once again be in sight.

The benchmark index rose 1.8 percent, pushing past its previous peak at the start of June and capping a strong rebound that has lifted the index nearly 6 percent over the past week.

After a jittery response to last week’s comments from Kevin Warsh, the new Federal Reserve chairman, stocks have been lifted by the prospect of fewer immediate rate increases, strong financial results from some big technology companies, cooling tensions between Iran and the United States and a rare intervention in global markets by the Treasury Department that also helped prop up domestic markets.

Investors have latched onto comments from the Trump administration in recent days that Iran and Qatar were making progress in talks to reopen the straight of Hormuz, a vital oil shipping route, helping extend a turnaround in technology stocks that began last week.

Investors remain concerned, however, that artificial intelligence companies that have been spending hundreds of billions of dollars building out data centers may yet run into trouble, such as from less expensive models being developed primarily by China.

The S&P 500 has swung high and low over the past two months, at times rising on hopes that the conflict with Iran was nearing an end or because of strong earnings by a large A. I. company, only for negotiations between Tehran and Washington to fall apart, or for fears about tech overspending to re-emerge.

Last week, the Nasdaq Composite index, which includes big technology companies, came close to a correction, Wall Street’s term of a drop of 10 percent or more from its recent peak.

By the end of the week, investors’ fears began to ease and the market stirred to a rally again. The Nasdaq has risen more than 9 percent since last Wednesday.

Stocks have been supported by continued strong corporate earnings, with companies recently reporting financial results for the three months through June.

Eighty-six percent of the S&P 500 companies that have reported this earnings season have posted earnings-per-share results that beat analysts’ forecasts, as of Friday’s market close, according to FactSet.

In another move that helped ease the market’s jitters, the Treasury Department stepped in to stabilize Japan’s weakening currency.

The yen had fallen to a 40-year low of 164 per dollar in recent weeks, in part because of worries over the government’s spending plans. The currency’s drop was intensified by a rise in oil prices.

Japan is a large holder of Treasuries, and the risk of the Japanese government selling U. S. assets to support the yen had fanned concerns about the sustainability of the U. S. debt, too. Higher Treasury yields also risk destabilizing the A. I. trade. By helping with the intervention, the Treasury Department was able to limit the direct selling of U. S. assets.

On Tuesday, international oil prices fell below $80 a barrel for the first time in three weeks, as investors were hopeful that a lull in fighting in the Middle East would hold.

Gas prices fell 1 cent on Tuesday to a national average of $4.09 a gallon, according to the AAA motor club.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio expressed optimism about negotiations to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, a waterway through which a fifth of the world’s crude oil is normally shipped. There had been “progress in talks,” he said, “but not finality yet.”

Some analysts said that they expected the rally in stocks to continue.

“The excesses that defined the early summer have largely been unwound,” said Scott Rubner, a strategist at Citadel Securities.

At the same time, the broader economy remains solid, despite lingering inflation worries.

“For the first time in several months, we believe investors can spend less time focused on positioning and more time focused on fundamentals,” Mr. Rubner said.

Joe Rennison writes about financial markets, a beat that ranges from chronicling the vagaries of the stock market to explaining the often-inscrutable trading decisions of Wall Street insiders.

Aruni Soni is a business reporter and a member of the 2026-27 Times Fellowship, a program for journalists early in their careers.

Dolphin Carries Dead Calf in What Experts Call Grieving

The New York Times August 04, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Footage posted by a conservancy group offers an unusual glimpse of a common behavior by dolphins that often goes unobserved.

By Sopan Deb

The video is haunting: A dolphin carries the deceased body of her two-week-old calf amid a pod of dolphins south of Perth, Australia.

The footage was posted on July 20 by Geographe Marine Research, a whale conservation organization. The group is familiar with this particular mother, whom it has named Fraggle, and her struggles. She had already lost three other calves, and giving birth to a fourth during winter in the Southern Hemisphere posed an immediate challenge to the calf’s survival.

“We still had hope she had a chance to be a mum again,” the group wrote in a widely shared social media post.

The group proposed that Fraggle’s calf had died of pneumonia.

Different types of dolphins are known to carry their dead offspring for days, if not weeks, said Lori Marino, a neuroscientist and the founder of the Whale Sanctuary Project.

“It’s absolutely clear that this is a mother grieving for her child,” Dr. Marino said.

She noted that while other footage of grieving dolphins has been captured, what was notable in this video was the placement of the surrounding dolphins.

“They are close to her,” Dr. Marino said in an interview. She added, “It’s not just her with her dead calf. There’s a recognition on the part of the whole pod that there is something going on here.”

Groups of cetaceans — a term for a marine mammal that includes dolphins and whales — are known for their emotional bonds with one another. That includes birth as well as death. For example, scientists have observed groups of sperm whales assisting a mother in giving birth, part of a growing body of research illustrating the depths of community among groups of some nonhuman animals.

Scientists say such expressions of grief are ordinary behavior for cetaceans.

In 2018 an orca named Tahlequah was seen carrying her dead calf near British Columbia for more than two weeks in 2018 over a thousand miles, although that many days was considered an outlier by scientists. She appeared to be in mourning again last year.

Experts say that mothers like Fraggle and Tahlequah appear to desire close contact with the corpse.

“What is most remarkable in these cases is that the mothers don’t have hands and live in an aquatic medium where they have to regularly surface to breathe as well as hunt,” Susana Monsó, a philosopher and the author of “Playing Possum: How Animals Understand Death,” wrote in an email. “This makes holding on to the corpse something very difficult and shows a strong motivation on the part of the mother.”

Such behavior is not unique to dolphins or whales. Scientists have documented the carrying of infant corpses for extended periods by nonhuman primates, including chimpanzees, gorillas and baboons, said Abigail McClain, a doctoral candidate at Center for the Advanced Study of Human Paleobiology at George Washington University.

“Again and again we see mothers carrying infants for days to weeks, sometimes even when there is evidence that the mother knows the infant has died, which opens the door to some really interesting conversations about grief in nonhuman species,” Ms. McClain wrote in an email.

Lauren Brandkamp, the stranding coordinator at Whale and Dolphin Conservation North America, noted that while humans find these videos interesting, they shouldn’t be surprised.

“It’s a natural behavioral response in animals,” Ms. Brandkamp said. “They form these bonds with their offspring, with other members of their pod or their species. And when a life is lost, they also experience that kind of mourning and sadness.”

Sopan Deb is a Times reporter covering breaking news and culture.
