Eaton Fire Caused by Utility’s Transmission Tower, Report Says

The New York Times August 04, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The 2025 fire, which killed 19 people and destroyed the Altadena community in Los Angeles County, began at an inactive tower belonging to Southern California Edison, officials said.

By Livia Albeck-RipkaIvan Penn and Shawn Hubler

The deadly blaze that devastated the Altadena neighborhood in Los Angeles County early last year was ignited by a transmission tower belonging to the utility company Southern California Edison, fire officials said in a report released on Tuesday.

The county’s fire department said the blaze, known as the Eaton fire, which killed 19 people and destroyed more than 9,400 buildings, was started by electrical sparks coming off the tower, according to a joint investigation by the department and Cal Fire, the state’s firefighting agency. The tower was out of service at the time.

Though Edison had previously acknowledged that its equipment most likely started the Eaton fire, the cause had not been officially confirmed.

Fire officials took 18 months to review evidence with experts, including video footage that showed “an unknown burning material” falling from the tower to the dry fuel bed below in the Eaton Canyon area, according to the report. The blaze ignited about 12 seconds later, officials said, quickly spreading into the surrounding neighborhoods, where it burned homes, businesses and schools.

Anthony C. Marrone, the county fire chief, said in a statement on Tuesday that he recognized that no investigation could ease the pain of residents affected by the Eaton fire.

“While the cause has been determined, our focus remains on assisting our residents to rebuild their homes and livelihoods, and ensuring lessons learned drive meaningful and impactful change in memory of the 19 lives lost,” Chief Marrone said.

On Tuesday, Kathleen Dunleavy, a spokeswoman for Southern California Edison, acknowledged the findings.

“We have taken our potential role in the start of this fire seriously from the beginning,” she said.

In a recent earnings call, company officials noted that their equipment was likely associated with the fire, she said, but they have also pointed out that wildfires of the Eaton fire’s magnitude “are rarely the result of a single factor.”

Livia Albeck-Ripka is a Times reporter based in Los Angeles, covering breaking news, California and other subjects.

Ivan Penn is a reporter based in Los Angeles and covers the energy industry. His work has included reporting on clean energy, failures in the electric grid and the economics of utility services.

Shawn Hubler is The Times’s Los Angeles bureau chief, reporting on the news, trends and personalities of Southern California.

Warsh Wanted ‘Regime Change.’ A Reset Might Need to Come First.

The New York Times August 04, 2026

U. S. Economy

Advertisement

Supported by

After his latest appearance set off a bout of volatility, Kevin M. Warsh, the chairman of the Federal Reserve, is under pressure to clear up mixed signals about his commitment to getting inflation down.

By Colby Smith

Colby Smith covers the Federal Reserve.

Before long, every head of the Federal Reserve learns the lesson. Their words are parsed so closely that anything short of absolute precision has the power to upend financial markets and force the central bank to walk back a message that had become misconstrued.

Janet L. Yellen learned this at her first news conference as chair in March 2014 when she inadvertently suggested the Fed could raise interest rates much sooner than many had expected.

Jerome H. Powell exacerbated a market meltdown when, just months into the top job in December 2018, he characterized the Fed’s plan to reduce its portfolio of government bonds and mortgage-backed securities as on “autopilot” and signaled further rate increases to come. Mr. Powell changed tack just over two weeks later, helping to alleviate concerns that the Fed was dismissive of the warning shots that the markets were sending.

Kevin M. Warsh, roughly two months into his tenure as chairman, is facing his own reckoning after a news conference following the Fed’s July meeting that confused investors and called into question his commitment to quelling inflation, which has remained above the Fed’s 2 percent target for more than five years. It was a costly blunder, setting off a sharp market move that economists at Bank of America said was typically associated with “credibility shocks” faced by central banks in emerging markets.

Since last week, markets have stabilized, largely because of renewed hope that a deal to end the war with Iran is close. Stock markets are hitting new highs, although longer term U. S. borrowing costs are still higher than they were before the Fed’s latest gathering.

The onus is now on Mr. Warsh to reset the narrative and make clear what it means in practice for the Federal Open Market Committee to have “no tolerance” for elevated inflation.

His next scheduled opportunity will be at the central bank’s annual conference in Jackson, Wyo., at the end of the month. Mr. Warsh, who has vowed “regime change” at the Fed and has been highly critical of past leadership, had initially wanted the speech to get at what he called the “big questions,” such as how a wave of higher productivity fueled by artificial intelligence is impacting the economy.

But more traditional, policy-focused remarks might be unavoidable to sidestep another bout of market indigestion. After that, the Fed’s next policy meeting, in September, will be another crucial test, especially if inflation does not moderate in the coming months.

“Every opportunity he has now to speak either with the F. O. M. C. or with the public is very important,” Jon Faust, a fellow at the Center for Financial Economics at Johns Hopkins University and a former senior adviser to Mr. Powell, said of Mr. Warsh. “There’s damage control to do.”

Already, several of Mr. Warsh’s colleagues have spoken out, emphasizing their willingness to raise rates if inflation does not begin to ease. They join three officials who believe the Fed should have already lifted borrowing costs by a quarter of a percentage point.

On Friday, Alberto G. Musalem, president of the St. Louis Fed, said he “expressed a preference” for higher rates at the meeting. Thomas I. Barkin of the Richmond Fed, said it was a “close call” whether rates were high enough to bring inflation down.

Those comments were followed by John C. Williams, president of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, who on Monday said it would “absolutely be appropriate to act to get us on a trajectory that does bring inflation back ​to 2 percent” if price pressures did not abate as he expected. Mr. Williams is a member of the “troika,” the central bank’s internal policy-steering group that includes Mr. Warsh and Philip N. Jefferson, the vice chair.

Another voter on this year’s policy-setting committee, Anna L. Paulson, president of the Philadelphia Fed, said on Tuesday that “the passage of time without progress would itself signal that more restrictive policy is needed.”

Mr. Warsh might benefit from being as specific. But having made sending fewer signals a central pillar of his approach, it would require a shift in his communications strategy.

“This is a teething process,” Randall S. Kroszner, a University of Chicago economist who served as a governor at the central bank alongside Mr. Warsh, said of the leadership transition. “It’ll take a little while for the markets to figure out his seriousness about inflation and that he’s not going to tell them exactly what he’s going to do.”

“You don’t want to ignore market movements, but you also don’t want to be a slave to them,” Mr. Kroszner added.

There is a middle ground, suggested Donald Kohn, who served as vice-chair of the Fed from 2006 and 2010 when Mr. Warsh was a governor. What was most notably missing from Mr. Warsh’s latest appearance, he said, was “his sense of where he sees the economy going and how certain policy changes, or lack of changes, in the near term might help to advance toward their goals.”

That need not constitute “forward guidance” — a longstanding practice of the Fed to help guide markets during times of crisis that Mr. Warsh has sought to do away with — Mr. Kohn said. Rather, it would provide a framework to better understand Mr. Warsh’s objectives and how he would go about achieving them.

When Mr. Kroszner and Mr. Kohn worked with Mr. Warsh, the future chairman often framed the Fed’s institutional credibility as synonymous with its inflation-fighting one.

In a 2010 speech, Mr. Warsh warned about the risks of changing the inflation goal posts. “Substantial harm would be done to a central bank’s institutional credibility, and perhaps lead to an unmooring of inflation expectations,” he said. “Such damage could lead investors to seek alternative currencies, with prices of commodities and other hard assets likely to increase.”

He echoed a similar point more recently at congressional hearings last month. In one exchange with lawmakers on the House Financial Services Committee, he said, “My commitment to you is to take sticky prices and to unstick them.” In another, he stressed that his definition of price stability was something beyond just meeting the 2 percent target — a world in which price changes are mild enough “such that no one’s talking about it.”

In his opening remarks at last week’s news conference, Mr. Warsh emphasized that the Fed did not have a “soft inflation target,” meaning it would not accept anything more than 2 percent, as measured by the Personal Consumption Expenditures price index. He also said, “Where necessary and appropriate, we will not hesitate to act.”

But his responses later on at the same news conference sent an entirely different message, most notably his suggestion that the 2 percent goal was subject to debate.

“Who knows, come after next January, what we might say about strategy,” he said in reference to the Fed’s annual affirmation of its approach. He also mentioned his five task forces, one of which will take up the issue of how inflation is best measured. A change of that magnitude would require the backing of a majority of Fed officials, support that Mr. Warsh will not be able to amass at the very least until the current goal is met in a durable way.

Investors also struggled to look past Mr. Warsh’s hesitation to reiterate that rate adjustments were the primary tool at the Fed’s disposal.

The amount of pressure on Mr. Warsh to adjust course will depend in large part on how the data evolve. Next week’s Consumer Price Index report, which will capture the period after which the Iran war flared up again and oil prices revisited recent highs, will be of particular importance.

Before the September meeting, the Fed will have two full months of data related to inflation, the labor market and consumer spending, among other metrics. There is still a plausible case, according to officials, that higher rates will not be necessary and that inflation will retreat to 2 percent on its own.

A string of benign data would carve out a path for Mr. Warsh to once again stand pat when policymakers next gather. It will also give him the opportunity to flesh out in more detail how he sees other tools, such as shrinking the central bank’s large holdings of investment securities, helping on the margins. But having sent mixed signals about his own commitment to getting inflation down, inaction on rates will keep doubts aflame.

“The only way you regain confidence is actually hiking,” said Greg Peters, co-chief investment officer of PGIM fixed income. “The action is the most important at this point."

Colby Smith covers the Federal Reserve and the U. S. economy for The Times.

Dismissing Trump’s Warning, Max Miller Won’t Step Aside Amid Abuse Claims

The New York Times August 04, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Republicans hoped a shove from President Trump would persuade the embattled congressman to drop his re-election bid in the face of abuse allegations.

By Emily Davies and Annie Karni

Emily Davies, who covers politics, reported from Ohio’s Seventh Congressional District. Annie Karni, who covers Congress, reported from the Capitol.

When President Trump called Representative Max Miller, his former loyal aide, to warn him the domestic abuse allegations he was facing would make it tough for him to win re-election, Republican officials at the White House and in Ohio hoped it would be enough to get the embattled congressman to drop out.

But Mr. Trump stopped short of asking Mr. Miller to step aside, and the congressman made it clear he had no intention of doing so, according to two people familiar with the call who spoke about the confidential conversation on the condition of anonymity.

The president, who endorsed Mr. Miller in May, has yet to publicly withdraw his support, leaving other Republicans reluctant to do so themselves.

The exchange, which was reported earlier by Axios, has left the G. O. P. in a bind as officials scramble to figure out how to protect a House seat that the party cannot afford to lose in the midterm elections, with a headstrong candidate and a fast-approaching deadline to get him out of the race.

If Mr. Miller were to drop out by the end of the day on Tuesday, there would be a special primary election to replace him on the ballot. Otherwise, Ohio law suggests he would need to resign by Friday to trigger a meeting of state party chairs, who would have to choose a new candidate by Monday.

The tight time frame has transformed what up until recently had been a family feud between two of the state’s most powerful families into a political crisis that has forced Republican officials to consider picking sides.

The drama, which has played out for months in court and in dueling media appearances and leaks, has pitted Mr. Miller, 37, against his ex-wife, Emily Moreno, 32, who has accused him of abusing her and their toddler daughter. Mr. Miller has denied the claims and said that Ms. Moreno, the daughter of Senator Bernie Moreno, also an Ohio Republican, is mentally unstable, accusing her of stalking and lying about him and endangering their daughter.

The concern from the highest levels of the Republican Party is not personal but political. The approaching ballot deadline has focused fresh attention on Mr. Miller’s case, including court filings that detail Ms. Moreno’s charges that he held a gun to her head, scalded her with water and fractured their daughter’s collarbone.

Mr. Moreno, who had initially made little in the way of public statements about the matter, issued a blistering one on Sunday calling his former son-in-law unfit for public office. But few other Republican leaders have openly criticized the congressman over the accusations, even as they privately worry that the scandal could put Ohio’s Seventh Congressional District at risk.

The district, which stretches from the Cleveland suburbs to Amish country, is solidly Republican. But with anti-Trump sentiment sweeping the country, it is not a lock, especially given that Mr. Miller’s Democratic challenger, Brian Poindexter, is a union ironworker who could appeal to working-class voters.

White House officials have been strategizing on how to most effectively prod Mr. Miller to withdraw. They have also explored possible replacements should Mr. Miller exit the race, according to a person familiar with the conversations.

Jane Timken, a state senator and former state party chair who unsuccessfully sought the G. O. P. nomination for Senate in 2022, has been floated as a possible alternate — though she has made clear that she does not want the job.

Mr. Miller, though, has insisted in private and public that he can still win a third term, and angrily rejected any suggestion that he step aside. He broadcast a lengthy livestream over the weekend in which he appeared agitated as he denied the allegations against him. On Tuesday, after having spoken with Mr. Trump, he announced that he would open an ethics investigation into himself “to clear my name from these horrific attacks on myself and family.”

Not long afterward, the House Ethics Committee said in a statement that it was “reviewing allegations that Representative Max Miller may have engaged in domestic violence and abuse or illegal drug use.”

A long paper trail of court filings, including for dueling restraining orders, as well as a file that Mr. Miller released on Sunday in an apparent effort to clear his name, paint the picture of an increasingly ugly family dispute in which each side has gone to great lengths to make the other look as violent, unstable and dishonest as possible.

The back-and-forth is full of tragic details, including a story that Mr. Moreno told on Tuesday at the Capitol, in which he said he had once picked up his granddaughter at a police station and that Mr. Miller had refused to hand over her favorite stuffed blue bunny.

Also on Tuesday, Ms. Moreno’s lawyers pointed to a picture of the couple’s toddler that had been included in the file Mr. Miller posted on Sunday and accused him of publishing an image that could be considered child sexual abuse material, noting that it had been viewed at least 204,000 times before it was removed.

A lawyer for Mr. Miller said the inclusion of the photograph was a mistake and that he had taken it down, according to Punchbowl News.

On the ground in Mr. Miller’s district this week, there was little sign of the chaos sweeping the race and alarming Republicans at the highest levels. Mr. Miller showed up on Monday at a county fair, where he campaigned before a hog show and among constituents who mostly said they had not heard about the week’s developments.

Local officials also stayed mostly silent about the race. Three of the four Republican county chairs in Mr. Miller’s district did not respond to questions on Monday about whether they supported his candidacy. Matt Miller, the chairman of Ashland County and the mayor of Ashland, said he “did not have a final opinion on the matter.”

Gov. Mike DeWine of Ohio, a Republican, told a reporter for Signal Ohio on Tuesday: “I’m not going to weigh in on it. These are very serious allegations that he vehemently denies.”

Vivek Ramaswamy, another Republican who is in a competitive race for governor, did not respond to inquiries about Max Miller’s situation. And Senator Jon Husted, who is facing his own tough race to keep his seat, told Newsmax on Tuesday only that he hoped “the president’s intervention can help move things along.”

Behind closed doors, however, some local officials were working to figure out how to compel Mr. Miller to step aside, according to two people briefed on the conversations, and what would happen if he did. They had come to the conclusion that only Mr. Trump himself had a chance of changing Mr. Miller’s mind.

Former Representative Jim Renacci, a Republican and former small-town mayor who represented a House district that covered much of the same area from 2011 to 2019, said he had been fielding calls about stepping in to seek the seat.

“I am convinced of this: The only person that would have a chance, and might not even have a chance, is me,” he said from a bench in downtown Wadsworth on Monday night, citing his name recognition in the district and the difficulties of running a potentially short race. “And even when I think of it, it would be a daunting challenge.”

Mr. Renacci also stopped short of saying that Mr. Miller should withdraw.

At the Medina County Fair, where Mr. Miller appeared on Monday, the Republican Party booth was advertising his picture next to a sign that said “RE-ELECT.”

Volunteers declined to discuss his campaign, saying only that they were praying for him.

Across the aisle, at the Democratic Party booth, volunteers were registering voters.

Tyler Pager contributed reporting from Washington.

Emily Davies is a political correspondent for The New York Times.

Annie Karni is a congressional correspondent for The Times.

Near Center of Palisades Fire, a Sign of a Comeback

The New York Times August 04, 2026

Rick Caruso, the billionaire real estate developer and former Los Angeles mayoral candidate, is reviving a property still surrounded by burned-out lots.

Rick Caruso, the billionaire real estate developer and former Los Angeles mayoral candidate, is reviving a property still surrounded by burned-out lots.

Palisades Village mall, which was largely intact after the devastating Los Angeles wildfire last year, is nearly complete and set to reopen Aug. 15. Credit... Ariana Drehsler for The New York Times

Supported by

By Kim Bhasin and Shawn Hubler

Reporting from Los Angeles

About 300 construction workers last month milled around Palisades Village, an outdoor shopping mall in Los Angeles, one of the few structures that didn’t completely burn down during the wildfire last year.

Rick J. Caruso, the billionaire owner of the property and several other upscale malls across the city, greeted the workers with a smile as they placed brick paths and installed doorways.

“Everything was gutted, and everything was built back the way it was,” Mr. Caruso, in sunglasses and a suit, said as he walked down an outdoor pathway that runs through the mall with his impeccably groomed golden retriever, Hudson, in tow. “It’s going to feel alive and full and busy.”

The surrounding neighborhood looked starkly different from his vision. It bore the scars of blazes that killed 31 people, burned over 38,000 acres and destroyed more than 16,000 structures across Southern California in January 2025.

Pacific Palisades, a neighborhood of about 23,000 on the western edge of Los Angeles with a median household income of about $190,000, was one of the worst-hit areas. Tucked in canyons between the Santa Monica Mountains and the ocean, it remains full of burned-out lots, vacant storefronts and the wood frames of homes in various stages of construction, a year and a half later. Many residents have yet to move back.

In a landscape where so many are still struggling to rebound, however, the short stretch of clean sidewalk, with its upscale boutiques and restaurants, is offering a long-yearned-for burst of evidence that the fire zones are finally poised for a comeback. It also is offering Mr. Caruso a victory lap of sorts.

Since the fires, Mr. Caruso, 67, a longtime civic and business leader who in 2022 ran unsuccessfully for mayor, has been among the most vehement voices demanding a speedy recovery, and among the most vocal critics of Mayor Karen Bass, who is running for re-election.

As Pacific Palisades burned, he was among the first to assail Ms. Bass for having been out of the country when the flames erupted. But he also faced criticism himself, for paying a private firefighting force to set up a perimeter around Palisades Village.

The private force, he later argued, freed city firefighters to better protect homes and other buildings, but some anguished property owners accused him of saving his own property while hundreds of others, including some just across the street, succumbed to the inferno.

With the refurbished mall set to reopen on Aug. 15, however, criticism on both sides has receded. Mr. Caruso and Ms. Bass have become partners on a host of rebuilding issues, and Ms. Bass — who has lobbied state legislators and the Trump administration aggressively for reforms in insurance and mortgage forbearance — has applauded the mall’s swift resurrection.

“The reopening of Palisades Village is very important, because it is imperative that residents have commercial spaces within close range — places to eat, shop, and come together so that they don’t have to leave their community,” the mayor said in a statement on Monday.

“The restoration of these essential commercial spaces is about more than a return to normalcy, it’s about restoring the places that make up a community and directly serve the people who live there.”

Mr. Caruso was at the gym near his home in Brentwood, a neighborhood adjacent to the Palisades, when he heard on Jan. 7, 2025, that the Palisades fire had erupted. Two of his children, Justin and Gianna, lived there.

“‘Dad, there’s smoke I can see in my rearview mirror,’” his son, Justin, told him over the phone as he drove away from the growing calamity.

Mr. Caruso called his head of security to get an update on the mall. He had built his fortune on commercial and residential real estate as the founder of Caruso, his development company.

Shopping malls are his specialty, and he has a portfolio that includes California properties such as the Grove in Los Angeles, the Commons in Calabasas, the Americana in Glendale, and the Promenade in Thousand Oaks. But he has long been especially proud of Palisades Village, which is near his home.

“I made a big investment when I built this seven years ago and bet on the Palisades community,” Mr. Caruso said. “And it worked.”

The threat of fire was familiar to him, however.

One of Mr. Caruso’s properties, the Rosewood Miramar Beach resort, in Montecito, had its own wildfire scare in 2018 when Santa Barbara County was besieged by flames that tore through nearly 300,000 acres of land. That fire never reached the resort.

That close call prompted management to devise an emergency plan for Palisades Village: hire a private fire brigade. In the days before the fires reached the Palisades last year, Mr. Caruso mobilized about 35 firefighters. They brought water trucks to the mall, sprayed the area with fire retardant and stood sentry.

Those efforts paid off, and Mr. Caruso’s business was saved. But it wasn’t all good news. His son and daughter each tried to return to their houses to retrieve some valuables before the flames began to singe their walls. Both lost their homes.

“It became very personal, very quickly,” Mr. Caruso said.

In the aftermath, some residents and business owners bristled at the sight of the intact shopping mall sitting within a residential grid blanketed in ash and rubble, and the firefighters who guarded it for two more weeks.

Looking back, Mr. Caruso said, he understood their anger and insisted that the sentiment has shifted over time as crews reconstruct the neighborhood and residents trickle into new homes on old lots.

“I’ve never been part of losing a town,” Mr. Caruso said. “It’s like, holy God, what more can happen to you?”

Until early this year, he had seriously considered challenging Ms. Bass’s re-election. A centrist Democrat and former Republican in a deeply liberal city, he abandoned his effort after polls showed that, while she was politically weakened by the fire, his prospects were uncertain too.

He said he was still interested in running for office at some point, though he would not say for what seat. “If I could serve in an official capacity, great. If I can’t, it’s not going to change my commitment to the city,” he said.

Although it looked unharmed on the outside, Palisades Village had underlying problems caused by smoke and toxins in the air.

Mr. Caruso and his staff considered closing down the mall. He said that would have been the easier and more financially prudent decision. But he wanted to bring the mall, which opened in 2018, back to life.

“So we took everything down to the studs,” Mr. Caruso said. “We treated the wood, retested the wood, and then we rebuilt everything all over again.”

The mall needed tenants, and it was unclear which of the stores would want to stay in the Palisades after such a crisis.

Mr. Caruso’s first call was to Elyse Walker, a New York fashion designer and boutique owner who lost one of her stores in the Palisades to the flames, to ask for her commitment to return and her help in convincing others to join them.

Ms. Walker said she decided soon after the fire that she would revive her shop, rather than move to another town. It will return just feet away from its old spot on opening day.

“You’re trying to balance putting your business back together, but also being respectful of the healing times,” Ms. Walker said. “There’s no place we would rather be.”

Palisades Village lost about 30 percent of its customers because of the fires. The rest, Mr. Caruso said, remained in range. Most shoppers came from less-affected areas, like Santa Monica and Brentwood, and he expected those people to come back.

The scarred landscape also presents an odd atmosphere for a high-end mall. The Grove, Mr. Caruso’s mall near Beverly Hills — and consistently among the most productive shopping centers in the United States — is surrounded by tidily trimmed sports fields, a historic ranch and a landmark farmer’s market. Palisades Village, for now, is encompassed by barren lots of dirt.

Mr. Caruso said Palisades Village would have a 99 percent occupancy rate when it opens. Fashion labels that have agreed to rent space include Zimmermann, Toteme and Anine Bing. Erewhon, the high-end grocery store, has also decided to return. Nancy Silverton, the chef known for Osteria Mozza, her Michelin-star restaurant, will open an eatery with an all-new concept: Spacca Tutto, an Italian steakhouse.

Ms. Silverton said she found the Palisades “eerie” on her first visit after the disaster, but it didn’t take much convincing from Mr. Caruso to get her on board.

“It’s still going to have that feeling, but having that focal point, that center, open again, it’s just going to be very emotional,” she said.

Kim Bhasin is a business reporter covering the retail industry for The Times.

Shawn Hubler is The Times’s Los Angeles bureau chief, reporting on the news, trends and personalities of Southern California.

The Parking Sticker of Shame Is Back in New York City

The New York Times August 04, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

After 14 years, the city has returned to slapping bright stickers on cars that do not move for street sweepers.

By Emma G. Fitzsimmons

Seven minutes after street sweeping began on the Upper West Side of Manhattan on Tuesday morning, sanitation workers and the local city councilwoman hit the streets to deliver justice.

“Move your car!” the councilwoman, Gale Brewer, shouted as she slapped a large neon-green, shield-shaped sticker on a Jeep Grand Cherokee.

Nearby, a driver got in his parked car and peeled away to avoid being next.

The stickers, which shame New Yorkers for failing to make way for street sweepers, are back after a 14-year hiatus. Coupled with a $65 ticket, they are designed to serve as a public slap on the wrist.

The stickers were used for 25 years before the City Council banned them in 2012. Ms. Brewer sponsored a bill this year to bring them back.

The new sticker carries the rebuke: “This vehicle violated N. Y. C. street cleaning rules. As a result, this street could not be properly cleaned.”

Then, in smaller print: “Remove this sticker with warm water and a scraper.”

The tree-lined stretch of West 90th Street near Columbus Avenue where the sticker campaign began is known for poor compliance with the city’s alternate-side parking rules, sanitation officials said. Drivers who park on the street are required to move their cars twice a week, on Tuesday and Friday, from 8:30 a. m. to 10 a. m.

Many New Yorkers ignore the rules, accepting the tickets as a cheaper alternative to paying for a garage. Others deeply resent having to stay home and sit in a double-parked car as they wait for the sweeper to go by.

Mary O’Reilly, who lives on the block and diligently moved her car on Tuesday, said she thought the stickers could change behavior.

“It is frustrating when you come out to move your car and others haven’t,” she said. “Then you’re navigating around them, as well as trying to get out of the way of the sanitation truck.”

Ms. O’Reilly said there was “incessant horn honking” on street-sweeping days and that she would welcome a reprieve. Moments later, a driver started leaning on a horn.

Mayor Zohran Mamdani expressed support for the enforcement effort at an unrelated news conference on Tuesday.

“It’s critically important that the Sanitation Department be able to conduct street cleaning,” he said.

The old, much-hated stickers were notorious for leaving behind adhesive on windows. David G. Greenfield, a former councilman who sponsored the bill to get rid of the stickers, said on Tuesday that they had damaged cars.

“A ticket is a penalty,” he wrote on social media. “Gluing trash to someone’s windshield is vandalism.”

The sanitation commissioner, Gregory Anderson, said that the effort was not meant to be punitive.

“The goal is not to put stickers on cars — the goal is to clean the street,” he said.

Mr. Anderson said the city was also starting a pilot program in the Prospect Heights neighborhood of Brooklyn to reduce the number of weekly street-cleaning days from two to one in the hope that drivers actually move that day.

“We’re using the carrot and the stick approach,” he said. “The sticker, unfortunately, is the stick. Reducing frequency is the carrot. We’ll see what works.”

Ms. Brewer, a neighborhood fixture who also took on illegal cannabis stores, said that something had to change.

“People in the neighborhood are livid,” she said. “The streets are filthy. It is really depressing to see the sweeper go down the middle of the street because every single space has a car in it.”

New York City used to slap giant neon stickers on cars that didn't move for street sweeping to shame drivers into complying. The City Council did away with the practice in 2012, and now it's back. I went out with sanitation workers this morning as they made their first rounds with the new stickers. I'm curious to see if the stickers will change behavior. It's annoying to stay home and move your car once or twice a week, and some New Yorkers have decided they'd rather just pay the $65 ticket.

Emma G. Fitzsimmons is a public policy correspondent for The Times, covering New York City.

An Angry Trump Struggles to Understand Iran’s Defiant Leaders

The New York Times August 04, 2026

War in the Middle East

Advertisement

Supported by

News Analysis

Iran’s leaders have perplexed several American presidents, perhaps none more than President Trump.

By Michael Crowley

Michael Crowley covers the State Department and U. S. foreign policy. He has reported from nearly three dozen countries.

President Trump’s angry claim on Monday that Iran was being “unbelievably duplicitous” in its dealings with the United States was just the latest sign of his struggle to understand his rivals in Tehran.

Mr. Trump considers himself a master of sizing up and exploiting his adversaries. But Iran’s leaders have baffled him.

“All they do is make me angry,” he told reporters last week. “They just make me angry.”

More frustration could be in store for the American president. Trump officials say a new deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz may be near, but Iran continues to insist on collecting fees there that Mr. Trump has ruled unacceptable.

Mr. Trump’s inability to strike a favorable deal with Iran has not only cost him politically among war-weary voters, but continued strife around the crucial waterway has made for volatile oil prices at the expense of American consumers and the global economy.

Mr. Trump is hardly the first U. S. president who has struggled to read Iran. Each of his predecessors since the country’s 1979 Islamic Revolution has tried to decode Iran’s murky power structure and the mind-set of its political leadership.

Most have come up short; some have been burned badly. A rare exception is President Barack Obama, whose 2015 nuclear deal with Iran was a 20-month diplomatic effort. Mr. Obama considered it a major achievement, despite criticism from Republicans and some Democrats that Iran had lured him into a flawed deal by feigning moderation.

But Mr. Trump may be the president who “has least understood Iran’s leadership,” said Kenneth Pollack, a former C. I. A. analyst and National Security Council official who has studied Iran for decades.

“In many ways, Trump represents the epitome of America’s frustrations with Iran,” Mr. Pollack said. “He has been both the most desirous of making a deal with Iran, and the one who used the most force against it. He has found that neither got him what he wanted.”

Mr. Trump often speaks as though massive force will produce a quick deal.

After the war opened with a Feb. 28 airstrike that killed Iran’s supreme leader of nearly 40 years, Ali Khamenei, Mr. Trump called on Iran’s people to rise up and “take over” their government. He added that he would then “choose” Iran’s next leader.

More senior Iranian officials would also be killed in airstrikes. But no popular uprising emerged.

Iran’s hard-line government instead doubled down. In March, it named a new supreme leader, Mr. Khamenei’s son, Mojtaba Khamenei. U. S. officials consider him even more rigid — and more interested in acquiring a nuclear bomb — than his father.

Iran had simply ignored Mr. Trump’s public declaration that the younger Mr. Khamenei would be an “unacceptable” choice. And Mr. Khamenei did not respond to a public offer from Mr. Trump for an in-person meeting.

Even so, Mr. Trump retained hope for major change. “Iran can get themselves on a very good footing if they make a deal,” he said in late April. Iran, he said, could become “a legitimate country, not a country based on death and horror.”

Iranian officials say they can negotiate with Mr. Trump on matters such as the Strait of Hormuz and their nuclear program, even as they rule out many of his core demands.

But in a political system premised on hatred of the United States, none show interest in a larger reconciliation with the United States.

There are few signs that Mr. Trump’s months of dealing with Iran’s regime have given him a clearer understanding of it. Over the course of the conflict, Mr. Trump has constantly revised his assessment of Mr. Khamenei and his deputies. He has branded them “lunatics,” “reasonable,” “crazy bastards,” “very smart” and “stone cold crazy.”

Mr. Trump is to some degree experiencing frustrations that have bedeviled several of his predecessors who also hoped for grand bargains with Iran.

“For decades, American policymakers have consistently underappreciated the ideological commitment and deeply institutionalized structure of power in the Islamic Republic,” said Suzanne Maloney, vice president and director for foreign policy at the Brookings Institution in Washington.

One problem, Maloney noted, is how little direct exposure U. S. officials have had to top Iranian leaders. No U. S. official ever met Iran’s first supreme leader, Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, or the late Mr. Khamenei, nor his son.

Ms. Maloney said that war appears to have strengthened the power of Iran’s religious and military leadership, leaving no “viable alternative power center.”

Iran’s semi-democratic political system, which features a president and parliament under the total religious authority of its supreme leader, has at times included high-level officials open to friendlier relations with the United States.

But past appeals by Washington to those figures have mostly ended in regret.

Dennis Ross, a veteran of Middle East diplomacy who served presidents of both parties, said that “the Iranians seem to understand us better than we understand them.”

In 1980, President Jimmy Carter approved secret talks with Iran’s foreign minister in an effort to free the 52 American hostages seized from the U. S. Embassy in Tehran the year before.

Mr. Carter’s diary entries show him obsessing, much like Mr. Trump, on details of Iran’s political machinations — including feuds among top Iranian officials.

In early 1980 Mr. Carter thought he had struck a deal to free the hostages in return for the release of billions in frozen Iranian assets and a pledge of American noninterference in Iranian affairs, among other things.

But in what Mr. Carter called “a bitter disappointment,” Mr. Khomeini shot down the idea, blindsiding American officials and his own subordinates. Mr. Carter would eventually order a hostage rescue mission that failed before finalizing a deal that freed the Americans on his last day in office.

Five years later, President Ronald Reagan directed aides to explore a message from an Iranian arms dealer who claimed that moderate Iranian officials would be open to establishing friendly ties once the aging Mr. Khomeini had died.

In what Mr. Reagan later called a search for “a strategic opening,” he approved the secret sale of U. S. weapons to Iran in exchange for the release of American hostages held in Lebanon. The arrangement became part of what is known as the Iran-contra affair because money from the arms sales was covertly diverted, in defiance of Congress, to an anti-communist rebel group in Nicaragua known as the contras.

The affair’s exposure engulfed Mr. Reagan’s presidency in scandal, as several U. S. officials pleaded guilty or were convicted of felonies; Mr. Reagan’s former national security adviser attempted suicide.

The opening with Iran turned out to be a mirage. No friendly moderates emerged in Tehran, and the C. I. A. believed the arms dealer who began it all was a fraud. Mr. Reagan, denying knowledge of key events, apologized in a national address, while defending his original goal of courting Iranian moderates.

A more tangible opportunity emerged for President Bill Clinton in 1997, when Iran elected a reformist candidate, Mohammad Khatami, as its president. Mr. Khatami called for good relations with the United States, and even expressed regret for the embassy hostage crisis.

This was the real thing.

Mr. Clinton reciprocated with gestures such as the restoration of U. S. imports of Iranian pistachios and carpets, and conciliatory remarks acknowledging some of Iran’s historical grievances.

Secretary of State Madeleine Albright even issued a public apology for the C. I. A.’s backing of a 1953 coup that overthrew Iran’s prime minister after he nationalized the country’s Western-dominated oil industry.

But powerful hard-liners opposed Mr. Khatami’s moderate vision, in part because reconciliation with the United States threatened the foundations of their anti-Western ideology.

Days after Ms. Albright’s speech, the elder Mr. Khamenei, who became supreme leader after Mr. Khomeini’s death in 1989, dismissed her words — and any possibility of dialogue with Washington.

Mr. Khatami later said privately that Mr. Khamenei believed that Iran could never make peace with the United States, according to Karim Sadjadpour, an Iran expert at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.

Only Mr. Obama has pulled off a major diplomatic agreement with Iran, in the form of the 2015 nuclear deal that placed limits on Iran’s atomic program lasting up to 15 years in exchange for relief from economic sanctions.

Many officials in the Obama administration hoped that agreement, negotiated with another moderate Iranian leader, Hassan Rouhani, might be a first step toward better relations. But that was not to be. Mr. Khamenei approved the deal, but showed no desire for taking things further; critics said that confirmed their warnings that Mr. Rouhani would amount to a replay of Mr. Khatami.

Iranian suspicions that the U. S. could not be trusted were soon affirmed. In 2018, Mr. Trump withdrew from the nuclear deal and imposed even harsher economic sanctions than had been in place before the agreement.

Iran responded by accelerating its nuclear program, putting it on course for a violent collision with the United States and the war Mr. Trump initiated in February.

Since then, Mr. Ross said, Iran has continued to outmaneuver Washington, which Mr. Trump’s obvious impatience to conclude the war has made easier.

“They tend to read our sense of urgency as a form of leverage,” Mr. Ross said. “We always seem in a hurry to get things done. They operate under the premise that time serves their interests more than ours.”

Michael Crowley covers the State Department and U. S. foreign policy for The Times. He has reported from nearly three dozen countries and often travels with the secretary of state.

Workers Disassemble Parts of Trump’s White House Helipad, Photos Show

The New York Times August 04, 2026

Trump Remakes Washington

Advertisement

Supported by

Last week, construction workers had begun to decorate the new South Lawn helipad with a giant presidential seal. By Tuesday, the design was gone.

By David A. Fahrenthold

President Trump has been building a huge new helipad at the White House. But on Tuesday, workers seemed to be reversing course on the project.

As of last week, the helipad appeared to be nearing completion. After starting work in June, workers had built a circle 100 feet in diameter in the middle of the green expanse of the South Lawn. They were starting to add the finishing touches in granite, laying out the lettering of the presidential seal along the edge of the pad.

But then, on Sunday, photos showed that some of the lettering had been removed. Where it had said “Seal of the President of the United States,” only “eal of the” was left in place. By Tuesday, photos of the helipad showed all the granite letters were gone: It was back to what appeared to be bare concrete.

The Washington Post reported on Tuesday that Mr. Trump had ordered contractors to redo weeks of work on the project, unhappy that the helipad — like the South Lawn it sits on — had a noticeable slope.

A White House spokesman, Davis Ingle, declined on Tuesday to say why the helipad’s lettering had been removed, or what would be changed about the project.

Mr. Trump has said he needs a helipad on the South Lawn to accommodate a new kind of helicopter now used to transport him, under the call sign Marine One. The new helicopters, made by Sikorsky, produce engine exhaust so hot that it can scorch the grass.

“For years, the White House has desperately needed a proper Helipad on White House grounds that will allow the President to land safely and also protect the beautiful South Lawn grass from the fierce exhaust fumes of the incredible Marine One,” Mr. Ingle said in a statement.

Lockheed Martin, which owns Sikorsky, has said it is paying to build the helipad as a donation. Mr. Trump said it would cost between $5 million and $6 million.

The change would alter the character of the South Lawn, which has been used for social gatherings and White House events. Mr. Trump did not seek permission to build the helipad from Congress or from the architectural review panels that often vet projects in Washington’s monumental core. The White House has said that “operational upgrades” like this one do not need outside review.

David A. Fahrenthold is a Times investigative reporter writing about nonprofit organizations. He has been a reporter for two decades.

Talks With Iran to Reopen Strait of Hormuz Make Progress, Officials Say

The New York Times August 04, 2026

War in the Middle East

Advertisement

Supported by

Qatar said that draft language of a deal was being circulated, while Secretary of State Marco Rubio expressed optimism about the talks but added that nothing was final yet.

By Aaron Boxerman and Ismaeel Naar

Negotiations to reopen the Strait of Hormuz are making progress, American and Qatari officials said Tuesday, but a deal with Iran has yet to be announced that could pave the way to reviving a broader cease-fire with the United States.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there had been “progress in talks, but not finality yet.” Iran blockaded the Strait of Hormuz — a critical conduit for global oil and gas shipping — after the U. S.-Israeli assault began in late February, causing widespread economic shock.

Iran and neighboring Oman, which also abuts the Persian Gulf waterway, were holding the talks with U. S. input, Mr. Rubio said. The two countries were discussing an immediate solution to the crisis in the strait ahead of a longer-term goal of curbing Iran’s nuclear program, he said.

In Qatar, which has previously acted as a mediator between Iran and the United States, officials expressed a similar measure of optimism. Majed al-Ansari, the Qatari foreign ministry spokesman, told reporters that the negotiations on the strait were in “very progressive stages” as draft language of a possible agreement had been “circulated among the parties.”

Iran’s blockade over the Strait of Hormuz throttled global energy markets and raised pressure on President Trump to end the war. Now, Iran hopes to cement its control over the critical waterway, which has served as a major source of leverage in its dealings with the United States.

U. S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a televised interview on Tuesday that he believed an agreement could be imminent. “We are in talks with the Iranians, and I think there is a chance we may have a deal today or tomorrow,” Mr. Bessent said on CNBC.

The price of Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, fell more than 2 percent to about $82 a barrel on Tuesday, as markets appeared to respond to optimism about a potential deal. But repeated pledges of diplomatic progress between the United States and Iran have failed to materialize, with the war now in its sixth month.

The Trump administration had hoped that the short-lived cease-fire, agreed on in June, would reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Instead, it collapsed into renewed fighting, as Iran has sought to impose its authority there.

Iran has enforced its claim by attacking commercial ships as they have tried to transit the strait. That has prompted American bombing runs inside Iran, as well as a U. S. blockade of Iranian ports — neither of which has successfully forced Iran’s leadership to back down.

On Monday, a cargo ship, the Greek-owned Minoan Pioneer, was hit near Oman and one of its crew members was missing, according to the International Maritime Organization. It was unclear who struck the vessel.

Mediators hope that restoring the flow of ships through the Strait of Hormuz will end the current cycle of attacks and counterattacks between the United States and Iran and allow the two countries to return to the June cease-fire agreement. That was supposed to pave the way for talks on the Iranian nuclear program and sanctions relief for Iran’s battered economy.

Over the weekend, Mr. Trump threatened an immense military escalation against Iran before abruptly pulling back, citing pleas for calm from regional allies.

“Our focus right now is on avoiding escalation, reopening the strait and reopening the door for diplomacy between the parties,” said Mr. al-Ansari, the Qatari official. “What we do not want to see right now is a major escalation in our region.”

An arrangement with Iran to reopen the strait could come with a geopolitical cost for the United States. Iranian officials say they are designing the accord to affirm their capacity to control the strait and retain strategic leverage they did not exercise before the war.

Officials familiar with the emerging proposal have said that under the new framework, vessels entering the Persian Gulf would have to transit a channel controlled by Iran, while outbound ships would travel through a channel near Oman.

In recent weeks, the fighting has spread to another vital maritime corridor in the Middle East: the Red Sea. The Houthis, an Iran-backed group that rules much of northwestern Yemen, have vowed to enforce a naval blockade on U. S.-allied Saudi Arabia.

Clashes between the two sides rapidly escalated last month for the first time in years, as Saudi-backed forces bombarded Houthi sites and the Houthis said they had fired at oil and gas facilities in Saudi Arabia.

On Tuesday, the Indian government said a projectile had sunk an Indian-flagged commercial vessel off the Yemeni coast. All 13 Indian nationals on board were rescued, the Indian foreign ministry said. The Houthis did not immediately comment.

Reporting was contributed by Peter Eavis, David E. Sanger, Farnaz Fassihi and Eric Schmitt.

Aaron Boxerman is a Times reporter covering Israel and Gaza. He is based in Jerusalem.

Ismaeel Naar is an international reporter for The Times, covering the Gulf states. He is based in Dubai, United Arab Emirates.

How Well Is the Progressive Left Actually Doing?

The New York Times August 04, 2026

Advertisement

Newsletter

Its wins have been largely confined to highly educated and heavily Democratic parts of urban America. But two races could change that.

By Nate Cohn and C. J. Robinson

After racking up a series of high-profile wins this summer, the left looks ascendant in blue America.

In open Democratic congressional primaries this year, candidates endorsed by progressive-left groups like Our Revolution, Justice Democrats and the Democratic Socialists of America have won nearly one-third of contests in places where Kamala Harris won at least two-thirds of the presidential vote in 2024.

For all of those impressive victories, there’s still one big asterisk on the activist left’s success this primary season: Its wins have been largely confined to the most highly educated and heavily Democratic parts of urban America, the places where Ms. Harris did the best.

Note: “Other progressive left” indicates candidates endorsed by Our Revolution, but not by the Democratic Socialists of America or Justice Democrats. Open races include those without a Democratic incumbent and where Trump won by at most 15 points in 2024.

Based on the same endorsements, the left has almost entirely failed to break through in battleground or red districts. Where it has broken through, it’s often with candidates who are white, male, blue-collar populists in the mold of Graham Platner (before his race exit) and John Fetterman (2022 edition) — not with the young democratic socialists who seem unstoppable in New York City or who surged in Colorado.

As long as the progressive left doesn’t win outside of heavily Democratic areas, it won’t be more than a large and vocal faction in the Democratic House caucus. The red states and battlegrounds may not embody the Democratic base, but they usually decide control of Congress and the party’s presidential nomination.

That’s what makes the Democratic primaries in Michigan (Tuesday) and Wisconsin (Aug. 11) significant tests of the rise of the left. The polls show wide leads for Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan’s Senate primary and Francesca Hong in the Wisconsin governor’s primary. If they prevail, it will deal a blow to whatever remains of the assumption that candidates of the progressive left can’t compete nationwide in 2028.

Of course, it’s always a mistake to read too much into one or two idiosyncratic primary elections. Both Dr. El-Sayed and Ms. Hong have benefited from favorable matchups. In Michigan, the Democratic establishment has put forward a staunchly pro-Israel candidate (Haley Stevens) in a state where progressive activists are especially mobilized against Israel’s conduct in Gaza. In Wisconsin, the Democratic establishment has struggled to put forward a candidate at all.

But in the past, candidates of the progressive left like Ms. Hong, a democratic socialist, or Dr. El-Sayed, who doesn’t call himself a democratic socialist but seems indistinguishable from his vocal democratic socialist allies, have found it almost impossible to win primaries in battleground states, even under favorable circumstances. Now they’re positioned to win, and candidates like them could find favorable matchups in the future — even in the next presidential primary.

The progressive left has had its best primary season in memory, including high-profile victories against well-established Democratic incumbents. But it’s not clear whether the left is anywhere near as strong as its flashiest wins can make it seem.

Most obviously, mainstream Democrats have won most Democratic primaries so far this year. That’s partly because most incumbents are mainstream Democrats (and incumbents almost always win), but it’s not just about incumbency. Mainstream Democrats have also tended to prevail in races without a Democratic incumbent — both in Republican-held seats and in the districts where Democratic incumbents are retiring.

Another issue is that it’s challenging to define whether someone actually is a candidate of the progressive left. Everyone can agree that the self-identified democratic socialists, like Zohran Mamdani and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, are at the core of this new left, but it’s not limited to the people who adopt that label. Dr. El-Sayed, for instance, does not identify as a democratic socialist, even though he has few policy differences with Ms. Ocasio-Cortez or Bernie Sanders.

At the same time, simply identifying as “progressive” doesn’t automatically put you in this group. Progressives have been winning for years. Many of the progressive left’s big victories over Democratic incumbents this cycle have come against other self-identified “progressive” members of the Congressional Progressive Caucus who support Medicare for all. What’s different this cycle is the success of a new kind of young, populist, activist-backed progressive who’s either a democratic socialist or indistinguishable from one on the issues.

One of the better ways to judge whether someone is ideologically aligned with the activist left is to use endorsements from progressive-left groups and individuals, like Mr. Sanders’s Our Revolution, the Democratic Socialists of America, Ms. Ocasio-Cortez herself and Justice Democrats (basically the so-called Squad and a handful of their colleagues in Congress). This measure isn’t perfect, either. Not every candidate with progressive-left views earns such an endorsement, and progressive-left groups will sometimes choose to endorse a relatively moderate candidate in a moderate district. It’s a rough proxy at best.

But by this measure, the progressive left has won less than 20 percent of primary races in open districts where Democrats are either strongly favored to win or are expected to be competitive in November. Among these races, progressives have done quite well in solidly blue districts but struggled to win at all in the battlegrounds.

Only three candidates backed by the progressive left have prevailed in the battlegrounds, based on endorsements, and even they are not necessarily representative of the new activist left that’s shaking up Democratic politics. None identify as democratic socialists. They were each endorsed by only one progressive group: Our Revolution, which routinely endorses the most progressive candidate in a race, even if that person is not necessarily part of the activist-backed progressive left. The Texas Senate candidate James Talarico, for instance, was endorsed by Our Revolution. In more heavily Republican districts, two more progressives prevailed in Democratic primaries; they tend to be blue-collar populists in the mold of a Mr. Platner or Mr. Fetterman.

Of the progressive groups that make endorsements, only Justice Democrats and the Democratic Socialists of America appear to award endorsements exclusively to this narrower kind of activist-backed candidate. By this narrower definition, no progressive left candidate has won in a battleground district or state so far this cycle.

Just as strikingly, there are many races without any progressive-left-endorsed candidate at all. This could be interpreted as a sign of even more profound weakness for the activist left, which might be so concentrated in urban areas that it can’t recruit and elevate candidates elsewhere. Alternately, it could suggest that progressives have focused on building strength in more solidly Democratic districts, which would leave open the possibility that the left could fare relatively well in the battlegrounds if and when it wages a viable campaign.

Against that backdrop, victories for Dr. El-Sayed and Ms. Hong would be a significant breakthrough. It wouldn’t be completely without precedent; Mr. Sanders won Michigan and Wisconsin in the 2016 primaries. But since then, the progressive left — including Mr. Sanders himself in 2020 — has failed to match that support among white working-class Democrats.

If Dr. El-Sayed and Ms. Hong win, it doesn’t prove that democratic socialists are now ascendant in battleground America and sure to win the 2028 presidential nomination. It’s still just two races. But it does show that the new, activist-backed progressive left can win outside of the most Democratic districts, at least under favorable circumstances. That’s not something they’ve shown before.

Nate Cohn is The Times’s chief political analyst. He covers elections, public opinion, demographics and polling.

C. J. Robinson is a reporting fellow at The Upshot and a member of the 2026-27 Times Fellowship, a program for journalists early in their careers.

Ronald Lauder, a Billionaire G. O. P. Backer, Closes His Wallet

The New York Times August 04, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Times Exclusive

Ronald S. Lauder, a major funder of conservative political causes, has not given a single dollar this year to Republicans in his home state, and his super PAC has gone idle.

By Nicholas Fandos

For decades, Ronald S. Lauder, the billionaire cosmetics heir and philanthropist, has been something like a one-man bank for Republicans in New York.

He personally funded a campaign to impose term limits in New York City, helped pay for a lawsuit to overturn the state’s gerrymandered congressional map and, just four years ago, plowed close to $13 million into races that helped Republicans flip the House.

Now, in the middle of another crucial midterm election year, Mr. Lauder, 82, appears to have abruptly closed his political checkbook, and the ramifications for the conservative movement he has nurtured in his home state could be significant.

He has yet to make a single donation to Republicans in his home state this year, according to campaign finance records. The super PAC he long maintained to advance Republican candidates and causes is also sitting idle.

And behind the scenes, Mr. Lauder has quietly dismissed a stable of well-paid advisers, ad makers and other consultants who regularly reported to his personal office in the Estée Lauder headquarters overlooking Central Park in Manhattan. Some had been with Mr. Lauder since 1989 when he ran his own quixotic race for mayor.

His motivation is not entirely clear. Three associates said that Mr. Lauder recently confided in them, saying that his adult children have stepped in to try to reduce his lavish spending on politics, art and philanthropy and suggesting reluctantly that he could not spend what he once did. The associates pointed to public securities filings showing that his stake in the family business, Estée Lauder, has lost at least $1.2 billion in value as the stock plummeted 77 percent from its 2021 high.

A person close to the Lauder family did not dispute that Mr. Lauder’s political spending was being curtailed, but said it was not because of a financial pinch.

Rather, the person said that he and his adult children had agreed that he would simplify the reach of his activities — involving extensive travel, large paid staff and public speeches — as he prepared for the last years of his life in order to prioritize art and philanthropic projects that could secure his legacy.

The New York Times pieced together this account of one of New York City’s most publicly engaged donors and philanthropists by examining public campaign finance records and corporate disclosures by Estée Lauder, and interviewing more than a dozen of his associates. Most insisted on anonymity to avoid crossing him.

Mr. Lauder himself did not respond to a detailed list of questions from The Times about his financial position or decision making.

In a written statement, he said that he had used political giving and philanthropy over the years to “strengthen” the city, adding, “I intend to continue dedicating my time, resources and energy to advancing those democratic principles and to ensuring that New York remains a place where people, families, businesses and communities can thrive.”

Some Republicans are holding out hope that Mr. Lauder might still involve himself in this year’s races. But Gerard Kassar, the chairman of the New York Conservative Party, said he had been advised by Allen Roth, a longtime Lauder lieutenant who recently left, that the billionaire “got to a certain age that his family and him all decided he wasn’t going to be as active the way he has been.”

Mr. Kassar said he did not know anything about Mr. Lauder’s personal finances, but was led to believe he would no longer be a major funder.

“Can anyone replace him in New York financially?” Mr. Kassar said. “The simple answer is no.”

Edward F. Cox, Mr. Kassar’s counterpart at the state Republican Party and a longtime friend of the Lauder family, declined to comment.

There is little doubt that Mr. Lauder is still enormously wealthy. He owns one of the world’s most respected private art collections, a Gulfstream with custom Hermès interiors and compounds in Palm Beach and the Hamptons. Forbes estimates that he and both of his adult daughters are worth billions of dollars.

There are signs that Mr. Lauder is taking other significant actions that could reverberate far beyond the political world. Many of the maneuvers, including giving up his Estée Lauder board seat, are consistent with the kind of estate planning typical of a wealthy person of his age.

But some of the moves he initiated over the past few years have also either generated substantial cash or offloaded tens of millions of dollars in future obligations at a time when the family business had taken a sharp downward turn.

In the most high-profile case, Mr. Lauder announced in May that his beloved Neue Galerie, the Upper East Side museum he founded to showcase the culture of prewar Austria and Germany, would be merging with the Metropolitan Museum of Art.

Both sides framed the blockbuster merger as a way to preserve the museum well beyond Mr. Lauder’s lifetime and strengthen the Met’s collection. But it would also be likely to save Mr. Lauder millions of dollars a year that he contributes to covering its operating expenses, according to the organization’s financial disclosures.

Mr. Lauder also recently announced that he would leave the presidency of the World Jewish Congress, an international federation of Jewish groups, where he has been the major funder and leader for two decades.

At the same time, Mr. Lauder, who began collecting as a teenager — real estate, planes and, most of all, art — has quietly been selling at a notable clip.

In late 2023, as the Estée Lauder stock slide accelerated, he sold a Philip Johnson-designed home in Manhattan for $20 million in an off-market deal. In late 2024, he sold 30 acres of land to the Town of East Hampton’s preservation fund for $56 million, and put his collection of World War II fighter planes on the market, according to an aviation enthusiasts’ website.

Mr. Lauder’s retrenchment has played out at a time of significant change for his storied family. His older brother, the businessman and philanthropist Leonard A. Lauder, died last year. His son-in-law, Kevin M. Warsh, was recently nominated to the chairmanship of the Federal Reserve by President Trump, a longtime friend of Ronald Lauder.

While Leonard Lauder spent his career leading the family business, Ronald Lauder carved out a path as an independent investor, philanthropist, art collector and political player, serving as a U. S. ambassador under Ronald Reagan.

Those pursuits were expensive, and in addition to outright selling his stock, Mr. Lauder long made a practice of using shares in the family business as collateral for bank loans and other financial transactions to help fund it all. (Estée Lauder’s most recent annual federal securities filing disclosed that he had pledged nearly all his remaining shares to a bank.)

The maneuver is popular among people who derive their wealth from stocks as a way to generate cash from their holdings without selling them and paying taxes. It would have had little downside when the company’s stock was going up in value. Estée Lauder shares peaked, at the end of 2021, at around $370 a share.

But there can be risks if the stock used as collateral loses considerable value. If the assets’ values fall far enough, a lender may ask the borrower to repay part of the loan or pledge more assets to maintain it.

The terms of Mr. Lauder’s borrowing are not specified in the Estée Lauder disclosures. As of this week, the stock was trading at around $85 a share.

The person close to the Lauder family conceded that the stock price’s slide could limit Mr. Lauder’s overall capital, but asserted that he did not have a meaningful liquidity problem. (The person declined to share financial records that would substantiate the claim.)

Mr. Lauder’s political giving has been relatively less expensive than his other pursuits. (He once spent $135 million on a single Gustav Klimt painting, which became the centerpiece of the Neue Galerie.) Over the last decade, public records show he has spent more than $40 million on state and federal races.

But in New York, he developed a reputation as a singular donor engaged not just in backing candidates but in embracing causes with outsize impact. In the 1990s, Mr. Lauder bankrolled a campaign that won term limits for public officials in New York City. In the 2010s, he was instrumental in stopping Mayor Bill de Blasio’s push to change the admissions test for city’s specialized public high schools.

As recently as last year, Mr. Lauder was spending aggressively on politics. He gave $5 million to MAGA Inc., a super PAC backed by Mr. Trump, in March 2025. (Mr. Lauder has gotten credit for giving Mr. Trump the idea to buy Greenland.) He donated another $1 million to a super PAC opposed to Zohran Mamdani’s mayoral campaign.

His free-spending ways caused Leonard Lauder to once say to an admirer who had confused him with his brother: “I’m the one who made the money. He is the one who spends the money.”

But the political contributions came to an abrupt stop at the beginning of this year, just as Bruce Blakeman, the Republican nominee for governor in New York, needed his help trying to narrow Gov. Kathy Hochul’s fund-raising advantage.

Mr. Lauder could theoretically decide to restart his giving. His decision to cull his longtime political staff was more lasting, and one that he indicated to associates he was not eager to make.

While it is difficult to independently determine the full cost of his personal office, Estée Lauder securities filings give some hints.

Mr. Lauder long had an arrangement with the company to house his personal office in the company’s Midtown headquarters. As part of the deal, Estée Lauder would provide some services, like payroll and phone systems, and Mr. Lauder would reimburse. The cost during the 2025 fiscal year, the filings show, was nearly $22 million.

As Mr. Lauder was cutting staff this spring, his chief financial officer sent an email that made it clear that the billionaire was facing new constraints even in his own office.

“Please note that if you are asked by Mr. Lauder or anyone else on his behalf to perform future work you must get my prior written approval,” the chief financial officer, Joseph F. Tuite Jr., wrote in the email, reviewed by The Times. “Should you perform services without this written approval, you will not be paid.”

Zachary Small contributed reporting.

Nicholas Fandos is a Times reporter covering New York politics and government.
